pages.title: Prophet Abraham and Tawhid
pages.content: In the Holy Qur’an, Prophet Abraham (pbuh) is presented as the messenger and representative of the monotheistic belief. Monotheistic belief means bearing witness that there is no god but Allah. He has no partner, rival, or helper. Allah is unique in every way. Abraham (pbuh) is also a fundamental figure in the three great monotheistic religions (Judaism, Christianity, and Islam). The fourteenth surah of the Qur’an is named Surah Ibrahim. Abraham (pbuh) is the father of two prophets: Prophet Ishmael (pbuh) and Prophet Isaac (pbuh). Prophet Ishmael (pbuh) is the direct forefather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh). Prophet Isaac (pbuh) is the father of Prophet Jacob (pbuh). Prophet Jacob is the father of Joseph (pbuh) and an ancestor of Moses (pbuh), Aaron (pbuh), Jonah (pbuh), and Jesus (pbuh). Abraham (pbuh) was also given the unique name of “Allah’s friend” (Khalilullah; see Surah an-Nisa: 125). This title was not given to any other prophet before. The Qur’an presents in detail his discovery of the oneness of Allah (Tawhid) in the middle of an idol-worshipping nation.

Believing that there is only one God.
Someone or something that competes with another for the same position.
A person from an earlier generation of your family; an ancestor.
Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else.
The Islamic belief that Allah is one and has no partner.
Worshipping statues or objects as gods.
Being one and only one.

exercises.title: One Family, Many Prophets
exercises.instructions: Match each prophet with what Chapter 1 says about him.
exercises.question: How does Chapter 1 connect Abraham’s sons and grandson with later prophets?

matchingPairs.right: the direct forefather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
the father of Prophet Jacob (pbuh)
the father of Joseph and an ancestor of Moses and Jesus (pbuh)

correctAnswer.Ishmael: the direct forefather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)

exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “Prophet Ishmael (pbuh) is the direct forefather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh). Prophet Isaac (pbuh) is the father of Prophet Jacob (pbuh).” Jacob is then named as “the father of Joseph” and an ancestor of Moses, Aaron, Jonah and Jesus. This is why Abraham is a central figure in all three monotheistic religions.

feedback.correct: Well done. Through Ishmael and Isaac, Abraham’s family line reaches Muhammad, Moses and Jesus (pbuh).
feedback.incorrect: Look at the middle of Chapter 1, where the writer moves from Abraham to his two sons and then to Jacob. Follow the family line one step at a time.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Is Presenting Whom?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the first sentence of Chapter 1. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “In the Holy Qur’an, Prophet Abraham (pbuh) is presented as the messenger and representative of the monotheistic belief.” Why does the writer say “is presented as”?
options: It shows that the description comes from a source, the Qur’an, so the writer is reporting how that source portrays Abraham.
It shows that the writer is not sure the description is true, so the reader should treat it as a weak and doubtful claim.
It shows that Abraham described himself in this way when he spoke to his people in Babylon.
It shows that the description was true only in the past and is no longer accepted today.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Be presented as / be described as” frames a statement: It tells the reader where a description comes from. Here the frame “In the Holy Qur’an … is presented as” makes the Qur’an the source of the portrait. A frame like this does not express doubt; it shows the reader whose presentation is being reported. The chapter returns to the Qur’an as a source in its last sentence.

feedback.correct: Correct. The frame names the source of the description; it does not weaken it.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the words before the verb: “In the Holy Qur’an”. Whose presentation of Abraham is the writer reporting?

languageFocusExercises.title: Define, Add, Expand
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 1 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words explain an idea, add a role and give more detail?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: Monotheistic belief [blank] bearing witness that there is no god but Allah. … Abraham (pbuh) is [blank] a fundamental figure in the three great monotheistic religions (Judaism, Christianity, and Islam). … The Qur’an presents [blank] his discovery of the oneness of Allah (Tawhid) in the middle of an idol-worshipping nation.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “X means + -ing form” unpacks an abstract term into an action. (“Means that” needs a full clause with its own subject, not an -ing form.) “Also” adds a second role to the earlier description without replacing it; “instead” would cancel the first role. “Presents in detail” tells the reader that the Qur’an gives a fuller account, not just a short mention.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the expressions that define, add and expand.
feedback.incorrect: Check what follows each gap: An -ing form (bearing witness …), an extra role, and a whole account. Then compare with the first paragraph of Chapter 1.

languageFocusExercises.title: Same Fact, New Focus
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence. Start with the words given and keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can the sentence start with the person or with the thing given?

transformItems.source: This title was not given to any other prophet before.
transformItems.frame: No other prophet [blank] this title before.

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) was also given the unique name of “Allah’s friend” …
transformItems.frame: The unique name of “Allah’s friend” [blank] to Abraham (pbuh).

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Give has two objects (give someone something), so its passive can start with the person (“No other prophet had been given this title”) or with the thing (“The unique name … was given to Abraham”). The giver is left out because the reader already knows it, and the focus stays on the title and how unique it is. When the thing comes first, use “to” before the person.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved the focus while keeping the passive and the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Keep a form of be + given. If the thing comes first, add “to” before the person. Check the sentences about “Allah’s friend” near the end of Chapter 1.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Framed B2 Explanation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 7–9 sentences about a famous person or an important idea.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can you explain a person or an idea clearly?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should not merely include the target expressions. It should use each one for a clear discourse purpose: Framing a source, unpacking meaning, adding a related point and foregrounding selected information.

feedback.correct: Check that every target expression has a real discourse function and that the paragraph develops in a clear sequence.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Name the source: “In …, … is presented as …”
discussionPrompts.example: In many science books, Marie Curie is presented as a pioneer of research on radioactivity. The words “is presented as” show that the description comes from these books.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Explain one idea: “… means that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The abstract idea is radioactivity. Radioactivity means that some atoms give off energy on their own.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Put the prize or title first: “She was awarded …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her two Nobel Prizes matter more than the committee that gave them. So I will write: “She was awarded the Nobel Prize twice.”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Check: Does each sentence name a source, explain, or add with “also”?
discussionPrompts.example: Yes. One sentence frames the source, one defines the idea, and the “also” sentence adds her work as a teacher. The passive sentence keeps the focus on her prizes.

pages.title: Hanifism and the One True Faith
pages.content:
He challenged the idol worship of his time and taught people to believe in Allah alone. His life mission was to spread the message of Tawhid—the belief that Allah is One and He has no partners. During his struggle, he had very difficult tests and he passed the tests with his full trust in Allah.

In the Holy Qur’an, Abraham (pbuh) is often described as a hanif; a hanif is a monotheist who is not a Jew, a Christian, or an idolater (see Surah Al Imran: 67) and is also morally upright. Hanifism is the belief in the oneness of Allah taught by Prophet Abraham (pbuh). We may say that it is the former version of Islam. Human beings are capable of discovering Hanifism; that is, the existence of Allah can be found through reasoning. Actually, all prophets taught this religion. As human conditions and capacities changed over time, some changes in details became necessary. So, the difference between the monotheism taught by Abraham (pbuh) and the Islam taught by Muhammad is only in the acts of worship.

vocabulary.definition: An important task or purpose that someone is given or chooses to follow.
A long, hard effort against difficulties or opposition.
Honest, fair and always behaving in a decent way.
The process of thinking about something in a logical way to reach a conclusion.
The abilities that people have to understand or do things.
To pray to someone or something and show it great love and respect.

hotspots.title: A Life Mission
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) spent his life teaching people to believe in Allah alone, and he passed hard tests with full trust in Him.

hotspots.title: The Hanif Path
hotspots.description: The Qur’an describes Abraham (pbuh) as a hanif: A monotheist who was neither a Jew, a Christian nor an idolater.

exercises.title: One Faith, Changing Details
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 2.
exercises.question: According to the writer, why did some details of the religion change between the time of Abraham and the time of Muhammad (pbuh)?
options: People had forgotten the belief in one God over time.
Human conditions and capacities changed over time.
Reasoning had replaced the teaching of the prophets.
The hanifs had mixed their belief with idolatry.
exercises.explanation: The writer says: “As human conditions and capacities changed over time, some changes in details became necessary.” The core belief stayed the same; the difference is “only in the acts of worship.”

feedback.correct: Right. The writer links the changes in details to changing human conditions and capacities, while the belief in one God stays the same.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last three sentences of Chapter 2. Find the sentence that begins with “As …” and explains why changes “became necessary”.

languageFocusExercises.title: How the Chapter Defines Its Terms
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each term with the definition the chapter gives for it.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does each word mean in Chapter 2?

matchingPairs.right: the belief that Allah is One and He has no partners
a monotheist who is not a Jew, a Christian, or an idolater
the belief in the oneness of Allah taught by Prophet Abraham (pbuh)
the only point where Abraham’s monotheism and the Islam taught by Muhammad differ

correctAnswer.Tawhid: the belief that Allah is One and He has no partners
correctAnswer.a hanif: a monotheist who is not a Jew, a Christian, or an idolater
correctAnswer.Hanifism: the belief in the oneness of Allah taught by Prophet Abraham (pbuh)
correctAnswer.the acts of worship: the only point where Abraham’s monotheism and the Islam taught by Muhammad differ

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter defines its terms in different ways: With a dash (“Tawhid—the belief that …”), with a relative clause (“a monotheist who is not …”), and with a participle phrase (“the belief … taught by Prophet Abraham”). Its last sentence limits the difference with “only”: the difference is “only in the acts of worship”. A hanif is a person; Hanifism is the belief system.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the person (a hanif) from the belief (Hanifism) and read the limiting “only”.
feedback.incorrect: Find each term in Chapter 2 and read what comes straight after it: a dash, “who …”, or “taught by …”. The last sentence of the chapter says where the difference lies.

languageFocusExercises.title: Definition or Interpretation?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Compare the two sentences from Chapter 2. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Hanifism is the belief in the oneness of Allah taught by Prophet Abraham (pbuh).” / “We may say that it is the former version of Islam.” What does “We may say that” add to the second sentence?
options: It presents the claim as the writer’s interpretation, offered with some caution.
It shows that the writer is quoting another scholar’s exact words.
It makes the second claim stronger and more certain than the definition.
It shows that the writer disagrees with the claim.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The first sentence is a direct definition with “is”. “We may say that …” is a stance marker: The modal “may” and the verb “say” show that the writer is offering a way of describing Hanifism, not a simple fact. Careful academic writers use this move for claims that are interpretations.

feedback.correct: Correct. “We may say that” marks a careful interpretation, not a plain definition.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the plain verb “is” in the definition with the modal “may” in the second sentence. Which one is more cautious?

languageFocusExercises.title: Reason, Result and Reformulation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 2 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 2?

transformItems.source: As human conditions and capacities changed over time, some changes in details became necessary.
transformItems.frame: Some changes in details became necessary [blank] human conditions and capacities changed over time.

transformItems.source: Human beings are capable of discovering Hanifism; that is, the existence of Allah can be found through reasoning.
transformItems.frame: … that is, people [blank] the existence of Allah through reasoning.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As” at the start of a sentence often gives a reason, like “because” or “since”; when the cause moves to the end, “because” is the clearest choice. “That is” introduces a reformulation: It says the previous idea again in plainer words. The passive “can be found” focuses on the existence of Allah; the active “people can find” focuses on human ability, which matches “capable of discovering”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the reason and the reformulation clear.
feedback.incorrect: In the first item, “As” gives a reason. In the second, change “can be found” into an active verb with “people” as the subject. Check the second paragraph of Chapter 2.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain Continuity and Change
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a tradition that has changed in some ways over time.
languageFocusExercises.question: What stayed the same, and what changed?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should organize ideas rather than simply insert target phrases. The reader should be able to see what the concept means, which statement is interpretive, why a change occurred, and what conclusion follows.

feedback.correct: Check that the paragraph distinguishes definition from interpretation and that the cause–result chain leads naturally to the final contrast.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Explain a key word: “A … is a … which …”
discussionPrompts.example: The term “marathon” needs a precise definition. A marathon is a race which covers about 42 kilometres.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give a careful opinion: “We may say that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The claim that the modern Olympics continue the ancient Games should be cautious. We may say that they are a new version of an old idea.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give a reason and a result: “Due to …, … . So …”
discussionPrompts.example: Due to faster travel, athletes from every continent can now take part. So the Games changed from a Greek festival into a world event.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Say what stayed and what changed: “The core stayed …; the details changed …”
discussionPrompts.example: Yes. The core stayed the same: Athletes compete in peace and the best win. The details changed: the sports, the countries and the rules for women.

beforeYouRead.quote: Actually, all prophets taught this religion.

pages.title: Hanifism Before Islam
pages.content:
In fact, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are all based on the religion of Abraham (pbuh). At the beginning of Prophet Muhammad’s mission, there was a group in the Hijaz who called themselves hanifs. They stayed away from idolatry and its practices. However, later on, this belief became mixed with idolatry and, like Judaism and Christianity, it was corrupted. One of the last hanifs we can mention is Waraqa ibn Nawfal, the cousin of Muhammad’s wife Khadija. He went to Damascus in search of Hanifism and accepted Christianity, which was the least corrupted religion at that time. When the first revelation (wahy) came to Muhammad (pbuh), Waraqa ibn Nawfal welcomed his prophethood. One day, while he was in the desert, Waraqa saw Bilal al-Habashi lying under the burning sun, punished by his master. At that moment, Bilal was saying, “Ahad, Ahad,” meaning “One, One.” Hearing his words, Waraqa replied, “I swear, O Bilal, One, One.”

As the last faith, Islam includes not only what Allah told Abraham (pbuh), but also what Allah told Noah (pbuh), Moses (pbuh), Jesus (pbuh), and all the other prophets (see Surah al-Baqarah: 285).

__historical_entity__:abraham-hijaz
__historical_entity__:abraham-hanifs
__historical_entity__:abraham-waraqa-ibn-nawfal
The worship of statues, stars or other created things instead of Allah.
Changed from its pure, original form into something false.
A message from Allah given to a prophet.
The position of someone chosen by Allah to carry His message to people.
Accepted something gladly and with approval.

hotspots.title: The Hanifs of the Hijaz
hotspots.description: Before Islam, a group in the Hijaz called themselves hanifs and stayed away from idolatry.

hotspots.title: Bilal’s Cry: “One, One”
hotspots.description: Waraqa ibn Nawfal saw Bilal being punished under the burning sun while he kept repeating “Ahad, Ahad.”

exercises.title: Waraqa’s Search
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 3 in order.
exercises.question: In what order does Chapter 3 tell the story of Waraqa ibn Nawfal?

sequencingItems.text: Waraqa goes to Damascus in search of Hanifism.
Waraqa accepts Christianity, the least corrupted religion at that time.
When the first revelation comes to Muhammad (pbuh), Waraqa welcomes his prophethood.
In the desert, Waraqa hears Bilal saying “One, One” and answers him.

exercises.explanation: Waraqa, “one of the last hanifs”, went to Damascus “in search of Hanifism and accepted Christianity”. When the first revelation came, he “welcomed his prophethood”. Later he saw Bilal punished in the desert and replied, “I swear, O Bilal, One, One.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Waraqa’s search for the pure faith of Abraham ends with him welcoming the Prophet (pbuh) and supporting Bilal’s words.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the middle of Chapter 3: Waraqa’s journey comes first, then his choice of religion, then the first revelation, then the day in the desert.

languageFocusExercises.title: An Evaluation with a Time Limit
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 3. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “He went to Damascus in search of Hanifism and accepted Christianity, which was the least corrupted religion at that time.” What does “at that time” do?
options: It limits the evaluation “the least corrupted” to that period, instead of making it true for all times.
It shows that Christianity became the least corrupted religion only later, after Waraqa’s death.
It shows that Waraqa left Christianity after some time and went back to the religion of Mecca.
It means that Christianity was not corrupted at all in that period, so it was completely pure then.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The non-defining relative clause “which was the least corrupted religion” adds the writer’s evaluation of Christianity. “At that time” limits this evaluation to Waraqa’s period. Also note that “the least corrupted” is a comparison: It does not mean “not corrupted at all”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The time phrase limits the evaluation to one period.
feedback.incorrect: Read the whole relative clause again. What is being evaluated, and for which period? Does “least corrupted” mean “not corrupted”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Turning Points in the Argument
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 3 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank], Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are all based on the religion of Abraham (pbuh). … They stayed away from idolatry and its practices. [blank], later on, this belief became mixed with idolatry and, [blank] Judaism and Christianity, it was corrupted. … As the last faith, Islam includes [blank] what Allah told Abraham (pbuh), but also what Allah told Noah (pbuh), Moses (pbuh), Jesus (pbuh), and all the other prophets.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “In fact” strengthens the opening claim. “However, later on” turns from the hanifs who stayed away from idolatry to a later, opposite development; “Therefore” would wrongly present the corruption as a result of staying away from idolatry. “Like Judaism and Christianity” places the change in a wider pattern; “unlike” would say the opposite. “Not only … but also” adds the other prophets to Abraham.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the chapter from claim to contrast, comparison and addition.
feedback.incorrect: Ask whether each gap strengthens, contrasts, compares or adds. Notice “but also” later in the last sentence. Then check Chapter 3.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Layered Scene
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to rebuild this sentence from Chapter 3.
languageFocusExercises.question: When, where and what did Waraqa see?
sentenceChunks: while he was in the desert,
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “One day” moves to one specific event, and “while he was in the desert” gives the ongoing background. The main clause is “Waraqa saw Bilal al-Habashi”. Then two participle phrases describe Bilal: “lying” (active, what he was doing) and “punished” (passive, what was being done to him). The chapter uses the same compact style in “Hearing his words, Waraqa replied …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. The time frame comes first, then the main event, then the details about Bilal.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the time frame, then the background with “while”, then who saw whom. The -ing and -ed phrases describe Bilal, so they come after his name.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Coherent Contrast-and-Extension Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a place or an idea that changed but kept its main purpose.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did it change, and what did it keep?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should show controlled progression: Establish a point, mark change, locate events in time, add a qualified description, and widen the conclusion without overclaiming.

feedback.correct: Check that each connector has a real discourse purpose and that your relative-clause evaluation is limited to the context you actually describe.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say what stayed the same: “In fact, … have … for centuries.”
discussionPrompts.example: The main purpose of a library has stayed the same. In fact, libraries have kept and shared knowledge for centuries.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show a real change: “However, …”
discussionPrompts.example: A real change came with the internet. However, many people now read online, so libraries added computers and digital books.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Limit your opinion to a time: “…, at that time, …”
discussionPrompts.example: My evaluation of printed catalogues needs a time limit. They were, at that time, the most practical way to find a book.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Widen your last point: “… not only … but also …”
discussionPrompts.example: Today libraries are not only places to borrow books but also community centers where people take classes and meet.

beforeYouRead.quote: Bilal was saying, “Ahad, Ahad,” meaning “One, One.”

pages.title: Abraham’s Land and Time
pages.content:
In the Holy Qur’an, the name of Abraham (pbuh)’s father is Azer. He is described as an idol worshipper (see Surah al-An’am: 74). Azer is presented in Islamic sources as Nimrod’s idol maker. There are different ideas about the birthplace of Abraham (pbuh). Some sources say that he was born in the land of Sumer, Mesopotamia, and migrated from there to Harran. Most generally speaking, we can say that Abraham was born in the city of Ur or Babylon, the country of King Nimrod. Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC. Some sources suggest that he lived between 2200–2000 BC. During the time of Abraham (pbuh), the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in many aspects, such as agriculture and industry. Abraham (pbuh)'s message of monotheism was a belief that had existed in these lands before, but it had been forgotten over time. In the time of Abraham (pbuh), Allah was believed to be in the heavens.

People worshipped the planets, stars, sun, and moon; some people worshipped idols of stone and wood; still others worshipped their kings and rulers.
