hotspots.title: The Land of Nimrod
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) was probably born in Ur or Babylon, the country of King Nimrod, around the 20th century BC.

hotspots.title: Many Objects of Worship
hotspots.description: People in Abraham’s (pbuh) time worshipped planets, stars, the sun, the moon, idols of stone and wood, and even their kings.

exercises.title: Checking the Source
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 4.
exercises.question: Which of these statements does the writer base on the Holy Qur’an itself?
options: Azer made idols for King Nimrod and sold them in the market.
Abraham was born in the city of Ur or in Babylon, in Mesopotamia.
Abraham lived in Mesopotamia in the 20th century BC.
Abraham’s father was called Azer and worshipped idols.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says: “In the Holy Qur’an, the name of Abraham (pbuh)’s father is Azer. He is described as an idol worshipper.” The other statements come from different sources: Azer as Nimrod’s idol maker is from “Islamic sources”, Ur or Babylon is what “we can say” “most generally speaking”, and the period is what Abraham “is believed” to have lived in.

feedback.correct: Correct. Only the father’s name and his idol worship are linked to the Qur’an; the other details come with more careful source words.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentences of Chapter 4 again. Look for the words “In the Holy Qur’an” and see which information follows them.

languageFocusExercises.title: Fact or Reported View?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put each part of Chapter 4 in the right group: Stated directly, or reported.
languageFocusExercises.question: Is the writer sure, or passing on a view?

items: Some sources say that he was born in the land of Sumer, Mesopotamia …
Most generally speaking, we can say that Abraham was born in the city of Ur or Babylon …
Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC.
In the time of Abraham (pbuh), Allah was believed to be in the heavens.
In the Holy Qur’an, the name of Abraham (pbuh)’s father is Azer.
There are different ideas about the birthplace of Abraham (pbuh).
During the time of Abraham (pbuh), the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in many aspects …

Reported or hedged: Some sources say that he was born in the land of Sumer, Mesopotamia …
Most generally speaking, we can say that Abraham was born in the city of Ur or Babylon …
Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC.
In the time of Abraham (pbuh), Allah was believed to be in the heavens.
Stated directly by the writer: In the Holy Qur’an, the name of Abraham (pbuh)’s father is Azer.
There are different ideas about the birthplace of Abraham (pbuh).
During the time of Abraham (pbuh), the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in many aspects …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Where sources disagree, the writer does not state a single fact. “Some sources say” attributes a claim to part of the tradition, “is believed to have lived” passes on a general belief without proof, and “Most generally speaking, we can say” offers a careful summary. “Was believed to be” reports what people of that time believed. The writer states directly what is not in doubt, including the fact that “there are different ideas”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated reported or hedged claims from direct statements.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the frame: some sources say, generally speaking, is believed, was believed. A sentence without such a frame is stated directly, even if it talks about disagreement.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Summary That Keeps the Caution
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the summary that keeps the level of certainty of Chapter 4.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which summary of Abraham’s birthplace and dates is faithful to the chapter?
options: Accounts differ, but broadly speaking Abraham was born in Mesopotamia, probably around the 20th century BC.
The chapter states that Abraham was born in Ur in 1990 BC and later migrated with his family to Harran.
The sources agree that Abraham was born in Sumer and lived in the 20th century BC, so there is no doubt about it.
Because the sources disagree, the chapter says nothing about where or when Abraham lived.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A good B2 summary keeps the writer’s caution. The chapter reports different views (“Some sources say …”) and then gives a general conclusion (“Most generally speaking, we can say …”) and a careful estimate of the period (“is believed to have lived …”). The wrong summaries either join different sources into one certain fact, claim agreement that is not there, or say nothing can be concluded.

feedback.correct: Correct. This summary keeps both the disagreement and the careful general conclusion.
feedback.incorrect: Does the chapter say the sources agree? Does it give one exact city and year? Does it avoid any conclusion? Check the hedged sentences in the first paragraph.

languageFocusExercises.title: Earlier Past and Social Variety
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Abraham’s time?

errorItems.sentence: Abraham (pbuh)’s message of monotheism was a belief that has existed in these lands before, but it had been forgotten over time.
Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to live in the 20th century BC.
People worshipped the planets, stars, sun, and moon; some people worshipped idols of stone and wood; still other worshipped their kings and rulers.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The past perfect “had existed” looks back from Abraham’s time to an even earlier period, and it matches “had been forgotten”. After “is believed”, a perfect infinitive (“to have lived”) is needed for a past time: The belief is present, the life is past. “Some people … still others …” divides society into groups; “others” is a pronoun here, so it needs the plural -s.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the earlier past, the past-time infinitive and the pronoun.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is the time earlier than Abraham’s time? Is the belief present but the life past? Is the word standing alone as a pronoun? Then check the end of Chapter 4.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Qualified Historical Overview
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a place in history that experts still disagree about.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is known, and what is still not sure?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should organize evidence and uncertainty explicitly: attribute claims, synthesise cautiously, locate an earlier state in time, mark change, and distinguish groups rather than overgeneralising.

feedback.correct: Check that every uncertain point is visibly qualified and that your paragraph still reaches a useful synthesis instead of becoming a list of disconnected caveats.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Pass on a source: “Some sources say that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The purpose of Stonehenge belongs to sources, not to me. Some sources say that it was a calendar for farmers.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give a careful summary: “Broadly speaking, we can say that …”
discussionPrompts.example: Broadly speaking, we can say that it was an important meeting place. The sources disagree about the details, but most agree that it was built in several stages.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Say what happened earlier: “Before …, people had already …”
discussionPrompts.example: Before the large stones arrived, people had already dug a round ditch on the site. I need “had dug” to show this earlier stage.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Show different views: “Some … think …, while others …”
discussionPrompts.example: Some researchers think it was a temple, while others believe it was a place for burials. Still others see it as a kind of calendar.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Where was Abraham (pbuh) born, most generally speaking?
options: in the city of Ur or Babylon
beforeYouRead.quote: Abraham was born in the city of Ur or Babylon

iCan: I can describe Abraham’s land and time and the different ideas about his birthplace.
I can show which facts come from sources and which are uncertain.
I can write a careful paragraph about a topic where experts disagree.

pages.title: Nimrod’s Fear and Abraham’s Birth
pages.content:
The head of Abraham (pbuh)’s family was an idolater who totally rejected Allah and made idols with his own hands. Abraham (pbuh) was born into that atmosphere and family. Very soon, he was going to fight against his family and the whole system in his society. As a prophet who lived before Jacob (pbuh), Joseph (pbuh), Moses (pbuh), and Jesus (pbuh), Abraham (pbuh) tried to spread the belief in monotheism in the land of Mesopotamia and the lands where he migrated. Nimrod, the king of Babylon, had many fortunetellers and astrologers. One year, around the 20th century BC, they predicted that a child named Abraham (pbuh) would be born in the region, would change the religion of the people, and would end the reign of Nimrod. According to another narration, Nimrod had a dream that a child in the region would challenge his throne. So, he gathered pregnant women in one place and ordered that all male children be killed.

Upon this, Azer took his wife, who was pregnant with Abraham (pbuh), to a safe place and hid her in a cave, where Abraham (pbuh) was born.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-babylon
__historical_entity__:abraham-mesopotamia
__historical_entity__:abraham-nimrod
The general mood and influences that surround a person or place.
People who claim to know the future by studying the movement of the planets.
Said that something would happen in the future.
The period during which a king or queen rules.
A report of past events passed on from person to person.

hotspots.title: The Astrologers’ Warning
hotspots.description: Nimrod’s astrologers predicted that a child named Abraham (pbuh) would change the people’s religion and end the king’s reign.

hotspots.title: Born in a Cave
hotspots.description: To protect the baby from Nimrod’s order, Azer hid his pregnant wife in a cave, where Abraham (pbuh) was born.

exercises.title: Born in a Cave
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 5.
exercises.question: Why did Azer take his pregnant wife to a cave?
options: Nimrod had ordered that all male children be killed.
Nimrod’s astrologers had asked Azer to bring the child to the palace.
Azer wanted his son to be born far from the idols he made.
exercises.explanation: Nimrod feared a child who would end his reign, so “he gathered pregnant women in one place and ordered that all male children be killed. Upon this, Azer took his wife … to a safe place and hid her in a cave.” The chapter gives two reports of how Nimrod learned about the child: His astrologers’ prediction and, “according to another narration”, his own dream.

feedback.correct: Yes. The words “Upon this” show that Azer hid his wife because of Nimrod’s order.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 5. What did Nimrod order just before the sentence that begins “Upon this, Azer …”?

languageFocusExercises.title: The Future Seen from the Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Did it happen, or is it a later event seen from the past? Put each part in a group.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was still in the future at that time?

dragDropGroups.group: A later event seen from the past
items: Very soon, he was going to fight against his family and the whole system in his society.
a child named Abraham (pbuh) would be born in the region
a child in the region would challenge Nimrod’s throne
Nimrod, the king of Babylon, had many fortunetellers and astrologers.
Nimrod gathered pregnant women in one place
Azer took his wife … to a safe place

A later event seen from the past: Very soon, he was going to fight against his family and the whole system in his society.
a child named Abraham (pbuh) would be born in the region
a child in the region would challenge Nimrod’s throne
An event that happened: Nimrod, the king of Babylon, had many fortunetellers and astrologers.
Nimrod gathered pregnant women in one place
Azer took his wife … to a safe place

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Was going to” and “would” are the future seen from a past moment. The narrator uses “was going to” to look ahead from Abraham’s birth to his later struggle. “Would” reports what the astrologers predicted and what Nimrod’s dream showed. The past simple (had, gathered, took) tells what actually happened at that point in the story.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated past events from future events seen from the past.
feedback.incorrect: Look for “was going to” and “would”: they look forward from a past point. Past simple verbs tell events of the story itself.

languageFocusExercises.title: Another Narration
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 5. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “According to another narration, Nimrod had a dream that a child in the region would challenge his throne.” What does “According to another narration” tell the reader?
options: What follows is a different account of how Nimrod learned about the child, not a second event.
The dream happened after the astrologers’ prediction and was a second warning sent to Nimrod.
The writer believes this account is wrong and wants the reader to ignore it.
Nimrod told other people about his dream and asked them what it meant.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “According to …” attributes information to a source. “Another narration” shows that the tradition tells the story in more than one way: In one account the astrologers predict the child, in the other Nimrod dreams about him. The writer reports both without choosing and without saying one happened after the other.

feedback.correct: Correct. The phrase introduces an alternative account of the same development.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the prediction of the astrologers with the dream. Does the chapter say both happened, or does it give two versions?

languageFocusExercises.title: Linking Result, Person and Place
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each part of Chapter 5 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 5?

transformItems.source: So, he gathered pregnant women in one place and ordered that all male children be killed.
transformItems.frame: [blank], he gathered pregnant women in one place and ordered that all male children be killed.

transformItems.source: Upon this, Azer took his wife, who was pregnant with Abraham (pbuh), to a safe place …
transformItems.frame: Upon this, Azer took his wife, [blank] Abraham (pbuh), to a safe place …

transformItems.source: … and hid her in a cave, where Abraham (pbuh) was born.
transformItems.frame: … and hid her in a cave, [blank] Abraham (pbuh) was born.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So” at the start of a sentence introduces a result; in more formal writing we use “Therefore”, “As a result” or “Consequently”. A non-defining relative clause like “who was pregnant with Abraham” can be shortened to the adjective phrase “pregnant with Abraham”. “Where” after a place means “in which”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the result, the extra detail and the place link.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1 needs a formal result linker. In item 2, drop “who was”. In item 3, replace “where” with a preposition + which. Check the end of Chapter 5.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Layered Past Narrative
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a past event with two different accounts.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did people expect, and what do the two accounts say?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should control time from a past viewpoint, distinguish the status of an alternative account, connect causes and consequences, and embed background/place detail without breaking the narrative flow.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph keeps the alternative account visibly qualified and that each connector or clause has a clear discourse purpose.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Set the time and look ahead: “In …, … . They were going to …”
discussionPrompts.example: In 1950, the village was still dry and poor. The dam was still in the future: Workers were going to start building it two years later.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Report what people expected: “They predicted that … would …”
discussionPrompts.example: Engineers predicted that the dam would bring water to every field. They also said that it would create jobs for young people.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give another account: “According to another account, …”
discussionPrompts.example: I will begin the second version with “According to another account”. In that account, the dam was planned mainly for electricity, not for farmers.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Add details: “The …, who …,” and “The …, where …,”
discussionPrompts.example: The engineer, who had studied abroad, belongs in a “who” clause. The valley, where the river was narrow, belongs in a “where” clause.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Nimrod have many of?
beforeYouRead.quote: Nimrod, the king of Babylon, had many fortunetellers and astrologers.

iCan: I can tell why Nimrod was afraid and where Abraham (pbuh) was born.
I can talk about the future as people saw it in the past.
I can keep two different accounts of one event apart.

pages.title: Abraham’s Childhood
pages.content: Abraham (pbuh) came to know Allah when he was young in age. Allah cleared up Abraham (pbuh)’s heart and mind and gave him wisdom from childhood. Allah said: “And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgement before, and We were of him well-Knowing” (as to his belief in the Oneness of Allah etc.) (Surah al-Anbiya: 51). During his early childhood, Abraham (pbuh) realized that his father made strange statues, sculptures. One day, he asked his father about what he made. His father replied that he made statues of gods. Abraham (pbuh) was astonished and he spontaneously rejected the idea. Being a child, he played with the statues, sitting on their backs as people sit on the backs of donkeys. One day, his father saw him riding the statue of Marduk (the Chief God of Babylon) and he became furious. He ordered his son not to play with it again. Abraham (pbuh) asked: “What is this statue, father? It has big ears, bigger than ours.” His father answered: “It is Marduk, the god of gods, son!”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-babylon
Made something pure and free from anything wrong or confusing.
The ability to make wise and sensible decisions.
Extremely surprised.
Naturally and immediately, without planning or being told.
Figures of people or animals made from stone, wood or metal.

hotspots.title: Wisdom from Childhood
hotspots.description: Allah gave Abraham (pbuh) wisdom and sound judgement while he was still a child.

hotspots.title: Riding the Chief God
hotspots.description: Young Abraham (pbuh) rode on the statue of Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, and his father became furious.

exercises.title: The Statue of Marduk
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 6.
exercises.question: When Azer saw his son riding the statue of Marduk, he became furious and told him not to play with it again.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says his father “became furious. He ordered his son not to play with it again.” For Azer, Marduk was “the god of gods”, so he could not accept his son playing on it.

feedback.correct: Correct. For Azer, Marduk was “the god of gods”, so he could not accept his son playing on it.
feedback.incorrect: Read the part of Chapter 6 where Azer sees his son on the statue. Find the word that describes Azer’s feeling and the order he gives.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Being a Child” Add?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 6. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Being a child, he played with the statues, …” What does “Being a child” add to the sentence?
options: It gives the background reason for his behavior: because he was a child, he played with them.
It shows that he was playing with the statues and becoming a child at the same moment.
It describes his father, who was making the statues while the boy was playing with them.
It shows that he stopped being a child after this event and started working in the shop.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A participle clause with “being” at the start of a sentence often gives a reason or background state: “Being a child” = “As he was a child”. Its subject is the same as the subject of the main clause (he). This compact form keeps the main event, “he played with the statues”, in focus.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Being a child” explains why he treated the statues as toys.
feedback.incorrect: Who is the subject of “being”? Read the main clause that follows it. Why did Abraham play with the statues?

languageFocusExercises.title: Reported and Direct Speech
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 6 with the words given.
languageFocusExercises.question: What changes when we report words, or quote them?

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) asked: “What is this statue, father? …”
transformItems.frame: Abraham asked his father [blank].

transformItems.source: His father replied that he made statues of gods.
transformItems.frame: His father replied, “[blank] statues of gods.”

transformItems.source: He ordered his son not to play with it again.
transformItems.frame: He said to his son, “[blank] with it again.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order and moves the tense back: “What is this statue?” → “what that statue was”. A reported statement also moves back, so the direct words behind “he made” are “I make”. A reported order uses order + person + (not) to + verb; in direct speech it becomes an imperative: “Don’t play …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You changed the question, the statement and the order correctly.
feedback.incorrect: In a reported question the verb comes after the subject (what the statue was). In direct speech, go back to the present and use an imperative for the order.

languageFocusExercises.title: Making a Comparison
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 6 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words compare the idols with ordinary things?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: … sitting on their backs [blank] people sit on the backs of donkeys. … “What is this statue, father? It has big ears, [blank] [blank] ours.”
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As” + clause compares two actions: He sat on the statues in the same way people sit on donkeys. “Such as” introduces examples, not a clause. Short adjectives form the comparative with -er + than: “bigger than ours”; “more big” is wrong, and “then” is a time word. The comparisons make the “god of gods” look like an ordinary object.

feedback.correct: Correct. You completed both comparisons.
feedback.incorrect: The first gap is followed by a full clause (people sit …). The second comparison needs a short adjective + -er and the word that introduces what is compared.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Childhood Memory with Layered Language
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a memory from your childhood.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened one day when you were young?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should distinguish background from main events, preserve the different functions of reported speech, and use comparison to develop perspective rather than as an isolated sentence pattern.

feedback.correct: Check that every target form contributes to the narrative flow and that the reported speech functions remain distinct.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Set the time, then one event: “When I was young, … . One day, …”
discussionPrompts.example: “When I was young, we lived near the sea” sets the broad frame. “One day, a storm hit the town” moves to one specific event.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Add background: “Being the youngest child, I …”
discussionPrompts.example: Instead of “I was the youngest child. I could not go out,” I can write “Being the youngest child, I had to stay at home.”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Report a question, a statement and an order: “She told us not to …”
discussionPrompts.example: My brother asked my mother whether the boats were safe. She said that the fishermen had tied them well. Then she told us not to go near the window.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Compare: “The … looked as … as …”
discussionPrompts.example: I could write: “The waves looked as tall as our house.” This shows how frightening they seemed to a small child, not their real size.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Abraham’s father say he made?
beforeYouRead.quote: His father replied that he made statues of gods.

iCan: I can tell how the young Abraham (pbuh) questioned his father’s statues.
I can report a question, an answer and an order.
I can write a short childhood memory with one clear event.

pages.title: Hatred for Idols
pages.content:
His father continued, “These big ears show his deep knowledge.” This made Abraham (pbuh) laugh; he was only seven years old at that time.

Years passed and Abraham (pbuh) grew. From childhood, his heart was full of hatred for these idols. He could not understand how a reasonable person could make a statue and then worship what he had made. He realized these statues were lifeless, silent, and entirely helpless; when they fell, they could not get back up. It was impossible to understand how people could believe that such statues could harm or benefit them! Abraham (pbuh)'s people had a big temple full of idols, in the middle of which was a niche housing the biggest gods. Abraham (pbuh), who used to go to the temple with his father when he was a child, greatly disliked all that wood and stone. It shocked him to see people bowing, crying, and begging the idols for help, as if those lifeless idols were capable of hearing their prayers! At first, Abraham thought the sight was funny, but later his feelings turned into anger.

vocabulary.definition: A very strong feeling of dislike.
Without life; not living and unable to move or feel.
Completely unable to act or to protect oneself.
A hollow space in a wall where a statue or object is placed.
Asking for something in a desperate and humble way.

hotspots.title: Idols That Cannot Stand
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) saw that the idols were so helpless that they could not get up again when they fell.

hotspots.title: The Great Temple
hotspots.description: His people’s temple was full of idols, and the biggest gods stood in a niche in the middle.

exercises.title: Changing Feelings
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 7.
exercises.question: How did Abraham’s feelings change when he saw people begging the idols for help?
options: At first he was afraid of the idols, but later he felt calm.
At first he found it funny, but later he became angry.
At first he was angry, but later he found it funny.
exercises.explanation: The last sentence of Chapter 7 says: “At first, Abraham thought the sight was funny, but later his feelings turned into anger.” He could not accept that people begged lifeless idols as if they could hear their prayers.

feedback.correct: Right. What seemed funny to a child became a serious problem for him as he grew older.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 7 again. Look for “At first …” and “but later …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “As If” Tell Us?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 7. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: In “It shocked him to see people bowing, crying, and begging the idols for help, as if those lifeless idols were capable of hearing their prayers!”, the writer suggests that the idols may really have heard the prayers.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As if” + past form (were) describes behavior that suggests something unreal. The people behaved like the idols could hear, but the writer calls them “lifeless idols”, so the comparison shows a contradiction between the people’s behavior and reality.

feedback.correct: Correct. “As if … were” marks the idea as unreal.
feedback.incorrect: Notice the word “lifeless” in the same clause and the past form “were”. Does the writer think the idols could hear?

languageFocusExercises.title: Background Inside the Sentence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapter 7.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which form fits each sentence about the temple?

formChoices.sentence: … how a reasonable person could make a statue and then worship what he [choice].
Abraham (pbuh)’s people had a big temple full of idols, in the middle of [choice] was a niche housing the biggest gods.
Abraham (pbuh), [choice] used to go to the temple with his father when he was a child, greatly disliked all that wood and stone.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The past perfect “had made” shows that making the statue came before worshipping it. After a preposition, English uses “which” for things (“in the middle of which”), never “that”. In a non-defining clause between commas, a person takes “who”; “that” is not used in non-defining clauses.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the earlier past and the right relative words.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which action came first? What follows a preposition? Is the clause between commas? Then check the second paragraph of Chapter 7.

languageFocusExercises.title: From Evidence to Evaluation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 7 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 7?

transformItems.source: … when they fell, they could not get back up.
transformItems.frame: … when they fell, they [blank] get back up.

transformItems.source: It was impossible to understand how people could believe that such statues could harm or benefit them!
transformItems.frame: Abraham [blank] how people could believe that such statues could harm or benefit them.

transformItems.source: At first, Abraham thought the sight was funny, but later his feelings turned into anger.
transformItems.frame: Although Abraham [blank] the sight was funny, later his feelings turned into anger.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Could not” can express physical inability (the statues “could not get back up” = were unable to). The impersonal “It was impossible to understand …” is a strong evaluation; with a person as subject it becomes “Abraham could not understand …”. “At first …, but later …” shows a change; with “Although” the first feeling becomes a concession, and “but” is dropped.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the ability, the evaluation and the change of feeling.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1 needs “be able to”. Item 2 needs a verb of understanding with “Abraham” as subject. In item 3, “Although” replaces “but”. Check the second paragraph of Chapter 7.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write an Observation-to-Evaluation Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a habit that does not match the facts.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do people do, and what is really true?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should use the target structures to organize reasoning. The grammar should help the reader see how evidence leads to judgement and how the writer’s viewpoint develops.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph has a visible reasoning chain and that the two uses of “could” perform different functions.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Describe it with three facts: “It is cheap, … and …”
discussionPrompts.example: The “lucky” bracelet is cheap, plastic and completely ordinary. These three facts will be the basis of my judgement.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give an example: “When …, …” or “If …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: When students wear it during an exam, their marks do not change. If they study, their marks improve with or without it.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show the gap: “They … as if it could …”
discussionPrompts.example: Some students touch the bracelet before a test as if it could answer the questions for them. This shows the gap between what they do and what is true.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Show how your view changed: “At first, I …, but later …”
discussionPrompts.example: At first, I thought the habit was harmless and funny, but later I felt worried. I noticed that some friends were studying less because they trusted the bracelet.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How old was Abraham (pbuh) when he laughed at the idol’s big ears?
beforeYouRead.quote: he was only seven years old at that time

iCan: I can explain why Abraham (pbuh) disliked the idols.
I can use “as if” to show a gap between how things look and what is true.
I can write a paragraph that moves from what I notice to my judgement.

pages.title: Discovering Allah
pages.content:
Wasn’t it shocking that all of those people could be fooled? His father wanted him to become a priest when he grew up, which made things even worse. He only wanted his son to show respect to those statues, yet Abraham (pbuh) never stopped displaying his hatred.

One night, Abraham (pbuh) left his house to go to a mountain. He walked by himself through the darkness until he found a cave in the mountain, where he sat down to rest. He looked at the sky and saw the planets and stars which were worshipped by some people on earth. The Holy Qur’an told this incident in Surah al-An’am, verses 75–79: “Thus, We showed Abraham the empire of the heavens and the earth, that he might be one of those with certainty. When the night fell over him, he saw a planet. He said, ‘This is my lord.’ But when it set, he said, ‘I do not love those that set.’” Abraham (pbuh) saw that the stars couldn’t show up when they wanted to because they could only do so at night.

vocabulary.definition: A person who performs religious duties in a place of worship.
A very large area, or everything, under the rule of one power.
An event, especially an important or unusual one.
Complete confidence that something is true.
(Of the sun, moon, stars or planets) went down below the horizon.

hotspots.title: A Night in the Mountains
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) walked alone through the dark and rested in a cave in the mountains.

hotspots.title: The Setting Planet
hotspots.description: When the planet disappeared, Abraham (pbuh) said that he did not love things that set.

exercises.title: A Planet in the Night
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 8.
exercises.question: Why was the planet not worthy to be Abraham’s Lord?
options: It was smaller and weaker than the moon.
His father had told him to worship only the sun.
It disappeared and could not choose when to appear.
exercises.explanation: When the planet set, Abraham said, “I do not love those that set.” The chapter adds that the stars “couldn’t show up when they wanted to because they could only do so at night.” Something that disappears and has no control over itself cannot be the Lord.

feedback.correct: Correct. Setting and appearing only at night show that the planet has no power over itself.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 8. What happens to the planet, and what does the last sentence say about when the stars can appear?

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose in the Verse
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the lines from Surah al-An’am in Chapter 8. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Thus, We showed Abraham the empire of the heavens and the earth, that he might be one of those with certainty.” What does “that he might be …” express?
options: The purpose of showing him the heavens and the earth: So that he would reach certainty.
A doubt: The writer is not sure whether Abraham ever reached certainty.
A permission: Abraham was allowed to see the heavens and the earth if he wanted.
A result that had already happened before he was shown the heavens and the earth.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “That + subject + might/may …” is a formal way of expressing purpose, like “so that he would …”. In the verse, what Abraham was shown has a clear aim: His certainty. The chapter then tells how he looked at the planets and stars.

feedback.correct: Correct. The clause gives the purpose of what Abraham was shown.
feedback.incorrect: Ask why Abraham was shown the heavens and the earth. The clause after “that” answers this question.

languageFocusExercises.title: Persistence and Its Effect
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Abraham and his father?

errorItems.sentence: His father wanted him to become a priest when he grew up, what made things even worse.
He only wanted his son to show respect to those statues, yet Abraham (pbuh) never stopped to display his hatred.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A comment on a whole situation is added with “, which …”: “…, which made things even worse”. “What” cannot refer back to a clause, and “that” is not used after a comma. “Stop + -ing” means to end an activity: “never stopped displaying his hatred” shows persistence. “Stop + to” would mean stopping in order to do something else. “Yet” sets his persistence against the father’s wish.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the comment clause and the verb pattern.
feedback.incorrect: Which relative word comments on a whole clause after a comma? Which form follows “stop” when an activity continues or ends? Check the first paragraph of Chapter 8.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build the Narrator’s Conclusion
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to rebuild the last sentence of Chapter 8.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Abraham see about the stars, and why?
sentenceChunks: because they could only do so
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Saw that …” here means “understood that …”: it reports a conclusion. “Because” gives the reason. “Do so” replaces the verb phrase “show up”, so the writer does not repeat it. The sentence turns what Abraham observed in the night sky into evidence that the stars have no control over themselves.

feedback.correct: Well done. The conclusion comes first, then its reason.
feedback.incorrect: Start with who saw what. Then add when the stars wanted to appear, and finally the reason with “because … do so at night”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Change-as-Evidence Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone whose real talent shows over time.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did others expect, and what did time show?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make grammatical choices carry the reasoning: Pressure is contrasted with persistence, an action has an intended result, and change over time becomes evidence for the final judgement.

feedback.correct: Check that every target structure contributes to the argument rather than appearing as an isolated grammar example.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say what others expected: “His parents expected him to …”
discussionPrompts.example: My cousin’s parents expected him to study law. They wanted him to have a safe job.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show what continued: “He …, yet he never stopped …”
discussionPrompts.example: He worked hard for his law exams, yet he never stopped drawing in the evenings. “Yet” shows that his love of art continued under pressure.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show the change: “When …, … . But when …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: When he was fifteen, his drawings looked like a hobby. But when he won a national prize at eighteen, everyone saw a real talent.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Give your judgement: “This shows that …, which …”
discussionPrompts.example: This change shows that his interest was not a passing phase, which is a judgement, not just a story. So his parents should take his talent seriously.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Abraham (pbuh) never stop showing toward the statues?
beforeYouRead.quote: yet Abraham (pbuh) never stopped displaying his hatred

iCan: I can tell what Abraham (pbuh) saw and learned on the mountain at night.
I can show that something continues in spite of pressure with “yet”.
I can use a change over time as evidence for a conclusion.

pages.title: The Signs in the Sky
pages.content:
“Then, when he saw the moon rising, he said, ‘This is my lord.’ But when it set, he said, ‘If my Lord does not guide me, I will be one of the erring people.’ Then, when he saw the sun rising, he said, ‘This is my lord, this is bigger.’ But when it set, he said, ‘O my people, I am innocent of your idolatry. I have directed my attention towards Him Who created the heavens and the earth—a monotheist—and I am not of the idolaters.’” His young heart was filled with severe pain. He considered what was beyond the moon, the stars, and the planets (i.e., Allah). He was astonished that these heavenly bodies were worshipped by people, while in fact all those stars, asteroids, the Sun, the Moon, etc., had been created; they appeared and disappeared at the Creator’s command.

People who worshipped astronomical objects got into arguments with Abraham (pbuh). In that debate, Abraham (pbuh) demonstrated to the people that these heavenly bodies cannot be worshipped as partners with Allah.

vocabulary.definition: Having nothing to do with something wrong.
Natural objects in the sky, such as the sun, the moon, stars and planets.
Small rocky objects that travel around the sun.
A discussion in which people give opposing opinions and arguments.
Turned or pointed something towards a particular person or thing.

hotspots.title: The Moon and the Sun
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) watched the moon and then the sun rise and set, and turned away from worshipping them.

hotspots.title: A Debate About the Stars
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) showed the star worshippers that heavenly bodies could not be partners with Allah.

exercises.title: After Watching the Sky
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 9.
exercises.question: Abraham discussed his thoughts about the heavenly bodies with the people who worshipped them.
exercises.explanation: The chapter ends: “People who worshipped astronomical objects got into arguments with Abraham (pbuh). In that debate, Abraham (pbuh) demonstrated to the people that these heavenly bodies cannot be worshipped as partners with Allah.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham did not stay silent; he explained his reasoning to the star worshippers in a debate.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 9. Who argued with Abraham, and what did he show them?

languageFocusExercises.title: Condition and Guidance
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the line from the verse in Chapter 9. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: In “If my Lord does not guide me, I will be one of the erring people”, Abraham says that he has already gone astray.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: This is a real (first) conditional: if + present simple, will + verb. It describes a possible future result that depends on a condition. Abraham does not say he has gone astray; he says his right guidance depends on his Lord. This prepares his clear statement at the end of the verse: “I am not of the idolaters.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The sentence states a condition and a possible result, not a past fact.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb forms: “if … does not guide” and “will be”. Is this about the past or about a possible result?

languageFocusExercises.title: Appearance and Reality
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 9 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did people do, and what was really true?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: He was astonished that these heavenly bodies [blank] by people, [blank] all those stars, asteroids, the Sun, the Moon, etc., [blank]; they appeared and disappeared at the Creator’s command.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive “were worshipped by people” keeps the heavenly bodies as the topic and shows how people treated them. “While in fact” marks a correction: It moves from human practice to the reality the writer asserts. The passive past perfect “had been created” shows that these bodies are the results of creation, not creators; the active “had created” would say the opposite.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated human practice from the reality behind it.
feedback.incorrect: The heavenly bodies did not worship or create; something was done to them. Which linker corrects an appearance? Check the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 9.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Does What?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 9 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 9?

transformItems.source: In that debate, Abraham (pbuh) demonstrated to the people that these heavenly bodies cannot be worshipped as partners with Allah.
transformItems.frame: … Abraham (pbuh) demonstrated to the people that they [blank] these heavenly bodies as partners with Allah.

transformItems.source: People who worshipped astronomical objects got into arguments with Abraham (pbuh).
transformItems.frame: [blank] got into arguments with Abraham (pbuh).

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive “cannot be worshipped” focuses on the heavenly bodies; the active “they cannot worship” focuses on the people. A defining relative clause (“people who worshipped …”) can be shortened to an -ing phrase (“people worshipping …”) or replaced by a noun (“worshippers of …”).

feedback.correct: Well done. You changed the focus and kept the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: In item 1, “they” means the people, so use an active modal verb. In item 2, shorten “People who worshipped …”. Check the last paragraph of Chapter 9.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build an Evidence-to-Stance Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a popular idea that turned out to be wrong.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did people believe, and what did the evidence show?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should show reasoning developing across the paragraph: A possibility is examined, evidence changes the evaluation, and the final stance is expressed more explicitly.

feedback.correct: Check that each target structure advances the argument and that the final stance follows from the evidence.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Give a real condition: “If you …, your … will …”
discussionPrompts.example: If you eat a balanced diet, your eyes will stay healthy. The result depends on this real condition.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what seemed true, then what changed: “At first, it seemed …”
discussionPrompts.example: At first, it seemed true that eating lots of carrots gives you excellent night vision. Later research showed that extra carrots do not improve healthy eyes.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Correct the idea: “It is often repeated …, while in fact …”
discussionPrompts.example: The idea is often repeated by parents, while in fact it began as a story during a war. The passive “is often repeated” puts the idea at the front.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — End with your view: “Therefore, I now see …”
discussionPrompts.example: Study after study found no special effect on night vision. Therefore, I now see the claim as a myth, not a fact.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Abraham (pbuh) see rising after the moon had set?
beforeYouRead.quote: when he saw the sun rising

iCan: I can explain what Abraham (pbuh) understood from the moon and the sun.
I can correct an idea with “while in fact”.
I can move from a first impression to a position based on evidence.

pages.title: Challenging Star Worshippers
pages.content:
Indeed, these bodies are evidently created, controlled, managed, and made to serve a purpose. They come and go, sometimes fading from the world. However, Allah sees and knows everything; nothing can be hidden from Him. Allah is without end, everlasting without disappearance. There is no other god but Allah. Abraham (pbuh) clarified the situation for them, firstly, that the heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship and, secondly, that they are the signs of Allah. The Qur’an emphasizes this with simple logic: “And of His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not bow down to the sun, nor to the moon, but bow down to Allah, Who created them both, if you really worship Him” (Surah Fussilat: 37). Abraham (pbuh)'s rational thinking helped to uncover the truth, and then the conflict between him and the worshippers of the stars and planets started. They did not remain silent.

They began arguing and threatening Abraham (pbuh).

vocabulary.definition: Lasting for ever; never ending.
Not deserving respect, attention or a particular treatment.
Explained something so that it could be understood without confusion.
Gives special importance to an idea.
A serious disagreement or fight between people or groups.

hotspots.title: Signs, Not Gods
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) explained that the sun and the moon were signs of Allah, not gods to be worshipped.

hotspots.title: The Conflict Begins
hotspots.description: His reasoning started a conflict with the star worshippers, who argued with him and threatened him.

exercises.title: Two Points and a Conflict
exercises.instructions: Match each step with what Chapter 10 says.
exercises.question: How does Chapter 10 organize Abraham’s answer to the star worshippers?

matchingPairs.right: The heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship.
They point to Allah as His signs.
The star worshippers began arguing and threatening him.

correctAnswer.Firstly: The heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship.
correctAnswer.Secondly: They point to Allah as His signs.
correctAnswer.After the truth was uncovered: The star worshippers began arguing and threatening him.

exercises.explanation: The chapter says Abraham clarified the situation, “firstly, that the heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship and, secondly, that they are the signs of Allah.” Then “the conflict between him and the worshippers of the stars and planets started”, and “They began arguing and threatening Abraham (pbuh).”

feedback.correct: Well done. You followed the writer’s signposts “firstly” and “secondly”, and then the reaction of the star worshippers.
feedback.incorrect: Find the words “firstly” and “secondly” in the middle of Chapter 10. Then read the end of the chapter to see how the people reacted.

languageFocusExercises.title: Words That Describe Created Things
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 10 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the chapter say about the heavenly bodies?

matchingPairs.right: clearly brought into existence by Someone else
directed by a power outside themselves
existing to do a particular job
appear for a time and then disappear
not deserving to be worshipped

correctAnswer.evidently created: clearly brought into existence by Someone else
correctAnswer.controlled, managed: directed by a power outside themselves
correctAnswer.made to serve a purpose: existing to do a particular job
correctAnswer.come and go: appear for a time and then disappear

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive participles “created, controlled, managed, and made …” all present the heavenly bodies as things that something is done to: They do not act by themselves. “Evidently” means “clearly, as can be seen”. The prefix un- in “unworthy” means “not”. Together these words prepare the chapter’s conclusion that the sun and moon are signs, not gods.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each description with its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first two sentences of Chapter 10 again. Which words show dependence, which show purpose, and which show change?

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “However” Contrast?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the lines from Chapter 10. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “They come and go, sometimes fading from the world. However, Allah sees and knows everything; nothing can be hidden from Him.” What contrast does “However” mark?
options: Between created bodies that come and go and Allah, Who knows everything and does not disappear.
Between Abraham’s view of the stars and the view of the people who worshipped them.
Between the night, when stars appear, and the day, when they fade from the sky and cannot be seen.
Between what Abraham believed as a child and what he believed later as a grown man.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “However” links two sentences that contrast. Before it: The heavenly bodies are created, controlled and temporary. After it: Allah sees and knows everything and is “everlasting without disappearance”. The contrast is between the created and the Creator.

feedback.correct: Correct. “However” sets the limited, changing bodies against Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence just before “However” and the sentences just after it. Who or what is described on each side?

languageFocusExercises.title: Organizing a Two-Part Explanation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 10 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 10?

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) clarified the situation for them, firstly, that the heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship and, secondly, that they are the signs of Allah.
transformItems.frame: Abraham (pbuh) clarified [blank] the heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship but also that they are the signs of Allah.

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh)’s rational thinking helped to uncover the truth, and then the conflict between him and the worshippers of the stars and planets started.
transformItems.frame: [blank] Abraham (pbuh)’s rational thinking helped to uncover the truth, the conflict between him and the worshippers of the stars and planets started.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Firstly … secondly …” lists two points in order. “Not only that … but also that …” joins the same two points and shows that the second adds something important: The heavenly bodies are rejected as gods but reinterpreted as signs. “…, and then …” can become a time clause with “After” or “Once”, which puts the first event in the background.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept both points and the order of events.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1 needs the first half of “not only … but also”. Item 2 needs a time word that shows the first event came before the conflict.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Contrast-and-Reframing Argument
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about something old in your town and what it means now.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do people see, and what does it really mean?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make each language choice advance the reasoning: observation, limitation, contrast, two-part interpretation, and a final consequence.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph develops an argument rather than listing disconnected sentences.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Describe what people see: “It is covered with … and admired by …”
discussionPrompts.example: I will start with the old clock tower in our town square. It is covered with ivy and is admired by tourists.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Add a problem: “However, …”
discussionPrompts.example: “However” will introduce the problem: The clock has not shown the correct time for years.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give two points: “Firstly, … . Secondly, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Firstly, the tower is no longer a useful clock. Secondly, it is a sign of the town’s history, so it should be kept as a monument.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Say what people now argue about: “Some want …, while others …”
discussionPrompts.example: This reasoning leads to a debate in the town council. Some members want to repair the clock, while others want to turn the tower into a museum.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did the star worshippers begin to do?
beforeYouRead.quote: They began arguing and threatening Abraham (pbuh).

iCan: I can explain the two points Abraham (pbuh) made about the stars and planets.
I can organize an argument with “firstly” and “secondly”.
I can explain how evidence can lead to a debate.

pages.title: Arguing for Tawhid
pages.content: “And his people argued with him. He said, ‘Do you argue with me about Allah, when He has guided me? I do not fear partners you assign to Him, unless my Lord wills it. My Lord comprehends all things in knowledge. Will you not reconsider? And why should I fear the partners you give to Him, and you do not fear worshipping others alongside Allah for which He sent down to you no authority? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you are aware?’ They who believe, and do not mix their belief with injustice—those will have security, and they are (rightly) guided. That was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people.” (Surah al-An’am: 80–83). His people attempted to argue with him and present evidence to prove the correctness of their beliefs. That these arguments are not told in the verses shows the ridiculousness of their claims. It is understood from Abraham (pbuh)'s statement, “I do not fear partners you worship alongside Allah,” that his people threatened him with the punishment of their gods.

vocabulary.definition: To give reasons for or against something, often angrily.
The quality of being true or free from mistakes.
The quality of being so silly that nobody can take it seriously.
Statements that something is true, made without proof.
Said that they would cause harm or punishment to someone.

hotspots.title: Who Deserves Security?
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) asked which side had more right to security: Those who worshipped Allah alone or those who gave Him partners.

hotspots.title: Empty Arguments
hotspots.description: His people tried to prove their beliefs, but their claims were so weak that the verses did not even mention them.

exercises.title: Evidence of a Threat
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 11.
exercises.question: How does the writer know that Abraham’s people threatened him with the punishment of their gods?
options: The verses quote, word for word, the threats that the people made against Abraham.
Abraham’s father told him about the threat when they argued at home.
King Nimrod announced the threat in public in front of the whole city.
It is understood from Abraham’s words that he does not fear their partners.
exercises.explanation: The writer does not quote a threat. The chapter says it “is understood from Abraham (pbuh)'s statement”, “I do not fear partners you worship alongside Allah,” “that his people threatened him with the punishment of their gods.” This is an inference from Abraham’s answer. The writer also notes that the people’s own arguments “are not told in the verses”.

feedback.correct: Right. The threat is not reported directly; the writer infers it from Abraham’s reply.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 11. Look for the words “It is understood from …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: What the Verses Say, What the Writer Adds
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it from the verses, or the writer’s comment? Put each part in the right group.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words are from the verses, and which are the writer’s?

items: My Lord comprehends all things in knowledge.
… for which He sent down to you no authority?
So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you are aware?
His people attempted to argue with him and present evidence to prove the correctness of their beliefs.
That these arguments are not told in the verses shows the ridiculousness of their claims.
It is understood from Abraham (pbuh)’s statement … that his people threatened him with the punishment of their gods.

From the verses: My Lord comprehends all things in knowledge.
… for which He sent down to you no authority?
So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you are aware?
The writer’s comment or inference: His people attempted to argue with him and present evidence to prove the correctness of their beliefs.
That these arguments are not told in the verses shows the ridiculousness of their claims.
It is understood from Abraham (pbuh)’s statement … that his people threatened him with the punishment of their gods.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter first quotes Surah al-An’am: 80–83 and then comments on it. The writer’s sentences use their own framing: “attempted to …” reports; “That these arguments are not told … shows …” draws a conclusion from something missing; “It is understood from … that …” marks an inference. A careful reader keeps the quoted evidence and the writer’s interpretation apart.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the quoted evidence from the writer’s interpretation.
feedback.incorrect: Find where the quotation from Surah al-An’am ends. Sentences after it are the writer’s. Look for “shows”, “It is understood” and “attempted”.

languageFocusExercises.title: An Exception That Keeps the Claim
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the line from the verse in Chapter 11. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “I do not fear partners you assign to Him, unless my Lord wills it.” What does “unless my Lord wills it” do?
options: It keeps the main statement — no fear of the partners — and says that anything that happens to him depends only on his Lord’s will.
It shows that Abraham is sometimes afraid of the partners, especially when his angry people threaten him with their punishment.
It means that the partners can harm Abraham if they want to, so he must be careful not to anger them.
It shows that Abraham will begin to fear the partners later, when his people punish him for breaking the idols.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Unless” means “except if”. It adds one narrow exception without cancelling the main claim. Abraham still rejects any fear of the false partners; the only power he recognises over what happens to him is his Lord’s will.

feedback.correct: Correct. The exception points to his Lord’s will, not to the partners’ power.
feedback.incorrect: Who is the subject of “wills” in the exception: The partners or his Lord? Does the exception give power to the partners?

languageFocusExercises.title: Framing an Inference
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 11 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 11?

transformItems.source: That these arguments are not told in the verses shows the ridiculousness of their claims.
transformItems.frame: [blank] these arguments are not told in the verses shows the ridiculousness of their claims.

transformItems.source: It is understood from Abraham (pbuh)’s statement … that his people threatened him with the punishment of their gods.
transformItems.frame: We [blank] from Abraham (pbuh)’s statement … that his people threatened him with the punishment of their gods.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A that-clause can be the subject of a sentence (“That these arguments are not told … shows …”), but it is very formal; “The fact that …” is clearer. The impersonal passive “It is understood from … that …” marks an inference without naming who makes it; “We understand/infer from … that …” states the same inference in the active voice.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the evidence and the inference clear.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1 needs a noun phrase before “that”. Item 2 needs an active verb for drawing a conclusion. Check the last three sentences of Chapter 11.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Question-Led Evidence Argument
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a disagreement at school or in your town.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which side has better reasons?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should use language choices to organize reasoning: Challenge an assumption, qualify a claim, distinguish evidence from inference, and end with an evaluative comparison.

feedback.correct: Check that your questions advance the argument and that your inference is clearly marked as an inference.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Challenge an idea with a question: “Do … really …?”
discussionPrompts.example: My first question will challenge the idea that more homework means more learning. “Do students really learn more just because they work longer?”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Add one exception: “… unless …”
discussionPrompts.example: Homework should be short unless a big exam is coming. This exception keeps my claim narrow.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give the evidence, then a careful guess: “It can be inferred that …”
discussionPrompts.example: A school survey directly shows that students sleep less when they have a lot of homework. It can be inferred that tired students learn less, but the survey does not prove it.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — End with a question: “Which position is better supported?”
discussionPrompts.example: My final question will be: “Which position is better supported, the one based on habit or the one based on the survey?”

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Which surah are these verses from?
beforeYouRead.quote: (Surah al-An’am: 80–83)

iCan: I can explain how Abraham (pbuh) answered his people’s threat.
I can ask a question that makes a point and limit a claim with “unless”.
I can keep what is proved apart from what is only inferred.

pages.title: Confronting His People
pages.content:
Prophet Abraham (pbuh) paid no heed to this threat. As a true believer, he expressed his fear of Allah. In doing so, he declared his belief that both benefit and harm come from Allah. Abraham (pbuh) did his best to make his people mindful of the oneness of Allah and the need to worship Him alone. He told them to firmly reject the worship of idols. He said to his father and his people in Surah al-Anbiya, verses 52–56: “When he said to his father and his people, ‘What are these statues to which you are faithful?’ They said, ‘We found our parents worshipping them.’ He said, ‘You and your parents are in evident error.’ They said, ‘Are you telling us the truth, or are you just playing?’ He said, ‘Your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the One who created them, and I bear witness to that.’”

A bitter struggle began between Abraham (pbuh) and his people. The most amazed and furious was his father, for he not only worshipped idols but shaped and sold them as well.

vocabulary.definition: Completely ignored something.
Stated something clearly and publicly.
Aware of something important and giving it attention.
In a strong, determined way that will not change.
A mistake or false belief that is clear for everyone to see.

hotspots.title: No Fear of Idols
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) ignored the threat and declared that benefit and harm come only from Allah.

hotspots.title: The Angry Idol Maker
hotspots.description: His father was the most furious of all because he shaped and sold idols as well as worshipping them.

exercises.title: The Angriest Man
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 12.
exercises.question: Why was Abraham’s father the most amazed and furious of all his people?
options: Abraham had insulted him in front of the whole town.
He not only worshipped idols but also shaped and sold them.
He was the chief priest of the great temple.
exercises.explanation: The last sentence of Chapter 12 says: “The most amazed and furious was his father, for he not only worshipped idols but shaped and sold them as well.” Abraham’s message was a challenge to his father’s belief and to his work.

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham’s message touched both his father’s faith and his livelihood.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 12. The word “for” introduces the reason.

languageFocusExercises.title: Follow the Debate
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the lines from Surah al-Anbiya in Chapter 12 in order.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the debate move from a question to a clear belief?

sequencingItems.text: ‘What are these statues to which you are faithful?’
‘We found our parents worshipping them.’
‘You and your parents are in evident error.’
‘Are you telling us the truth, or are you just playing?’
‘Your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the One who created them, and I bear witness to that.’

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Each line does something in the argument. Abraham opens with a challenging question. The people justify their worship with tradition (“We found our parents …”). Abraham answers the justification directly: The parents were also in error. The people then question his seriousness, and Abraham replies with a positive statement of belief and his own witness.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the debate from question to justification, judgement, doubt and declaration.
feedback.incorrect: Look for links: “your parents” answers “our parents”, and “Are you telling us the truth” reacts to a strong judgement. Check the verses in Chapter 12.

languageFocusExercises.title: Words for Response and Conflict
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 12 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which expressions describe Abraham’s response and the people’s position?

matchingPairs.right: ignored; did not let it affect him
keeping something in mind and aware of it
that you stay loyal to
clearly mistaken
a hard and painful conflict

correctAnswer.paid no heed to: ignored; did not let it affect him
correctAnswer.mindful of: keeping something in mind and aware of it

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Several of these expressions are fixed combinations: Pay (no) heed to, be mindful of, be faithful to (in the verse the preposition moves to the front: “to which you are faithful”). Learn them with their prepositions. “Evident” means “clear, easy to see”, and “bitter” with “struggle” means painful and full of anger.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each expression with its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Find each expression in Chapter 12 and read the sentence around it: a threat, a duty, statues, a judgement, and the relationship with his people.

languageFocusExercises.title: Adding and Reporting
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 12 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 12?

transformItems.source: … for he not only worshipped idols but shaped and sold them as well.
transformItems.frame: Not only [blank] idols, but he shaped and sold them as well.

transformItems.source: He told them to firmly reject the worship of idols.
transformItems.frame: He said to them, “[blank] the worship of idols.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not only … but (also/as well)” adds a stronger second point: The father did more than worship idols, he made and sold them. When a sentence starts with “Not only”, the subject and auxiliary change places, as in a question: “Not only did he worship …”. A reported instruction (told them to + verb) becomes an imperative in direct speech.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used inversion after “Not only” and changed the instruction into direct speech.
feedback.incorrect: After “Not only” at the start, use question word order: did + subject + verb. For item 2, start with the base verb.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Stance-and-Response Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who stays calm under pressure.
languageFocusExercises.question: What pressure does the person face, and how do they answer?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should connect pressure, principle, action, interpretation and dialogue into one coherent argument rather than produce isolated grammar examples.

feedback.correct: Check that every language choice advances the paragraph’s stance and that the dialogue has a clear function.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Describe the pressure: “In the last minute, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In the last minute of a final, thousands of fans shout at the referee to give a penalty.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give the person’s principle: “As a …, she must …”
discussionPrompts.example: As a referee, she must follow the rules, not the crowd. This principle frames her whole response.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Write a short exchange: “Are you …?” “I …”
discussionPrompts.example: A player shouts, “Are you blind? That was a foul!” The referee calmly answers, “I saw it clearly, and the rules say it was not.”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — End wider: “She was not only … but also …”
discussionPrompts.example: In the end, she was not only fair to both teams but also a good example for the young referees watching the game.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Abraham (pbuh) declare comes from Allah?
beforeYouRead.quote: he declared his belief that both benefit and harm come from Allah

iCan: I can describe how Abraham (pbuh) spoke to his father and his people.
I can explain what an action shows with “In doing so”.
I can describe someone who answers pressure from a clear principle.

groupTask.title: From Tawhid to the First Debates

roles.name: Chapters 1–4 Expert

steps: Read your chapters again. Note two key facts and one phrase that shows whether the book states a fact, reports a source or gives an interpretation, such as “Some sources say” or “We may say that”.
Teach your facts to the group in your own words, then read the sentence from the book that supports each one.
Listen to the others and build one shared timeline from Abraham’s birth to the start of the struggle with his people.
Together, complete this sentence with three reasons, each backed by a quote: Abraham (pbuh) rejected the idols because … For example, he saw that they were “lifeless, silent, and entirely helpless”.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its timeline and its three reasons, and says which of its facts the book states directly and which it reports from sources.
groupTask.solo: Make a timeline of Chapters 1–12 with one event or idea from each chapter, and mark each one as a fact, a report from a source or an interpretation, according to the words the book uses.

pages.title: Speaking to His Father
pages.content:
Abraham (pbuh) felt that it was his duty as a good son to advise his father against this evil so that his father could be saved from Allah’s punishment. He was a wise son, so he did not make his father feel embarrassed, or make fun of his job. He told him that he loved him; in that way, he hoped to increase fatherly love. Then he kindly asked him why he worshipped lifeless statues who could not hear, see, or protect him. Before his father got angry, he quickly added an explanation, as recorded in Surah Maryam, verses 42–48: “He (Abraham) said to his father, ‘O my father, why do you worship what can neither hear, nor see, nor benefit you in any way? O my father, there has come to me knowledge that never came to you. So follow me, and I will guide you along a straight way.

O my father, do not worship Satan. Satan is disobedient to the Most Beneficent (Allah). O my father, I fear that a punishment from the Most Beneficent (Allah) will afflict you, and you become a friend of Satan.’”

vocabulary.definition: Something that you feel you must do because it is right.
Feeling ashamed and uncomfortable in front of others.
The warm affection that a father has for his child.
Refusing to do what one is told to do.
To cause pain, suffering or trouble to someone.

hotspots.title: Gentle Advice
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) advised his father kindly, without mocking his job, and told him that he loved him.

hotspots.title: A Warning About Satan
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) warned his father not to worship Satan, who had disobeyed Allah.

exercises.title: Advice to a Father
exercises.instructions: Put the steps from Chapter 13 in order.
exercises.question: How did Abraham advise his father, step by step?

sequencingItems.text: Abraham feels it is his duty as a good son to advise his father.
Abraham tells his father that he loves him.
Abraham kindly asks why his father worships lifeless statues.
Before his father gets angry, Abraham quickly adds an explanation.

exercises.explanation: Abraham “felt that it was his duty as a good son to advise his father”. He did not embarrass him: “He told him that he loved him”, then “kindly asked him why he worshipped lifeless statues”, and “Before his father got angry, he quickly added an explanation”.

feedback.correct: Well done. Abraham began with duty and love, and only then gave his reasons: a respectful way to speak to a parent.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Look for the order words “Then” and “Before his father got angry”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Fear or Certainty?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the line from Surah Maryam in Chapter 13. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: In “O my father, I fear that a punishment from the Most Beneficent (Allah) will afflict you …”, Abraham presents the punishment as certain.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “I fear that …” frames the future as a worry, not as a fact. Abraham speaks with concern for his father: He warns him about a possible consequence instead of announcing a certain one. This fits the chapter’s picture of a kind, respectful son.

feedback.correct: Correct. “I fear that” expresses concern about a possibility.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the words before “a punishment”. Does “I fear that” state a fact, or a worry?

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose and Reason
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 13 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 13?
