transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) felt that it was his duty as a good son to advise his father against this evil so that his father could be saved from Allah’s punishment.
transformItems.frame: … it was his duty as a good son to advise his father against this evil [blank] his father from Allah’s punishment.

transformItems.source: He was a wise son, so he did not make his father feel embarrassed, or make fun of his job.
transformItems.frame: [blank] a wise son, he did not make his father feel embarrassed, or make fun of his job.

transformItems.source: He told him that he loved him; in that way, he hoped to increase fatherly love.
transformItems.frame: He told him that he loved him, [blank] to increase fatherly love.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So that + could” gives a purpose; when the subject changes to Abraham, “to save / in order to save” is shorter. “…, so …” gives a result; turning the first part into “Being a wise son” or “As he was a wise son” presents it as the reason. “In that way, he hoped …” links a choice to its hoped-for effect; a participle (“hoping to …”) joins the two ideas in one sentence.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the purpose, the reason and the hope.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use to + verb (who saves whom?). Item 2: turn the first clause into a reason. Item 3: use an -ing form of “hope”. Check the first paragraph of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: Asking Without Offending
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each part of Chapter 13.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words fit when Abraham kindly asks his father?

formChoices.sentence: … lifeless statues who could not hear, see, [choice] protect him.
Then he kindly asked him why he [choice] lifeless statues …
Before his father [choice] angry, he quickly added an explanation …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: After “could not”, a list continues with “or”: could not hear, see, or protect. “Nor” is used after “neither” (as in the verse: “can neither hear, nor see, nor benefit you”). A reported question keeps statement word order and moves back in time: “why he worshipped”. After “before” in a past narrative, use the past simple (“got”), not “will”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right negative list, reported question and time clause.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which word continues a list after “not”? Is the question direct or reported? Is the time clause in the past? Check the first paragraph of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: Design a Respectful Persuasion Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about kindly persuading someone you respect.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can you persuade someone without hurting them?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should use language choices to manage both argument and relationship, rather than producing isolated grammar examples.

feedback.correct: Check that your wording explains both what the speaker wants and how the speaker protects the relationship.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say what you hope for: “… so that she can …”
discussionPrompts.example: The speaker hopes that her grandmother will try a hearing aid so that she can enjoy family dinners again. At the moment she often misses the conversation and feels left out.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Choose kind words: “Instead, she will say …; in that way, …”
discussionPrompts.example: She will not say, “You never hear anything.” Instead, she will say that she loves talking with her grandmother; in that way, her grandmother will feel respected.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give reasons in a row: “She can neither … nor …”
discussionPrompts.example: Without help, her grandmother can neither follow the news on the radio nor hear the doorbell. She also struggles to hear her friends on the phone.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Show care, not anger: “I’m worried that …”
discussionPrompts.example: She could say, “I’m worried that you may feel lonely if you miss our conversations.” This sounds like care, not an attack.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Who does Abraham (pbuh) tell his father not to worship?
beforeYouRead.quote: O my father, do not worship Satan.

iCan: I can explain how Abraham (pbuh) advised his father with respect.
I can give reasons in a parallel way with “neither … nor …”.
I can write a polite message that persuades without hurting anyone.

pages.title: Calling People to Reconsider
pages.content: “He (his father) said, ‘Are you rejecting my gods, O Abraham? If you do not stop this, I will stone you. So leave me alone for a while before I punish you.’ Abraham said, ‘Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you; He has been Kind to me. And I will turn away from you, and from what you pray to instead of Allah. And I will pray to my Lord, and I hope I will not be disappointed in my prayer to my Lord.’” Abraham (pbuh) kindly spoke to his father with clear logic and sense. His father’s harsh behavior towards Abraham (pbuh) did not stop him from carrying the message of truth. He was angry and sad to see people bow down before idols; he was determined to put an end to these practices and went to the town to debate with the people. In fact, he knew well that he might face negative consequences. Just as a wise doctor looks for the cause of an illness to find the right cure, or a clever judge questions a suspect to uncover the truth, Abraham (pbuh) questioned them to reveal the reality of their situation.

vocabulary.definition: Cruel, severe and unkind.
Having made a firm decision to do something.
The results of an action, often bad ones.
A person who is thought to have committed a crime.
To stop something completely.

hotspots.title: A Father’s Threat
hotspots.description: Abraham’s (pbuh) father threatened to stone him, but Abraham (pbuh) answered with peace and prayed for his forgiveness.

hotspots.title: Questions Like a Judge
hotspots.description: Like a clever judge questioning a suspect, Abraham (pbuh) asked people questions to reveal the truth.

exercises.title: The Doctor and the Judge
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 14.
exercises.question: Why does the writer compare Abraham to a wise doctor and a clever judge?
options: To show that he healed the sick among his people and cared for them
To show that he asked careful questions to reveal the truth about their beliefs
To show that he wanted to punish the idolaters for their crime against Allah
To show that he worked at the king’s court as a doctor and a judge
exercises.explanation: The chapter says: “Just as a wise doctor looks for the cause of an illness to find the right cure, or a clever judge questions a suspect to uncover the truth, Abraham (pbuh) questioned them to reveal the reality of their situation.” The comparison describes his method, not his job.

feedback.correct: Right. Like a doctor or a judge, Abraham used careful questions to find the real problem.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 14. What do the doctor, the judge and Abraham all do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Threat or Promise?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it a threat or a promise? Put each line from Chapter 14 in the right group.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can “will” carry a threat or a calm promise?

items: If you do not stop this, I will stone you.
So leave me alone for a while before I punish you.
I will ask my Lord to forgive you; He has been Kind to me.
And I will turn away from you, and from what you pray to instead of Allah.
I hope I will not be disappointed in my prayer to my Lord.

Threat or demand (the father): If you do not stop this, I will stone you.
So leave me alone for a while before I punish you.
Promise or hope (Abraham): I will ask my Lord to forgive you; He has been Kind to me.
And I will turn away from you, and from what you pray to instead of Allah.
I hope I will not be disappointed in my prayer to my Lord.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The father uses a first conditional (If + present, will + verb) to threaten, and an imperative to demand. Abraham answers with “will” as well, but for his own future actions: He promises to pray for his father’s forgiveness and to turn away. “I hope …” shows a hopeful stance, not certainty. The same grammar serves opposite purposes.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the father’s threats from Abraham’s promises and hope.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Who is the action aimed at, and is it harm or kindness? Check the verses at the start of Chapter 14.

languageFocusExercises.title: Knowing the Risk
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 14. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “In fact, he knew well that he might face negative consequences.” What does “might” show about Abraham’s decision to debate with the people?
options: The consequences were possible, not certain, and he went to the town knowing this.
He was sure that he would be punished, so he went to the town to accept it.
He had the king’s permission to face the consequences in the town.
The consequences had already happened before he went to the town.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Might” expresses a possibility that is not certain. Together with “he knew well” and “he was determined”, it presents Abraham’s persistence as a conscious choice: He knew there was a real risk and still went to debate. “In fact” adds this as an important, perhaps surprising, point.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Might” marks a possible risk that he chose to accept.
feedback.incorrect: Does “might” show certainty, permission or possibility? Read the sentences before it about Abraham’s determination.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reading the Comparison
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each part of the comparison at the end of Chapter 14 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the comparison explain Abraham’s way of questioning?

matchingPairs.left: looks for the cause of an illness
matchingPairs.right: searches for the root of a problem
so that the problem can be properly treated
asks someone questions to test their story
to find out what really happened

matchingPairs.left: to reveal the reality of their situation
matchingPairs.right: to make the people see their true position

correctAnswer.looks for the cause of an illness: searches for the root of a problem
correctAnswer.to find the right cure: so that the problem can be properly treated
correctAnswer.questions a suspect: asks someone questions to test their story
correctAnswer.to uncover the truth: to find out what really happened
correctAnswer.to reveal the reality of their situation: to make the people see their true position

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The sentence is built as “Just as A …, or B …, C …”. The doctor and the judge both ask questions for a purpose (to find the right cure, to uncover the truth), and Abraham does the same: He questions the people “to reveal the reality of their situation”. The comparison presents his questions as a careful method, not as an attack.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the comparison from the doctor and the judge to Abraham.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 14. Each person asks or looks for something with a purpose (to + verb). What is each purpose?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Risk-Aware Reasoning Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who keeps going despite a risk.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the person do, and what might happen?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should show why the person acts, what risk remains possible, what they commit to doing, and how the analogy clarifies the reasoning process.

feedback.correct: Check that each grammar choice contributes to stance, consequence, commitment or reasoning rather than appearing as an isolated example.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Give a condition: “If …, … will …”
discussionPrompts.example: If the factory continues to pour waste into the river, the fish will die. This future result depends on what the factory chooses now.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what the person will do: “She will … . She will also …”
discussionPrompts.example: The journalist will interview the families who live by the river. She will also send water samples to a laboratory.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Name a risk: “She might …”
discussionPrompts.example: Even if she continues, she might lose her job or receive angry calls from the company.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Compare: “Just as a doctor …, … to uncover …”
discussionPrompts.example: Just as a doctor runs tests to find the cause of an illness, a journalist asks questions to uncover the cause of the pollution.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Abraham’s father threaten to do?
beforeYouRead.quote: If you do not stop this, I will stone you.

iCan: I can tell how Abraham’s father answered and why Abraham (pbuh) went on.
I can explain an idea with a comparison that begins with “Just as”.
I can write about someone who continues a hard task despite the risks.

pages.title: Debating the Idolaters
pages.content:
“Do the idols see you when you bow down before them? Do they benefit you in any way?” They quickly tried to defend their beliefs. They argued that they knew the idols were lifeless but that their forefathers had worshipped them; to them, this confirmed their belief. Abraham (pbuh) explained that their forefathers had been wrong. This angered them and they responded: “Are you criticizing our gods and our forefathers? Or are you just joking?” Abraham (pbuh) showed no fear as he replied: “I am serious. I come to you with a true religion. I have been sent with guidance from our Lord, Who alone is worthy of worship. He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and He regulates all affairs of life, unlike the speechless idols which are just stone and wood.” To persuade them that the idols could not harm him, he challenged: “I have already criticized them; see if they have any power to harm me by now!”

Abraham (pbuh) did not give up arguing with the idolaters.

vocabulary.definition: To protect something from attack by arguing in its favor.
Saying what is wrong with someone or something.
Controls and organizes how something works.
To make someone agree to something by giving good reasons.
Meaning what you say; not joking.

hotspots.title: The Forefathers’ Excuse
hotspots.description: The idolaters admitted that the idols were lifeless but said that their forefathers had worshipped them.

hotspots.title: A Bold Challenge
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) had criticized the idols openly and challenged the people to see whether they could harm him.

exercises.title: The People’s Defense
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 15.
exercises.question: The people defended their idols by saying that the idols could see them when they bowed down.
exercises.explanation: The people did not claim that. “They argued that they knew the idols were lifeless but that their forefathers had worshipped them; to them, this confirmed their belief.”

feedback.correct: Correct. They admitted the idols were lifeless and relied only on what their forefathers did.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of Chapter 15. What did the people say they knew about the idols, and whose example did they follow?

languageFocusExercises.title: Testing or Defending?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the lines from Chapter 15: Abraham testing the idols, or the people defending them.
languageFocusExercises.question: How do the two sides use questions differently?

items: Do the idols see you when you bow down before them?
Do they benefit you in any way?
see if they have any power to harm me by now!
They quickly tried to defend their beliefs.
Are you criticizing our gods and our forefathers?
Or are you just joking?

Abraham tests the idols: Do the idols see you when you bow down before them?
Do they benefit you in any way?
see if they have any power to harm me by now!
The people defend their belief: They quickly tried to defend their beliefs.
Are you criticizing our gods and our forefathers?

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Abraham’s questions are rhetorical tests: They point to things people can check (Do the idols see? Do they benefit you?), and the expected answer is “No”. His challenge “see if …” turns the claim into an observable test. The people’s questions do not answer the test; they change the topic to disrespect (“criticizing our forefathers”) or try to reduce the challenge to a joke.

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham’s questions test the idols; the people’s questions avoid the test.
feedback.incorrect: Ask whether each line invites people to check the idols’ power, or protects the belief from being checked. Read Chapter 15 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Manner and Purpose
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 15 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 15?

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) showed no fear as he replied: …
transformItems.frame: [blank], Abraham (pbuh) replied: …

transformItems.source: To persuade them that the idols could not harm him, he challenged: …
transformItems.frame: He challenged them [blank] them that the idols could not harm him.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As he replied” describes the manner of the reply; a participle phrase (“Showing no fear”) or an adverb (“Fearlessly”) says the same more compactly. A to-infinitive of purpose can come at the start (“To persuade them …, he challenged”) or after the main clause (“He challenged them to persuade them …”); “in order to” makes the purpose even clearer.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the manner and the purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: describe how he replied in a short phrase. Item 2: keep the purpose with to + verb. Check the first paragraph of Chapter 15.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reporting the Argument
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the report of the argument?

errorItems.sentence: They argued that they knew the idols were lifeless but that their forefathers have worshipped them; to them, this confirmed their belief.
Abraham (pbuh) explained them that their forefathers had been wrong.
Abraham (pbuh) did not give up to argue with the idolaters.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In a report in the past, an action that happened even earlier takes the past perfect: “their forefathers had worshipped them”. “Explain” cannot take the person directly as its object: Say “explained that …” or “explained (something) to them”. “Give up” is followed by -ing: “did not give up arguing”. The people’s argument puts tradition (“but …”) against a fact they admit.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the earlier past, the verb pattern and the -ing form.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which action happened earlier? Can “explain” take the person directly as its object? Which form follows “give up”? Check Chapter 15.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build an Evidence-vs-Tradition Argument
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a rule people keep only because it is old.
languageFocusExercises.question: Does the old rule really work?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should acknowledge what people believe, distinguish inherited practice from evidence, test the claim through questions, define an alternative clearly, and conclude in a controlled way.

feedback.correct: Check that every structure contributes to the argument rather than appearing as an isolated grammar example.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Ask two testing questions: “Does … help …? Does it …?”
discussionPrompts.example: Does wearing a tie in hot weather help students learn? Does it make the school safer?

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Admit a fact: “Although …, the rule has never changed.”
discussionPrompts.example: Although everyone knows that the classrooms are very hot in June, the rule has never changed. The evidence says one thing, but the old practice says another.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Describe a better choice: “A better choice is … which …”
discussionPrompts.example: A better choice is a summer uniform which keeps students cool and still looks smart.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Suggest a test: “We could test whether …”
discussionPrompts.example: We could test whether students concentrate better without ties for one month. If their marks and behavior stay the same or improve, the tie rule becomes harder to defend.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What reason did the idolaters give for their belief?
options: The idols had spoken to them.
Their forefathers had worshipped the idols.
beforeYouRead.quote: their forefathers had worshipped them

iCan: I can explain how the idolaters defended their idols.
I can admit a fact with “although” and still disagree.
I can test an old habit by asking what we can observe.

pages.title: The Idols or the Creator
pages.content: Allah said in Surah ash-Shu’ara, verses 69–82: “And describe to them the story of Abraham. When he said to his father and his people, ‘What do you worship?’ They said, ‘We worship idols, and we remain faithful to them.’ He said, ‘Do they hear you when you pray? Or do they benefit you, or harm you?’ They said, ‘But we found our ancestors doing so.’ He said, ‘Have you considered what you worship— You and your ancient ancestors? They are enemies to me, but not so the Lord of the Worlds. He who created me, and guides me. He who feeds me, and waters me. And when I get sick, He heals me. He who makes me die, and then revives me. He who, I hope, will forgive my sins on the Day of Resurrection?’” He explained to them the beauty of Allah’s creation, His power, and His wisdom. Idol worship is hated by Allah, as Allah is the Lord of the universe Who created mankind, offers guidance, provides human beings with food and drink and heals the sick.

vocabulary.definition: Belonging to a time very long ago.
Wrong actions that break Allah’s law.
Everything that exists, including all stars and planets.
Gives people what they need.
Makes someone who is ill healthy again.

hotspots.title: What Do You Worship?
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) asked his people whether their idols could hear them, help them or harm them.

hotspots.title: The Lord of the Worlds
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) described Allah as the One who creates, guides, feeds, heals and brings the dead back to life.

exercises.title: The Lord of the Worlds
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 16.
exercises.question: After the verses, what reason does the writer give for why Allah hates idol worship?
options: The idols could harm the people who did not pray to them or bring them offerings.
Allah alone created mankind, guides them, gives them food and drink and heals the sick.
The people’s ancestors had never worshipped idols before, so it was a new and strange custom.
exercises.explanation: The writer says: “Idol worship is hated by Allah, as Allah is the Lord of the universe Who created mankind, offers guidance, provides human beings with food and drink and heals the sick.” The word “as” gives the reason.

feedback.correct: Correct. Worship belongs to the One who creates, guides, feeds and heals, not to lifeless idols.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 16. Find the word “as” and read what comes after it.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Abraham Says About His Lord
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line from the verses with what it says about the Lord.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do the “He who …” lines say about the Lord?

matchingHeadings.right: What it says about the Lord

matchingPairs.left: He who created me, and guides me.
matchingPairs.right: the Creator, Who also shows the way

matchingPairs.left: He who feeds me, and waters me.
matchingPairs.right: the Provider of food and drink

matchingPairs.left: And when I get sick, He heals me.
matchingPairs.right: the One Who restores health

matchingPairs.left: He who makes me die, and then revives me.
matchingPairs.right: the One Who has power over death and new life

matchingPairs.left: He who, I hope, will forgive my sins on the Day of Resurrection?
matchingPairs.right: the One Whose pardon is hoped for on the Last Day

the Creator, Who also shows the way
the Provider of food and drink
correctAnswer.He who makes me die, and then revives me: the One Who has power over death and new life
correctAnswer.He who, I hope, will forgive my sins on: the One Whose pardon is hoped for on the Last Day

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The verses repeat “He who …” to build one long description: Each line adds a new attribute in parallel form. The repetition contrasts with the idols, which “do not hear” and cannot benefit or harm. In the last line, “I hope” adds Abraham’s personal stance: Forgiveness is hoped for, not claimed.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the chain from creation to forgiveness.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb in each line (created, feeds, heals, makes … die, forgive) and find the matching attribute.

languageFocusExercises.title: Changing the Focus
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each part of the last sentence of Chapter 16. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say the last sentence of Chapter 16?

transformItems.source: Idol worship is hated by Allah, as Allah is the Lord of the universe …
transformItems.frame: Allah [blank] idol worship, as He is the Lord of the universe …

transformItems.source: … Who created mankind, offers guidance, provides human beings with food and drink and heals the sick.
transformItems.frame: … Who created mankind, offers guidance, provides [blank] human beings and heals the sick.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive “Idol worship is hated by Allah” keeps idol worship as the topic; the active “Allah hates idol worship” makes Allah the topic. “Provide” has two patterns: provide someone with something, or provide something to/for someone. The narrator’s sentence restates the verses in plain prose: creation, guidance, food and drink, and healing.

feedback.correct: Well done. You changed the focus and the verb pattern correctly.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: make Allah the subject of an active verb. Item 2: when the thing comes first after “provides”, which preposition comes before the person?

languageFocusExercises.title: One Clear Exception
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the line from the verses in Chapter 16. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “They are enemies to me, but not so the Lord of the Worlds.” What does “but not so” mean here?
options: The Lord of the Worlds is not an enemy to him; He is the one exception.
The Lord of the Worlds is not as great as people think.
The idols are not really enemies to him.
The Lord of the Worlds is also an enemy, but a less serious one.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So” replaces the words already said (“an enemy to me”), and “but not so” excludes one case: All the things they worship are enemies to Abraham, except the Lord of the Worlds. The line sets a strong contrast between the idols and the Lord, which the “He who …” lines then explain.

feedback.correct: Correct. “But not so” makes the Lord of the Worlds the exception.
feedback.incorrect: What does “so” stand for here? Read the words just before it: “They are enemies to me …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Cohesive Evaluation Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a school habit that may need to change.
languageFocusExercises.question: Is there a better way to do it?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should move logically from questioning to evaluation, use repeated clause structure for cohesion, and keep strong claims separate from local stance markers.

feedback.correct: Check that each language choice contributes to the argument and that your stance markers apply only where intended.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Ask two questions about its effects: “Does … help …?”
discussionPrompts.example: Does printing every worksheet help students remember more? Does it really save the teachers’ time?

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give the old reason: “We have always done it this way.”
discussionPrompts.example: Some teachers say, “We have always done it this way, and it works.” This is a conventional reason, not evidence.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Describe a better way: “… which …, that …, and which …”
discussionPrompts.example: The alternative is a shared online folder which every student can open, that teachers can update in seconds, and which helps students who often lose their papers.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Separate facts from hopes: “I expect that …”
discussionPrompts.example: “The school prints five thousand pages a week” is a firm fact. “I expect that an online folder would save money” is only an expectation.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What do the people say they do with the idols?
beforeYouRead.quote: We worship idols, and we remain faithful to them.

iCan: I can explain the questions Abraham (pbuh) asked about the idols.
I can describe something with a chain of “who” or “which” clauses.
I can write a fair evaluation of a habit or a rule.

pages.title: The Empty Temple
pages.content:
Allah also will cause them to die and bring them back to life again. However, idolaters would not give up but held on tightly to their idols. Abraham (pbuh) left his father’s house and distanced himself from his people and what they worshipped. Actually, he decided to do something shocking to show their error. He knew that there was going to be a great celebration outside the town. All the people would attend it. Abraham (pbuh) waited until the city was empty, then cautiously made his way to the temple. The streets leading to it and the temple itself were empty. The priests had also gone to the festival outside the city. Abraham (pbuh) went there with a sharp axe. He looked at the stone and wood statues of the gods and at the food put in front of them as offerings. He approached one of the statues and asked: “The food in front of you is getting cold.

Why don’t you eat?” The statue kept silent and rigid.

vocabulary.definition: Refused to let go of something.
Kept away from someone or something.
Carefully, trying to avoid danger or being noticed.
Things such as food given to a god as an act of worship.
Stiff and unable to move or bend.

hotspots.title: An Empty City
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) waited until everyone, even the priests, had gone to the festival outside the town.

hotspots.title: Food for the Idols
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) asked a statue why it did not eat the food in front of it, but it stayed silent.

exercises.title: The Day of the Festival
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 17.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham go to the temple on the day of the great celebration?
options: The priests had asked him to bring food offerings to the gods.
His father had asked him to guard the temple during the festival.
Everyone, even the priests, was at the festival outside the town.
exercises.explanation: Abraham knew that “All the people would attend it.” He “waited until the city was empty”, and “The priests had also gone to the festival outside the city.” So he could reach the temple without being stopped.

feedback.correct: Right. He chose a time when the temple was empty so that he could carry out his plan.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 17. Where were the people and the priests during the celebration?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Question That Is Not a Question
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read Abraham’s words at the end of Chapter 17. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The food in front of you is getting cold. Why don’t you eat?” Why does Abraham ask the statue this question?
options: It is an ironic test: He knows the statue cannot eat, so its silence exposes its helplessness.
He really wants to know whether the statues eat the offerings, because he has never seen them eat before.
He is politely offering the food to the statue, as the people did during their ceremonies.
He is asking the priests why the food is still there after the festival has started.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A rhetorical question is not a request for information. Abraham already knows the answer, so the question works as irony and as a test. The next sentence gives the result: “The statue kept silent and rigid.” The silence becomes evidence against the idols.

feedback.correct: Correct. The question is an ironic test, not a real request.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence after the question. What happens, and what does Abraham already know about the statues?

languageFocusExercises.title: Back to Abraham’s Thoughts
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write each idea from Chapter 17 as Abraham’s own thought.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Abraham think would happen?

transformItems.source: He knew that there was going to be a great celebration outside the town.
transformItems.frame: He thought, “There [blank] a great celebration outside the town.”

transformItems.source: All the people would attend it.
transformItems.frame: He thought, “All the people [blank] it.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The narrator tells the story in the past, so Abraham’s knowledge about a later event appears as “was going to” and “would”: the future seen from the past. In his own mind at that moment, the same ideas are simply future: “is going to be”, “will attend”. His knowledge of the festival is part of his plan.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved the future-in-the-past back to Abraham’s present viewpoint.
feedback.incorrect: Change “was going to” to “is going to” and “would” to “will”. Check the first paragraph of Chapter 17.

languageFocusExercises.title: Timing the Plan
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Abraham’s plan?

errorItems.sentence: Actually, he decided doing something shocking to show their error.
Abraham (pbuh) waited until the city will be empty, then cautiously made his way to the temple.
The priests have also gone to the festival outside the city.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Decide” is followed by to + verb: “decided to do”. In a past narrative, a time clause after “until” takes the past simple, not “will/would”: “waited until the city was empty”. The past perfect “had also gone” shows that the priests left before Abraham arrived, so the temple was empty.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the decision, the time clause and the earlier past.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which form follows “decide”? Which tense follows “until” in a past story? Did the priests leave before or after Abraham came? Check Chapter 17.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Plan-and-Test Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who plans a test to show a problem.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is the plan, and what does the test show?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make the time relations and the purpose of each action clear while using the final question as part of the argument rather than as a request for unknown information.

feedback.correct: Check that each tense and connector has a clear discourse function and that the test leads naturally to your conclusion.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Show that people will not listen: “Even after …, many people kept saying …”
discussionPrompts.example: Even after a critical review, many people kept saying that the cheap phone charger was perfectly safe.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what was going to happen: “She knew that … was going to …”
discussionPrompts.example: The engineer knew that the company was going to show the charger at a fair the next month. Everyone would be watching.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Say what happened earlier: “Before …, she had already …”
discussionPrompts.example: Before the fair began, she had already measured the charger’s temperature in her laboratory.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Ask a testing question: “If it is so …, why …?”
discussionPrompts.example: At the fair, she asked, “If it is so safe, why is it too hot to touch after ten minutes?” The heat was a result everyone could see.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. What did Abraham (pbuh) take to the temple?
beforeYouRead.quote: Abraham (pbuh) went there with a sharp axe.

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) found the temple empty.
I can talk about a plan that was going to happen and wait “until” the right moment.
I can describe a plan to test an idea.

pages.title: Breaking the Idols
pages.content: Abraham (pbuh) asked all the other statues around him: “Will you not eat of the offering before you?” (Surah as-Saffat: 91). He was mocking them, for he knew they would not eat. He once again asked them: “What is the matter with you that you do not speak?” (Surah as-Saffat: 92). He then raised his axe and started smashing the false gods worshipped by the people. He destroyed them all except one. On its neck, he hung the axe. He left the temple. He had fulfilled his duty to show his people a practical proof of their foolishness in worshipping something other than Allah. When the people returned, they were shocked to see their gods smashed into pieces, spread all over the temple. They tried to find out who had done that to their idols and Abraham (pbuh)'s name came to their minds. Allah said in Surah al-Anbiya, verses 59–67: “They said, ‘Who did this to our gods? He is certainly one of the wrongdoers.’”

vocabulary.definition: Laughing at someone or something in an unkind way.
To break something violently into many pieces.
Beings or things that people wrongly worship as divine.
A lack of good sense or judgement.
People who act unjustly and harm others.

hotspots.title: The Axe on the Idol’s Neck
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) broke all the idols except the biggest one and hung the axe on its neck.

hotspots.title: Shock in the Temple
hotspots.description: The people returned and were shocked to find their gods in pieces all over the temple.

exercises.title: In the Temple
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 18 in order.
exercises.question: What happened in the temple and after it?

sequencingItems.text: Abraham asks the statues why they do not eat or speak.
Abraham smashes all the statues except one.
Abraham hangs the axe on the neck of the statue he left.
Abraham leaves the temple.
The people return and think of Abraham’s name.

exercises.explanation: First Abraham spoke to the silent statues. “He then raised his axe and started smashing the false gods … He destroyed them all except one. On its neck, he hung the axe. He left the temple.” When the people returned, “Abraham (pbuh)’s name came to their minds.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You followed Abraham from his questions to the statues to the people’s return.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Chapter 18 from the beginning: First his questions, then the axe, then his leaving, and finally the people’s return.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “For” Introduce?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 18. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: In “He was mocking them, for he knew they would not eat”, the word “for” introduces the purpose of his mocking.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: In formal writing, “for” + clause gives a reason, like “because”: he was mocking them because he knew they would not eat. It does not express a purpose. The reason makes the irony of his question clear.

feedback.correct: Correct. “For” here means “because”; it gives a reason.
feedback.incorrect: Replace “for” with “because” and with “in order to”. Which one keeps the meaning of the sentence?

languageFocusExercises.title: Exception and Completion
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each part of Chapter 18 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 18?

transformItems.source: He destroyed them all except one.
transformItems.frame: He destroyed all of them; only one [blank].

transformItems.source: He left the temple. He had fulfilled his duty to show his people a practical proof of their foolishness …
transformItems.frame: [blank] his duty to show his people a practical proof of their foolishness, he left the temple.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “All except one” names a whole group and removes one member; the same idea can be split into two statements (“all of them … only one remained”). The past perfect “had fulfilled” shows that his task was already complete when he left. A perfect participle (“Having fulfilled …”) or “After -ing” puts the completed task first.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the exception and the order of events.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: what happened to the one statue? Item 2: use a form that shows the task was complete before he left. Check the first paragraph of Chapter 18.

languageFocusExercises.title: After the People Returned
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 18 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Abraham do, and how did the people react?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: On its neck, he [blank] the axe. … When the people returned, they were shocked [blank] their gods smashed into pieces, spread all over the temple. They tried to find out who [blank] that to their idols …
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Hang” has two past forms: “hung” for objects (he hung the axe) and “hanged” only for executing a person. Adjectives of feeling are followed by to + verb: “shocked to see”. “Who had done that” uses the past perfect because the damage happened before the people returned and asked.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right past form, the feeling pattern and the earlier past.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is an object or a person being hung? Which form follows “shocked”? Did the destruction happen before the people asked? Check the middle of Chapter 18.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write an Evidence-Building Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who tests a false claim in an advert.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can you show that a claim is false?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make each discourse move purposeful: The rhetorical question tests a claim, the reason explains the test, the exception matters to the logic, the past perfect clarifies sequence, and the quotation is explicitly sourced rather than blended into the narrator’s voice.

feedback.correct: Check that the quotation is clearly attributed and that each connector changes the relationship between ideas.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Ask a question you know the answer to: “Has anyone ever …?”
discussionPrompts.example: “Has anyone ever grown new hair just by using this shampoo?” The speaker already knows that the answer is no.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give the reason for asking: “She asks this, for …”
discussionPrompts.example: She asks this question, for the advert promises results that nobody has shown.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Add one exception: “She tested every … except one because …”
discussionPrompts.example: She tested every product on the shelf except one because that one made no claims on its label. This shows that she was testing claims, not products.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Name the source: “According to a report by …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: I will write: “According to a report by the national health office, none of the shampoos stopped hair loss.” The source is named clearly.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did the people say about the one who broke the idols?
options: “He is certainly one of the wrongdoers.”
beforeYouRead.quote: He is certainly one of the wrongdoers.

iCan: I can tell what Abraham (pbuh) did to the idols and what the people saw.
I can say what had happened before a later reaction.
I can support a claim with a short quote and name its source.

pages.title: Questioned Before the People
pages.content:
“They said, ‘We heard a youth mentioning them. He is called Abraham.’ They said, ‘Bring him before the eyes of the people, so that they may witness.’ They said, ‘Are you the one who did this to our gods, O Abraham?’ He said, ‘But it was this biggest of them that did it. Ask them if they can speak.’ Then they turned to one another and said, ‘You yourselves are the wrongdoers.’ But they reverted to their old ideas: ‘You certainly know that these do not speak.’ He said, ‘Do you worship, instead of Allah, what can neither benefit you in anything, nor harm you? Shame on you, and on what you worship instead of Allah. Do you not understand?’” They furiously demanded that Abraham (pbuh) be arrested and judged. Abraham (pbuh) did not resist. This was exactly what he was aiming for, so that he could demonstrate to them in public that their beliefs were foolish. At the trial, they asked him if he was responsible for breaking the idols.

Smiling, he told them to ask the biggest idol which was still undamaged.

vocabulary.definition: To see something happen with your own eyes.
Asked for something firmly, as if it were a right.
To fight back or refuse to accept something.
A formal process in which a court decides whether someone is guilty.
Not broken or harmed in any way.

hotspots.title: Ask the Biggest Idol
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) smiled and told them to ask the biggest idol, which was still undamaged.

hotspots.title: A Public Trial
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) did not resist his arrest because a trial let him show everyone that their beliefs were foolish.

exercises.title: No Resistance
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 19.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham not resist when the people demanded that he be arrested and judged?
options: He wanted to blame the biggest idol at the trial and escape punishment.
A public trial let him show everyone that their beliefs were foolish.
He hoped the king would forgive him and let him go if he did not fight.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says: “Abraham (pbuh) did not resist. This was exactly what he was aiming for, so that he could demonstrate to them in public that their beliefs were foolish.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The trial gave Abraham the public stage he wanted for his argument.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentences after “Abraham (pbuh) did not resist” in Chapter 19. What was he aiming for?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Lasting Change?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the lines from Surah al-Anbiya in Chapter 19. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: The words “You yourselves are the wrongdoers.” show that the people changed their minds for good.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The people’s words to one another show a moment of self-correction. The very next sentence reverses it: “But they reverted to their old ideas”. “But” and the verb “reverted” (went back) mark the return to their earlier position, which is why Abraham answers with more questions.

feedback.correct: Correct. The self-correction was only a moment; they soon reverted.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence after “You yourselves are the wrongdoers.” Which linking word and which verb show what happened next?

languageFocusExercises.title: Reporting the Trial
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about the trial?

errorItems.sentence: At the trial, they asked him if was he responsible for breaking the idols.
Smiling, he told them ask the biggest idol which was still undamaged.
They furiously demanded that Abraham (pbuh) be arrest and judged.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses if/whether + statement order: “asked him if he was …”. A reported instruction uses tell + person + to + verb: “told them to ask”. After “demand that”, formal English uses be + past participle for a passive: “that Abraham be arrested and judged”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the question, the instruction and the demand.
feedback.incorrect: Check the word order after “if”, the form after “told them”, and the passive after “be”. Then read the end of Chapter 19.

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose Behind the Calm
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 19 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 19?

transformItems.source: This was exactly what he was aiming for, so that he could demonstrate to them in public that their beliefs were foolish.
transformItems.frame: This was exactly what he was aiming for: He wanted [blank] to them in public that their beliefs were foolish.

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) did not resist.
transformItems.frame: Abraham (pbuh) [blank] no resistance.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So that + could” gives the purpose of accepting the arrest; “he wanted to demonstrate …” states the same aim directly. The verb “resist” can become the noun “resistance” in a fixed phrase: offer/put up/show no resistance. The narrator shows that Abraham’s calm was part of a plan: A public trial gave him a public audience.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the purpose and found a natural verb for “resistance”.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use want + to + verb. Item 2: which verb goes with “no resistance”? Check the last paragraph of Chapter 19.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Public Contradiction Test
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a public claim that someone tests.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can you test a claim in front of everyone?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make the language do argumentative work: The condition tests the claim, the reversal shows a change in stance, the purpose clause explains the speaker’s strategy, and the final rhetorical question crystallizes the contradiction.

feedback.correct: Check that every connector changes the relationship between ideas and that the final question is rhetorical, not a request for unknown information.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Open with a direct question: “Did your … really …?”
discussionPrompts.example: A student stands up in the school assembly and asks, “Did your app really raise our marks, as you claim?”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Test it with “if”: “If …, then …”
discussionPrompts.example: “If the app works, the students who used it should have better marks than those who did not.” This test makes the claim face its own logic.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show a short change of mind: “For a moment, … . But then …”
discussionPrompts.example: For a moment, the app’s supporters admit that the results are mixed. But then they go back to their old claim that the app was a success.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Say why you go on: “… so that everyone can see …”
discussionPrompts.example: The student continues the discussion so that everyone can see the real numbers. Without public evidence, the claim would never be checked.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: At the trial, what did Abraham (pbuh) tell the people to do?
beforeYouRead.quote: he told them to ask the biggest idol which was still undamaged

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) was questioned in front of the people.
I can test a claim with “if” and give a purpose with “so that”.
I can show how a group changes its mind and then goes back.

pages.title: The Decision to Burn Abraham
pages.content: He told them that it must be the culprit! They replied that he knew well that the idol could not speak or move. These words gave Abraham (pbuh) the chance to show the foolishness of worshipping these lifeless objects. They had no answer for Abraham (pbuh). In fact, they realized the stupidity of their beliefs; however, their arrogance would not allow them to admit their foolishness. All they could do was use their authority as tyrants to punish Abraham (pbuh). They kept him in chains and planned their revenge. Anger was burning in their hearts. They agreed that Abraham (pbuh) should be burned alive. They decided to throw Abraham (pbuh) into the biggest fire they could build. All the citizens were ordered to gather wood as a service to their gods. For several days they collected fuel. They dug a deep pit, filled it with firewood, and set it on fire. They brought a catapult with which to throw Abraham (pbuh) into the fire. Abraham (pbuh) was put on the catapult; his hands and feet were tied.

vocabulary.definition: The person who is responsible for a crime or wrong action.
Too much pride that makes a person unwilling to accept that they are wrong.
To accept that something is true, often unwillingly.
Rulers who use their power in a cruel and unfair way.
Harm done to someone as a punishment for harm they have done.

hotspots.title: Pride over Truth
hotspots.description: The people knew their beliefs were foolish, but their arrogance stopped them from admitting it.

hotspots.title: Preparing the Fire
hotspots.description: The citizens gathered wood for days and filled a deep pit to burn Abraham (pbuh) alive.

exercises.title: After the Trial
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 20.
exercises.question: Why did the people decide to punish Abraham instead of answering him?
options: They had no answer, and their arrogance would not let them admit their foolishness.
Abraham refused to answer their questions at the trial and stayed silent.
They proved that the biggest idol had broken the others, so Abraham was lying to them.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says: “They had no answer for Abraham (pbuh). In fact, they realized the stupidity of their beliefs; however, their arrogance would not allow them to admit their foolishness. All they could do was use their authority as tyrants to punish Abraham (pbuh).”

feedback.correct: Right. When they could not answer the argument, they used power instead of honesty.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of Chapter 20. Look for the word “however” and what stopped the people from admitting the truth.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Must” Mean Here?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from the start of Chapter 20. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “He told them that it must be the culprit!” What does “must” express?
options: A conclusion presented as the only logical one — said ironically because Abraham knew the idol could not act.
An obligation: The idol had to accept the blame for the broken idols because it was the biggest and the most important one.
Uncertainty: Abraham was not sure who had broken the idols, so he gave the people his best guess.
A fact that the idol itself had admitted when the people asked it who had broken the other idols.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Must be” is used for a strong conclusion (deduction), not only for obligation. Abraham uses it ironically: If the idols were gods, the biggest idol must be the one who did it. The people’s answer — the idol “could not speak or move” — shows that their own logic has failed.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Must” marks a strong, ironic deduction.
feedback.incorrect: Is Abraham giving an order, or drawing a conclusion? Read the people’s reply in the next sentence.

languageFocusExercises.title: From Argument to Force
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 20 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What could the people do, and what did they decide?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: All they [blank] do was use their authority as tyrants to punish Abraham (pbuh). … They decided [blank] Abraham (pbuh) into the biggest fire they could build. … They [blank] a deep pit, filled it with firewood, and set it on fire.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “All they could do was …” narrows their options to one: They had no argument left, only force. “Should” would give advice, not ability. “Decide” is followed by to + verb (“decided to throw”). “Dig” is irregular: dig – dug – dug.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed the narrowed choice, the decision and the preparation.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is the first gap about ability or advice? Which form follows “decided”? What is the past of “dig”? Check Chapter 20.

languageFocusExercises.title: Recognition, Refusal and Orders
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 20 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 20?

transformItems.source: In fact, they realized the stupidity of their beliefs; however, their arrogance would not allow them to admit their foolishness.
transformItems.frame: [blank] they realized the stupidity of their beliefs, their arrogance would not allow them to admit their foolishness.

transformItems.source: All the citizens were ordered to gather wood as a service to their gods.
transformItems.frame: They [blank] to gather wood as a service to their gods.

transformItems.source: They agreed that Abraham (pbuh) should be burned alive.
transformItems.frame: They agreed [blank] alive.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “…; however, …” sets two facts side by side; “Although …, …” puts the recognition in a concession clause and makes the refusal the main point. The passive “were ordered” hides who gave the order and stresses the command; the active version needs an object (ordered all the citizens to …). “Agree that … should be …” can become “agree to + verb”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the contrast, the order and the decision.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use a concession word and drop “however”. Item 2: add the object after “ordered”. Item 3: use agree + to + verb. Check Chapter 20.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write Recognition Without Admission
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a group that will not admit a mistake.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the group know, and what does it do?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should clearly separate what the group recognizes from what it is willing to admit, then show how the language shifts from reasoning to authority and organized action.

feedback.correct: Check that “must” signals inference, “however” creates a genuine reversal, the passive hides or backgrounds the commander, and the final purpose expression explains the action.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Draw a strong conclusion: “The plan must be weak because …”
discussionPrompts.example: The plan for the new car park must be weak because the experts found three serious problems in it.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show what they knew but would not admit: “In fact, … . However, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In fact, the committee recognized that the park was more useful than a car park. However, they refused to admit that their plan had been a mistake.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show their only choice: “All they could do was … . They decided to …”
discussionPrompts.example: All they could do was use their power to vote again. They decided to keep the plan without further discussion.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Give the order and its aim: “The workers were ordered to … to …”
discussionPrompts.example: The workers were ordered to start building on Monday. This was done to finish the project before the next election.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did the people decide to do to Abraham (pbuh)?
beforeYouRead.quote: They agreed that Abraham (pbuh) should be burned alive.

iCan: I can explain why the people decided to burn Abraham (pbuh).
I can show that a group saw the truth but refused to admit it.
I can report a group’s decision and its purpose.

pages.title: The Coolness of the Fire
pages.content:
The fire was ready, with its flames reaching the sky. The people stood away from the pit because of the great heat. Then, the chief priest gave his order to throw Abraham (pbuh) into the fire. The angel Gabriel came near Abraham (pbuh) and asked him: “O Abraham, do you wish for anything?” Abraham (pbuh) replied: “Nothing from you.” The catapult was fired, and Abraham (pbuh) was thrown into the fire. But his fall into the fire was like going down into a cool garden. The rising flames were still there, but they did not burn him, for Allah commanded: “O fire! Be coolness and safety for Abraham” (Surah al-Anbiya: 69). The fire obeyed the order of Allah. It became cool and safe for Abraham (pbuh). It only burned his ropes, and he sat in the middle of the fire as if he were sitting in a garden. He thanked Allah, with a heart full of His love and trust in Him.

There was no fear or worry. The air became more pleasant as the fire was turned into coolness.

vocabulary.definition: The bright, hot parts of a fire that rise into the air.
A large, deep hole in the ground.
A machine used in the past to throw heavy objects over a long distance.
Moving or growing upwards.
A pleasant, slightly cold quality.

hotspots.title: Nothing from You
hotspots.description: When the angel Gabriel asked whether he wished for anything, Abraham (pbuh) replied that he wanted nothing from him.

hotspots.title: Like a Cool Garden
hotspots.description: Allah ordered the fire to be cool and safe, so it burned only Abraham’s (pbuh) ropes.

exercises.title: Before the Fire
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 21.
exercises.question: When the angel Gabriel asked Abraham if he wished for anything, Abraham asked nothing from him.
exercises.explanation: Abraham answered: “Nothing from you.” He trusted in Allah alone, and Allah commanded: “O fire! Be coolness and safety for Abraham” (Surah al-Anbiya: 69).

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham asked Gabriel for nothing because his trust was in Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of Chapter 21. Find Gabriel’s question and Abraham’s short answer.

languageFocusExercises.title: Sitting in a Garden?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 21. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “… he sat in the middle of the fire as if he were sitting in a garden.” What does “as if he were” show?
options: It compares his real situation with an unreal one: He was in the fire, but it felt like a garden.
It shows that the fire had changed into a real garden with trees and flowers around him.
It shows that the narrator is not sure where Abraham was sitting: in the fire or in a garden.
It shows that Abraham closed his eyes and imagined a beautiful garden so that he could forget the fire.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As if” + past subjunctive (“were”) compares a real situation with an unreal one. Abraham was really in the middle of the fire; the comparison with a garden shows how safe and peaceful it was for him. The same comparison appears in “his fall into the fire was like going down into a cool garden”.

feedback.correct: Correct. “As if he were” marks an unreal comparison.
feedback.incorrect: Where was Abraham really? Read the whole sentence again: “he sat in the middle of the fire …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Did It?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each line from Chapter 21 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 21?

transformItems.source: The catapult was fired, and Abraham (pbuh) was thrown into the fire.
transformItems.frame: They fired the catapult, and they [blank] into the fire.

transformItems.source: Then, the chief priest gave his order to throw Abraham (pbuh) into the fire.
transformItems.frame: Then, the chief priest ordered that Abraham (pbuh) [blank] into the fire.

transformItems.source: The air became more pleasant as the fire was turned into coolness.
transformItems.frame: The air became more pleasant as Allah [blank] into coolness.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive (“was fired”, “was thrown”, “was turned”) keeps the focus on the catapult, on Abraham and on the fire, not on the people who acted. In the active, the agent must be named. “Order that + be + past participle” is a formal way to report a command. The last item names the real cause of the change: Allah’s command.

feedback.correct: Well done. You named the agents and kept the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: In the active, the subject does the action and the object follows the verb. After “ordered that”, use be + past participle. Check Chapter 21.

languageFocusExercises.title: Appearance and Effect
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 21 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why did the fire not burn Abraham?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: The rising flames were still there, [blank] they did not burn him, [blank] Allah commanded: “O fire! Be coolness and safety for Abraham” (Surah al-Anbiya: 69). The fire obeyed the order of Allah. It became cool and safe for Abraham (pbuh). It [blank] burned his ropes …
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “But” contrasts what stayed the same (the flames were still there) with what changed (they did not burn him). “For” + clause gives the reason; “because of” needs a noun, not a clause, and “so” would give a result. “Only” limits the fire’s effect to one thing, his ropes; “also” would wrongly suggest that it burned something else too.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed the contrast, the reason and the limit.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: What contrasts with the flames still being there? What introduces the reason (a full clause follows)? What did the fire burn and what did it not burn?

languageFocusExercises.title: Write Appearance Versus Effect
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about something that looks dangerous but actually helps.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does it look, and what does it really do?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make the contrast meaningful: The visible situation may remain similar while its consequence changes, and each connector or structure should perform a distinct discourse function.

feedback.correct: Check that “but” reverses an expectation, the passive foregrounds the event, “only” narrows the result, and “as if” remains a comparison rather than a literal claim.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say how it still looks: “The forest still looks …”
discussionPrompts.example: During a planned forest burn, the forest still looks frightening, with smoke and flames between the trees.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show the real effect: “But it only …”
discussionPrompts.example: But the fire only burns the dry grass on the ground, and the old trees stay healthy. The burn actually protects the forest.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give the reason: “This happens because …”
discussionPrompts.example: This happens because the fire was planned by experts on a cool, calm day. They control where it can go.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Compare: “It looks as if …”
discussionPrompts.example: After the burn, the forest looks as if it has been cleaned for spring. This is an image, not a literal claim.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. What did the fire burn?
beforeYouRead.quote: It only burned his ropes

iCan: I can describe what happened to Abraham (pbuh) in the fire.
I can use “only” and “as if” to describe a surprising effect.
I can write about something that looks dangerous but is not.

pages.title: Stepping Out Unharmed
pages.content: His trust in the true Allah was tested here. His last words before entering the flames were, “Allah is sufficient for me.” The large crowd, the leaders, and the priests were watching the fire from a distance. It was burning their faces and nearly made them breathless. The fire kept burning for such a long time that the disbelievers thought it would never be extinguished. Once the fire burnt out, they were shocked to see that Abraham (pbuh) had stepped out of the pit completely unharmed. The smoke blackened their faces, yet his face was bright. The burning fire had become cool for Abraham (pbuh) and had only blackened the ropes which held him. He walked out of the fire as if he were walking out of a garden. Cries of astonishment were heard from the unbelievers. “They wanted to harm him, but We made them the worst losers” (Surah al-Anbiya: 70). This miracle shamed the despotic rulers, but the fire of their rage did not cool down. Consequently, people did not dare to follow Abraham (pbuh) out of fear of rulers.

vocabulary.definition: Hardly able to take in air.
(Of a fire) put out so that it stops burning.
Made something dark in color, for example with smoke or fire.
Made someone feel disgraced in front of others.
To be brave enough to do something dangerous or difficult.

hotspots.title: Allah Is Sufficient
hotspots.description: Abraham’s (pbuh) last words before entering the fire were “Allah is sufficient for me.”

hotspots.title: Out of the Pit
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) walked out of the fire unharmed with a bright face, while smoke had blackened the faces of those watching.

exercises.title: A Picture in Words
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 22.
exercises.question: What does the writer mean by “the fire of their rage did not cool down”?
options: The fire in the pit kept burning for many more days.
The rulers were so ashamed that they stopped being angry.
The crowd’s faces were still hot from the flames.
The rulers stayed angry, even though the miracle had shamed them.
exercises.explanation: The writer says: “This miracle shamed the despotic rulers, but the fire of their rage did not cool down.” The real fire had become cool for Abraham, but the rulers’ anger did not. The chapter then says that people “did not dare to follow Abraham (pbuh) out of fear of rulers.”

feedback.correct: Right. “Fire” here is a picture of the rulers’ anger, which the miracle did not end.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence with “the fire of their rage” near the end of Chapter 22. Is the writer talking about the real fire or about a feeling? Notice the word “but”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Result or Reason?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the last sentence of Chapter 22. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Consequently, people did not dare to follow Abraham (pbuh) out of fear of rulers.” What do “Consequently” and “out of fear of” introduce?
options: “Consequently” introduces a result of the rulers’ rage; “out of fear of rulers” gives the reason why people held back.
Both introduce results of the rulers’ rage: first the people’s silence, and then their fear of following Abraham.
Both give reasons for the miracle of the fire and explain why Abraham was saved from it.
“Consequently” gives the reason for the rulers’ rage, and “out of fear of rulers” gives a result of that rage.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Consequently” (= as a result) links the sentence to the one before it: The rulers’ rage “did not cool down”, and as a result people did not dare to follow Abraham. “Out of + noun” (out of fear, out of love) gives the motive for an action: They held back because they were afraid. One sentence gives both the result and the motive.

feedback.correct: Correct. One phrase gives a result, the other a motive.
feedback.incorrect: Replace “Consequently” with “As a result” and “out of fear of” with “because they feared”. Which one is a result and which a reason?

languageFocusExercises.title: Duration and Result
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to rebuild this sentence from Chapter 22.
languageFocusExercises.question: How long did the fire burn, and what did people think?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Such + a/an + (adjective) + noun + that …” links a degree to its result: The time was so long that the disbelievers thought the fire would never go out. “Kept + -ing” shows continuing action, and “would never be extinguished” is their expectation, seen from the past.

feedback.correct: Well done. The duration comes first, then its result with “that”.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the fire, then say how long it burned (for such a long time), then the result with “that …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Turning Point and Contrast
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 22 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened when the fire burnt out?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank] the fire burnt out, they were shocked to see that Abraham (pbuh) had stepped out of the pit completely unharmed. The smoke blackened their faces, [blank] his face was bright. The burning fire [blank] cool for Abraham (pbuh) and had only blackened the ropes which held him.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Once” means “as soon as / after”: it marks the moment the fire ended and the next stage began. “Yet” sets two opposite results side by side: Their faces were black, his was bright. The past perfect “had become” shows that the fire had changed for Abraham before he walked out; it matches “had only blackened”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You marked the turning point, the contrast and the earlier change.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which word means “after/as soon as”? Are the two faces similar or opposite? Look at “had only blackened” in the same sentence.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Turning-Point Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a long problem that finally ends.
languageFocusExercises.question: What changed at the turning point?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should make the timeline clear and keep discourse relations distinct: Duration leads toward a turning point, contrast reverses an expectation, consequence follows from an event, and motive explains a person’s choice.

feedback.correct: Check that your timeline is coherent and that consequence and motive are not treated as the same relationship.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say how long it lasted: “… for such a long time that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The bridge in our town was closed for repairs for two years. The work went on for such a long time that people thought it would never end.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give the turning point: “Once …, … had finally …”
discussionPrompts.example: Once the bridge reopened, traffic in the center became much lighter. The repair had finally been completed.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show a surprise: “People expected …, yet …”
discussionPrompts.example: People expected long queues on the first day, yet the traffic moved smoothly.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Give a result and a reason: “Consequently, … . … out of fear of …”
discussionPrompts.example: Consequently, the shops near the bridge had more customers. However, some drivers still avoided the bridge out of fear of new problems.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How did Abraham (pbuh) come out of the fire?
beforeYouRead.quote: had stepped out of the pit completely unharmed

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) came out of the fire and how people reacted.
I can link a long situation to a turning point with “once”.
I can explain why people react differently to the same event.

pages.title: Debating King Nimrod
pages.content:
Abraham (pbuh) challenged those who declared themselves as gods, like King Nimrod. When King Nimrod heard that Abraham (pbuh) had emerged from the fire unharmed, he was filled with rage. He thought that his claim to be a god could not be questioned by an ordinary person. He wanted to know him personally and held a dialogue with him. Still a young man, Abraham (pbuh) was put on trial and stood by himself before a king. Even his father was not on his side; he was on the king’s side. Allah tells us about this scene in Surah al-Baqarah, verse 258: “Have you not thought about him who disputed with Abraham about his Lord (Allah) because Allah had given him the kingdom?” Abraham (pbuh)’s logic was undeniable; he said to him: “My Lord (Allah) is He Who gives life and causes death.” He said: “I give life and cause death.”

The king called up two men sentenced to death. He freed one and the other was put to death.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-nimrod
Normal and not special in any way.
Became extremely angry.
Argued against someone about something.
So clearly true that nobody can say it is false.
Officially ordered by a judge or ruler to be killed as a punishment.

hotspots.title: A King Who Claimed to Be God
hotspots.description: King Nimrod claimed to be a god and called Abraham (pbuh) to argue with him in person.

hotspots.title: Life and Death
hotspots.description: Nimrod freed one condemned man and had the other killed, claiming that he too gave life and caused death.

exercises.title: Before the King
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 23.
exercises.question: When Abraham stood before King Nimrod, even his father was on the king’s side.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says Abraham “stood by himself before a king. Even his father was not on his side; he was on the king’s side.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham stood alone; even his father supported the king.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 23. Look for the sentence that begins “Even his father …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Statement or Reported Claim?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Does the narrator say it, or report someone’s claim? Put each part in a group.
languageFocusExercises.question: Is it the narrator’s own statement, or someone else’s claim?

items: Still a young man, Abraham (pbuh) was put on trial and stood by himself before a king.
Even his father was not on his side; he was on the king’s side.
Abraham (pbuh)’s logic was undeniable

dragDropGroups.group: A claim or belief is reported
items: those who declared themselves as gods
Nimrod thought that his claim to be a god could not be questioned by an ordinary person.
Nimrod said: “I give life and cause death.”

The narrator states it: Still a young man, Abraham (pbuh) was put on trial and stood by himself before a king.
Even his father was not on his side; he was on the king’s side.
A claim or belief is reported: those who declared themselves as gods
