Nimrod thought that his claim to be a god could not be questioned by an ordinary person.
Nimrod said: “I give life and cause death.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Reporting verbs keep claims at a distance: “declared themselves as gods”, “He thought that …”, “He said …”. The narrator does not accept these claims; he only reports them. The narrator’s own statements have no such frame. “Still a young man” compresses background, and “Even” stresses how alone Abraham was.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the narrator’s statements from the claims he reports.
feedback.incorrect: Look for reporting words: declared, thought that, said. Sentences without them are the narrator’s own view.

languageFocusExercises.title: Cause and the Other One
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about the king?

errorItems.sentence: When King Nimrod heard that Abraham (pbuh) has emerged from the fire unharmed, he was filled with rage.
The king called up two men sentenced to death. He freed one and another was put to death.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Nimrod heard the news after Abraham came out of the fire, so the earlier event takes the past perfect: “had emerged”. With two people, “one … the other” is used: “the other” is the second, known member of the pair; “another” means one more from a larger group.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the earlier past and the pair “one … the other”.
feedback.incorrect: Which came first: Abraham leaving the fire or Nimrod hearing about it? How many men were there? Check Chapter 23.

languageFocusExercises.title: The Same Words, a Different Claim
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the exchange at the end of Chapter 23. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: Abraham says, “My Lord (Allah) is He Who gives life and causes death.” Nimrod answers, “I give life and cause death.” What do Nimrod’s almost-same words show?
options: He copies the wording but gives it a much narrower meaning, which he shows by freeing one prisoner and executing the other.
He agrees with what Abraham says about his Lord and accepts that only Allah gives life and causes death.
He admits in front of his people that he cannot really give life, so he loses the argument at once.
He uses completely different words to make a different claim about his own power over the people of Babylon.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Parallel wording can hide a change of meaning. Nimrod repeats Abraham’s words but uses them for something much smaller: deciding which prisoner lives or dies. The narrator shows this with the example of the two men. A careful reader compares not only the words but what each speaker means by them.

feedback.correct: Correct. Same words, different and much narrower meaning.
feedback.incorrect: What does Nimrod do after his answer? Compare that action with “gives life and causes death” in Abraham’s sense.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Claim-and-Counterclaim Exchange
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about two people who use similar words for different plans.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can the same words mean different plans?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should show who holds each viewpoint, order the events clearly, explain why the disagreement occurs, and use parallel wording as an argumentative device rather than as empty repetition.

feedback.correct: Check that your parallel claims are genuinely comparable but not automatically equivalent in meaning.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Report a belief: “She thought that her plan could not be questioned.”
discussionPrompts.example: Sara thought that her plan for a new science club could not be questioned. The belief is hers, so I report it with “thought that”.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what happened first: “When … had been …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: When the votes had been counted, the other candidate asked for a second debate. The past perfect shows that the counting came first.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give the reason for the disagreement: “They disagreed because …”
discussionPrompts.example: They disagreed because Sara wanted to spend the money on new clubs, while Omar wanted to spend it on books.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Use similar words: “I will … .” “I will … too, by …”
discussionPrompts.example: Sara said, “I will change our school.” Omar replied, “I will change our school too, by fixing what we already have.” The words are similar, but the plans are very different.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How did Nimrod feel when he heard that Abraham (pbuh) survived the fire?
beforeYouRead.quote: he was filled with rage

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) answered King Nimrod.
I can report what someone thought and what had happened before.
I can show that similar words can mean different things.

pages.title: Sarah and Lot Believe
pages.content:
This reply of the king was totally foolish, so Abraham (pbuh) put forth another challenge which would unquestionably and easily quiet him. Abraham (pbuh) said: “Verily, Allah causes the sun to rise from the east; then cause it to rise from the west.” He was utterly defeated. Allah does not guide the people who are Zalimeen (wrongdoers) (Surah al-Baqarah: 258). Abraham (pbuh)'s fame spread throughout the entire kingdom of Babylonia. People talked about how he was saved from the fire and how he debated with the king and left him unable to speak. In the meantime, Abraham (pbuh) continued calling people to believe in Allah and made a great effort to guide his people to the right path. He tried every means to persuade them. However, in spite of his love and care for his people, they left him alone. Only one woman and one man of his people shared his belief in Allah.

The woman’s name was Sarah and she became his wife. The man’s name was Lot and he later became a prophet.

vocabulary.definition: Offered an idea or argument for others to consider.
In a way that nobody can doubt.
Completely beaten, with nothing left to say.
The state of being known and talked about by many people.
Methods or ways of achieving something.

hotspots.title: The Sun from the West
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) challenged Nimrod to make the sun rise from the west, and the king could not answer.

hotspots.title: Only Two Believers
hotspots.description: Only Sarah and Lot (pbuh) shared Abraham’s (pbuh) belief; Sarah became his wife, and Lot later became a prophet.

exercises.title: The Sun From the West
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 24.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham’s challenge about the sun leave Nimrod unable to speak?
options: Nimrod could decide about prisoners, but he had no power over the rising of the sun.
Nimrod’s astrologers had already predicted the path of the sun, so he had nothing new to say.
Nimrod was afraid that the crowd would follow Abraham if he answered the question.
exercises.explanation: Nimrod had “proved” his power by freeing one prisoner and killing another. Abraham then said: “Verily, Allah causes the sun to rise from the east; then cause it to rise from the west.” No king can change the order of the sky, so “He was utterly defeated.”

feedback.correct: Right. The challenge moved from human decisions to something only Allah controls.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of Chapter 24. Compare what Nimrod did with the prisoners and what Abraham asked him to do with the sun.

languageFocusExercises.title: Words for Winning and Trying
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 24 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which expressions describe the debate and Abraham’s later efforts?

matchingPairs.right: offered a new test
beaten completely
made him fall silent
during the same period
used every possible way

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Put forth” is a formal phrasal verb meaning “present, offer”. “Utterly” is an intensifier (= completely). “Leave + person + adjective” describes the state someone is left in. “In the meantime” links two things happening in the same period: People talked about Abraham while he continued his call. “Means” (always with -s) here means “way, method”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each expression with its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Find each expression in Chapter 24 and read what happens around it: The debate with the king, its result, and Abraham’s efforts afterwards.

languageFocusExercises.title: Effort Against Result
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 24 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 24?

transformItems.source: However, in spite of his love and care for his people, they left him alone.
transformItems.frame: However, although he [blank] his people, they left him alone.

transformItems.source: Only one woman and one man of his people shared his belief in Allah.
transformItems.frame: [blank] one woman and one man of his people shared his belief in Allah.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “In spite of” is followed by a noun phrase (his love and care); “although” is followed by a clause with a verb (he loved and cared for …). Both set Abraham’s effort against the negative result. “Only X” can also be expressed with a negative + exception: “No one except X …”. Both stress how small the support was.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the concession and the limited result.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: turn the nouns love and care into verbs. Item 2: start with a negative word and add an exception. Check the end of Chapter 24.

languageFocusExercises.title: The Expected Effect
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 24. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “This reply of the king was totally foolish, so Abraham (pbuh) put forth another challenge which would unquestionably and easily quiet him.” What does “would” express here?
options: The effect the challenge was certain to have, seen from the moment Abraham put it forth.
A habit: Abraham used to put forth challenges like this to the king many times in the past.
A polite request: Abraham asks the king to answer the challenge quietly.
An imaginary situation: The challenge was never really put forth to the king.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Would” is the future seen from the past: At the moment Abraham gives his challenge, the narrator looks ahead to its effect. “Unquestionably and easily” show how sure the narrator is. The next sentences confirm it: “He was utterly defeated.”

feedback.correct: Correct. “Would” looks ahead from that moment to the challenge’s certain effect.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentences after the challenge. Does the effect happen? Is “would” about habit, politeness, or a future seen from the past?

languageFocusExercises.title: Write Effort, Resistance and Limited Outcome
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who works hard but gets little help.
languageFocusExercises.question: How much effort was made, and how much help came?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should show how an earlier event motivates a stronger action, how another development continues at the same time, why the eventual result is unexpected, and how a general reference can be developed into specific details.

feedback.correct: Check that your connectors build a real discourse progression and that “only” genuinely limits the outcome.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Give the problem and a step: “…, so she decided to … . She hoped it would …”
discussionPrompts.example: The school bins were always full of plastic, so Leyla decided to start a recycling campaign. She hoped it would make the school cleaner.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show two things at once: “She was … . In the meantime, …”
discussionPrompts.example: She was making posters for the corridors. In the meantime, she was writing to the head teacher to ask for new bins.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show the small result: “However, in spite of …, only …”
discussionPrompts.example: However, in spite of all her effort, only two students joined her team. The result was much smaller than she had hoped.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Name the helpers: “The first was …, and the second was …”
discussionPrompts.example: The whole class heard her speech, but only two classmates helped. The first was her best friend, Nur, and the second was a new student, Ali.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: According to the verse, whom does Allah not guide?
beforeYouRead.quote: Allah does not guide the people who are Zalimeen (wrongdoers)

iCan: I can explain how the debate ended and who believed in Abraham’s message.
I can show that great effort had a small result with “in spite of” and “only”.
I can write about an effort that received little support.

pages.title: Emigration and Ishmael’s Birth
pages.content: When Abraham (pbuh) realized that no one else was going to believe in his call, he decided to emigrate. He left his people and traveled with his wife Sarah and Lot to Egypt. Allah told us: “So Lot believed in him (Abraham’s message of Islamic Monotheism). He (Abraham) said, ‘I will emigrate for the sake of my Lord. Verily, He is the All Mighty, the All Wise.’” (Surah al-Ankabut: 26). After Egypt, Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Palestine and settled there. He called people to believe in Allah wherever he traveled, judged fairly between people, and guided them to truth and righteousness. Abraham (pbuh)'s wife Sarah was sterile. She had been given an Egyptian woman, Hagar, as a servant when they were in Egypt. Abraham (pbuh) had aged and his hair was gray after many years spent in calling people to Allah. Sarah thought she could not have a child. Therefore, she suggested Abraham (pbuh) get married to Hagar. Hagar gave birth to her first son, Ishmael, when Abraham (pbuh) was an old man.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-palestine-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-egypt-ancient
To leave your own country to live in another.
Behavior that is morally good and fair.
Unable to have children.
Grew old.
Put forward an idea for someone to think about.

hotspots.title: Journey to Egypt
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) left his people with Sarah and Lot (pbuh), traveled to Egypt and then settled in Palestine.

hotspots.title: The Birth of Ishmael
hotspots.description: Hagar gave birth to Ishmael (pbuh) when Abraham (pbuh) was already an old man.

exercises.title: From Babylon to Palestine
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 25 in order.
exercises.question: What happened after Abraham decided to emigrate?

sequencingItems.text: Abraham leaves his people with Sarah and Lot.
Abraham, Sarah and Lot travel to Egypt.
Abraham settles in Palestine.
Sarah suggests that Abraham marry Hagar.
Hagar gives birth to Ishmael.

exercises.explanation: Abraham “left his people and traveled with his wife Sarah and Lot to Egypt.” “After Egypt, Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Palestine and settled there.” Later Sarah, who thought she could not have a child, “suggested Abraham (pbuh) get married to Hagar”, and Hagar gave birth to Ishmael.

feedback.correct: Well done. You followed the journey and the family events in the right order.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Chapter 25 from the start: The journey comes first (Egypt, then Palestine), and the family events come at the end.

languageFocusExercises.title: Background or Main Event?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it earlier background, or does it move the story on? Sort the sentences.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which sentences go back to earlier events?

items: She had been given an Egyptian woman, Hagar, as a servant when they were in Egypt.
Abraham (pbuh) had aged and his hair was gray after many years spent in calling people to Allah.
He left his people and traveled with his wife Sarah and Lot to Egypt.
After Egypt, Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Palestine and settled there.
Hagar gave birth to her first son, Ishmael, when Abraham (pbuh) was an old man.

Earlier background (past perfect): She had been given an Egyptian woman, Hagar, as a servant when they were in Egypt.
Abraham (pbuh) had aged and his hair was gray after many years spent in calling people to Allah.
Main events (past simple): He left his people and traveled with his wife Sarah and Lot to Egypt.
After Egypt, Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Palestine and settled there.
Hagar gave birth to her first son, Ishmael, when Abraham (pbuh) was an old man.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The past simple moves the story forward: left, traveled, settled, gave birth. The past perfect steps back to explain the situation at that point: Hagar had been given to Sarah earlier in Egypt, and Abraham had aged over many years. This background explains why Sarah suggested the marriage.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated earlier background from the main events.
feedback.incorrect: Look for had + past participle: It steps back to an earlier time. Past simple verbs carry the story forward.

languageFocusExercises.title: Realisation and Recurring Action
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each part of Chapter 25 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 25?

transformItems.source: When Abraham (pbuh) realized that no one else was going to believe in his call, he decided to emigrate.
transformItems.frame: Abraham (pbuh) realized: “No one else [blank] in my call.”

transformItems.source: He called people to believe in Allah wherever he traveled …
transformItems.frame: He called people to believe in Allah [blank] he traveled …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Was going to” is the future seen from the past; in Abraham’s own thought at that moment it is “is going to”. His realisation leads directly to a decision (“he decided to emigrate”). “Wherever” means “in every place where”: it turns one action into a pattern repeated on the whole journey.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved the future back to Abraham’s viewpoint and kept the repeated action.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: change “was going to” to the present. Item 2: find another way to say “in every place where”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Sarah’s Thought and Suggestion
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix what Sarah thought and suggested?

errorItems.sentence: Sarah thought she cannot have a child.
Therefore, she suggested Abraham (pbuh) to get married to Hagar.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A thought reported in the past moves back in time: “She thought she could not have a child.” “Suggest” is never followed by person + to-infinitive. Use suggest (that) + person + base verb: “she suggested Abraham get married to Hagar”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the reported thought and the pattern after “suggest”.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Does the reported thought need a past form? Which form follows “suggested + person”? Check the end of Chapter 25.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Coherent Change-of-Plan Narrative
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who has to change plans.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did the person realize, and what did they do?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should distinguish what had happened earlier, what the person realized at a later moment, what decision followed, and how the new actions developed across time or place.

feedback.correct: Check that your tense choices show clear time relationships and that each connector advances the discourse.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say what had happened before: “He had … for five years.”
discussionPrompts.example: Emre had trained for the national swimming team for five years. He had won many local races before his shoulder injury.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what was not going to happen: “He realized that he was not going to …”
discussionPrompts.example: After the injury, he realized that he was not going to swim at the national level.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give the decision: “He decided to … . Therefore, he …”
discussionPrompts.example: He decided to become a swimming coach instead. Therefore, he took a coaching course and started work at a club.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Say what he did everywhere: “Wherever he …, he …”
discussionPrompts.example: Wherever he worked, he taught children to swim safely and to love the sport.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did Abraham (pbuh) do wherever he traveled?
options: called people to Allah and judged fairly
beforeYouRead.quote: He called people to believe in Allah wherever he traveled, judged fairly between people, and guided them to truth and righteousness.

iCan: I can tell why Abraham (pbuh) emigrated and how Ishmael was born.
I can say what someone decided after a realisation.
I can write about a change of plan in clear steps.

pages.title: The Journey to Mecca
pages.content: Some time later, Allah gave Abraham (pbuh) another son from his first wife, Sarah. The name of this second son was Isaac. Allah told Abraham (pbuh) that these two sons’ offspring would be the prophets of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. From Ishmael’s descendants came Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), while from Isaac’s came Moses (pbuh) and Jesus (pbuh). One day, Allah told Abraham (pbuh) that he should take Hagar and Ishmael to the Sacred City, Mecca. This was another test for Abraham (pbuh) while Ishmael was still a little child. It was part of Allah’s master plan. He informed Abraham (pbuh) that the sacred city would be built through Ishmael and that water would flow for him. In a few days, Abraham (pbuh) set out with his wife Hagar and their son Ishmael. Hagar was still nursing Ishmael and the child was still breastfeeding. Abraham (pbuh) walked through cultivated land, desert, and mountains until he reached the desert of the Arabian Peninsula and came to an uncultivated valley near two small hills called Safa and Marwa.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-mecca-valley-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-arabian-peninsula
__historical_entity__:abraham-safa-and-marwa-ancient
A person’s children, grandchildren and later generations.
People who come from a particular ancestor over many generations.
Told someone about something.
Feeding a baby with milk from the breast.
Not used for growing crops or plants.

hotspots.title: Two Sons, Many Prophets
hotspots.description: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) came from Ishmael’s (pbuh) descendants, and Moses (pbuh) and Jesus (pbuh) came from Isaac’s (pbuh).

hotspots.title: Across the Desert
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) led Hagar and baby Ishmael (pbuh) to a valley near the hills of Safa and Marwa.

exercises.title: A Journey With a Purpose
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 26.
exercises.question: Why was Abraham told to take Hagar and Ishmael to Mecca?
options: Hagar wanted to go back to her own people in Egypt, and Mecca was on the way.
It was part of Allah’s plan: The sacred city would be built through Ishmael.
The tribe of Jurham had invited the family to live with them in the valley.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says the journey “was part of Allah’s master plan. He informed Abraham (pbuh) that the sacred city would be built through Ishmael and that water would flow for him.” It was also “another test for Abraham”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The journey was a test and part of Allah’s plan for Mecca and Ishmael.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 26. Look for the words “master plan” and what Allah told Abraham about Ishmael.

languageFocusExercises.title: An Instruction and a Plan
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the two sentences from Chapter 26. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “One day, Allah told Abraham (pbuh) that he should take Hagar and Ishmael to the Sacred City, Mecca.” / “He informed Abraham (pbuh) that the sacred city would be built through Ishmael and that water would flow for him.” How are the two sentences different?
options: The first reports an instruction (should); the second reports a future plan (would).
Both report instructions: In each sentence, Allah tells Abraham what he should do.
The first reports a plan; the second reports an instruction.
Both report things that had already happened before Abraham went to Mecca.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Tell someone that he should …” reports an instruction: what Abraham had to do. “Inform someone that … would …” reports a plan for the future, seen from that past moment: The city and the water. The instruction is Abraham’s test; the plan explains its purpose.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Should” reports what to do; “would” reports what was going to happen.
feedback.incorrect: Compare “should” and “would”. Which one tells Abraham what to do, and which one tells what will happen later?

languageFocusExercises.title: Branches, Background and the End of the Journey
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 26 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words fit the lines about the family and the journey?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: From Ishmael’s descendants came Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), [blank] from Isaac’s came Moses (pbuh) and Jesus (pbuh). … Hagar was [blank] nursing Ishmael … Abraham (pbuh) walked through cultivated land, desert, and mountains [blank] he reached the desert of the Arabian Peninsula …
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “While” can set two parallel facts side by side (= whereas): one family line led to Prophet Muhammad, the other to Moses and Jesus. “Since” would wrongly give a reason. “Still” shows that a state continues: Ishmael was a baby who was still breastfeeding. “Until” marks the end point of the long walk.

feedback.correct: Correct. You placed the contrast, the continuing state and the end point.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Are the two family lines compared, or is one the reason for the other? Which word shows that a state continues? Which word marks where the walk ended?

languageFocusExercises.title: Time and Focus
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 26 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 26?

transformItems.source: Some time later, Allah gave Abraham (pbuh) another son from his first wife, Sarah.
transformItems.frame: Some time later, Abraham (pbuh) [blank] another son from his first wife, Sarah.

transformItems.source: In a few days, Abraham (pbuh) set out with his wife Hagar and their son Ishmael.
transformItems.frame: [blank], Abraham (pbuh) set out with his wife Hagar and their son Ishmael.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: With “give”, the passive can start with the person who receives: “Abraham was given another son”. This keeps Abraham, the main character, as the subject. “In a few days” in a past narrative means “a few days later”: the time phrase shows how soon Abraham obeyed.

feedback.correct: Well done. You changed the focus and kept the time.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: make Abraham the subject of a passive verb. Item 2: say “in a few days” in another way. Check Chapter 26.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Planned Journey with Layered Viewpoint
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a team that must move somewhere new.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was the team told, and what happened on the way?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should distinguish the instruction from the later intended result, keep the narrative viewpoint consistently in the past, and use the movement sequence to reach a clearly marked destination.

feedback.correct: Check that “would” is anchored to a past viewpoint and that “while” connects genuinely parallel information.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Report an instruction: “The team was told that it should …”
discussionPrompts.example: The research team was told that it should move to a station in the far north.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what would happen later: “The manager said that … would …”
discussionPrompts.example: The manager said that the station would open in the spring. The team would study the ice there for two years.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Compare two groups: “The older ones …, while the younger ones …”
discussionPrompts.example: The older scientists packed the instruments, while the younger ones prepared the computers.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Describe the journey: “They were still … . They sailed until …”
discussionPrompts.example: The team was still collecting data on the ship. They sailed for six days until they reached the station.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What was the name of Abraham’s second son?
beforeYouRead.quote: The name of this second son was Isaac.

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) took Hagar and Ishmael to the valley near Safa and Marwa.
I can report an instruction and a plan for the future.
I can describe a journey and how it ended.

groupTask.title: From Babylon to the Valley

roles.name: Reader A (Babylon or Ur)
roles.job: You know Chapters 4–5 and 20–22: the different ideas about his birthplace and the fire.

roles.name: Reader B (Egypt and Palestine)
roles.job: You know Chapters 24–25: why Abraham (pbuh) emigrated, where he went and where he settled.

roles.name: Reader C (Mecca)
roles.job: You know Chapter 26: the journey with Hagar and Ishmael to the valley near Safa and Marwa.

roles.name: Map Keeper
roles.job: You ask questions, draw the route on paper and write one reason next to each place.

steps: Each reader reads only his or her chapters and then closes the book.

The Map Keeper asks each reader where Abraham (pbuh) went, why he went there and who traveled with him. Places that the book gives only as one idea among several, like Harran, are marked with a question mark.
Each reader answers with one sentence from the book, for example: “After Egypt, Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Palestine and settled there.” The Map Keeper adds the place and the reason to the route.
Together, check your route against the map page “Abraham’s Journey” in the app and correct anything you placed wrongly.
groupTask.share: Each group traces its route for the class and gives a reason for each move, using phrases such as because he realized that …, he decided to … or Allah told him that he should …
groupTask.solo: Cover Chapters 4–26, draw the route Babylon or Ur → Egypt → Palestine → the valley of Mecca from memory with one reason for each move, then check it on the map page “Abraham’s Journey”.

pages.title: Hagar’s Trust in the Desert
pages.content: The valley had no fruit, no trees, no food, no water, and no sign of life. Abraham (pbuh) left them with a skin of water and a leather bag full of dates. As Abraham (pbuh) began walking away, leaving them behind, Hagar became anxious as to what was happening. Abraham (pbuh) continued walking. Hagar asked him: “Has Allah commanded you to leave us here?” He replied: “Yes. I am leaving you to Allah’s care.” Feeling a degree of comfort in this answer, this great woman said: “I am satisfied to be with Allah! We are not going to be lost, since Allah is with us.” Hagar came to understand that Abraham (pbuh) was not acting on his own decision; Allah had commanded him to leave them. Abraham (pbuh) advanced as far as the upper parts of Mecca. He stopped in a place where they could not see him.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-mecca-valley-ancient
Worried and nervous about what may happen.
A feeling of calm and relief after worry.
Pleased and content with something.
The sweet brown fruit of the palm tree.
Moved forward.

hotspots.title: In Allah’s Care
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) left Hagar and Ishmael (pbuh) in the empty valley with only water and dates, trusting them to Allah.

hotspots.title: Hagar’s Question
hotspots.description: Hagar asked whether Allah had commanded this, and when Abraham (pbuh) said yes, she was at peace.

exercises.title: Left in the Valley
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 27.
exercises.question: What gave Hagar a degree of comfort when Abraham was walking away?
options: He promised to come back with more water and food from Palestine in a few days.
She saw a caravan passing through the valley and knew that she would not be alone.
He told her that Allah had commanded it and that he was leaving them to Allah’s care.
exercises.explanation: Hagar asked: “Has Allah commanded you to leave us here?” Abraham replied: “Yes. I am leaving you to Allah’s care.” She then said: “I am satisfied to be with Allah! We are not going to be lost, since Allah is with us.”

feedback.correct: Right. Once she knew the command came from Allah, her worry turned into trust.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 27. Find Hagar’s question to Abraham and his answer.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Since” Mean Here?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read Hagar’s words in Chapter 27. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “I am satisfied to be with Allah! We are not going to be lost, since Allah is with us.” What does “since” introduce?
options: The time when her confidence began.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Since” has two meanings: Time (since 2020, since he left) and reason (= because). Here it is followed by a present fact, “Allah is with us”, which explains why she is sure they will not be lost. Her answer turns her anxiety into reassurance.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Since” here means “because”.
feedback.incorrect: Replace “since” with “because” and with “from the time when”. Which keeps the meaning of Hagar’s words?

languageFocusExercises.title: Absence, Movement and Place
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about the valley?

errorItems.sentence: The valley had no fruit, no trees, no food, not water, and no sign of life.
As Abraham (pbuh) began walking away, left them behind, Hagar became anxious as to what was happening.
He stopped in a place which they could not see him.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “No + noun” means “not any”: repeating “no … no … no …” piles up what was missing and makes the valley feel empty. “Not” cannot come directly before a noun here. “Leaving them behind” is a participle phrase that adds a second action at the same time. “Where” (= from which) links a place to what happens there.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the list, the participle and the place link.
feedback.incorrect: Check the pattern of the list, the form that adds a second action, and the word that links to a place. Then read Chapter 27 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Correction and Report
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each part of Chapter 27 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 27?

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) was not acting on his own decision; Allah had commanded him to leave them.
transformItems.frame: Abraham (pbuh) was acting not on his own decision [blank].
answers: but on the command of Allah

transformItems.source: Hagar asked him: “Has Allah commanded you to leave us here?”
transformItems.frame: Hagar asked him [blank] to leave them there.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not X but Y” rejects one explanation and puts the correct one in its place: Not his own decision, but Allah’s command. A reported yes/no question uses if/whether, statement word order, and moves back in time: “has commanded” → “had commanded”; “you … us here” → “him … them there”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You made the correction clear and reported the question.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: complete “not … but …”. Item 2: use if/whether and move the tense back. Check the middle of Chapter 27.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write from Uncertainty to Reassurance
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a hard move to a new place.
languageFocusExercises.question: How do the feelings change, from worry to understanding?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should use the language forms to move the reader through stages: difficult setting → uncertainty → clarification → reasoned response → spatial or narrative endpoint.

feedback.correct: Check that each connector changes the relationship between ideas, rather than merely decorating separate sentences.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — List what is missing: “There were no …, no … and no …”
discussionPrompts.example: At her new boarding school, Selin had no friends, no family nearby and no familiar food. Everything felt strange.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Ask for the reason: “Why do I have to …?”
discussionPrompts.example: As her parents prepared to leave, she asked, “Why do I have to stay here alone?” Her mother explained that the school had the best science programme in the country.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Correct the first idea: “It was not …; rather, it was …”
discussionPrompts.example: At first, Selin thought that her parents were sending her away. She understood that it was not a punishment; rather, it was a chance to follow her dream.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Mark the end of the trip: “… as far as …” or “… until …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her parents drove as far as the school gate and then left. Selin watched the road until she could no longer see the car.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What was the valley like?
options: without water or any sign of life

pages.title: Abraham’s Prayer for Mecca
pages.content:
He turned his face towards the direction where the Ka’ba stands today and raised his hands, praying as follows: “O Our Lord! I have made some of my offspring to dwell in a valley with no cultivation, by Your Sacred House (the Ka’ba at Mecca); in order, O our Lord, that they may offer prayers perfectly (Iqamat as salat); so fill some hearts among men with love towards them, and O Allah provide them with fruits so that they may give thanks” (Surah Ibrahim: 37). Abraham (pbuh) had to take Hagar and Ishmael away from Palestine to a new place. This was about the rebuilding of the temple, that is, the Ka’ba. According to Allah’s intention, Hagar and Ishmael had to leave Palestine and settle in the barren valley of Mecca, near the place of the old temple. The aim was to reconstruct the Holy Ka’ba, which was lost after Noah’s Flood. This made the place the renewed center of monotheism: Islam. Over the years, Ishmael’s children had children; one of them was Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam (pbuh).

They spread all over the Arabian Peninsula to carry their grandfather Abraham (pbuh)’s message of monotheism.

__historical_entity__:abraham-palestine-ancient

hotspots.title: A Prayer for the Valley
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) prayed that people’s hearts would love the family he had left near the Sacred House.

hotspots.title: The Ka’ba’s Lost Place
hotspots.description: Hagar and Ishmael (pbuh) settled near the site of the Ka’ba, which had been lost after Noah’s (pbuh) Flood.

exercises.title: The Ka’ba’s Past
exercises.instructions: Is the statement true or false? Use Chapter 28.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 28, Abraham and Ishmael would build the Ka’ba in a place where no temple had ever stood.
exercises.explanation: The chapter speaks of “the rebuilding of the temple”. Hagar and Ishmael settled “near the place of the old temple”. “The aim was to reconstruct the Holy Ka’ba, which was lost after Noah’s Flood.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The Ka’ba was to be rebuilt; an old temple had stood there before Noah’s Flood.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 28. Look for the words “rebuilding”, “old temple” and “Noah’s Flood”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reading Abraham’s Prayer
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each part of Abraham’s prayer (Surah Ibrahim: 37) with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does Abraham ask for, and why?

matchingPairs.left: in a valley with no cultivation
matchingPairs.right: in a place where no crops are grown

matchingPairs.left: that they may offer prayers perfectly
matchingPairs.right: so that they would worship in the right way

matchingPairs.left: fill some hearts among men with love towards them
matchingPairs.right: make people feel affection for them

matchingPairs.left: so that they may give thanks
matchingPairs.right: so that they would be grateful

correctAnswer.in a valley with no cultivation: in a place where no crops are grown
correctAnswer.that they may offer prayers perfectly: so that they would worship in the right way
correctAnswer.fill some hearts among men with love tow: make people feel affection for them
correctAnswer.so that they may give thanks: so that they would be grateful

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The prayer is built on purpose: “in order … that they may …” and “so that they may …” give the reasons behind each request. First Abraham explains why his family is in a barren valley (to pray), then he asks for love from people and for fruits, with a final purpose: gratitude.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the requests and their purposes.
feedback.incorrect: Read the prayer at the start of Chapter 28. Which part describes the place, which gives a purpose, and which asks for something?

languageFocusExercises.title: Why “Had To”?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapter 28. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Abraham (pbuh) had to take Hagar and Ishmael away from Palestine to a new place. This was about the rebuilding of the temple, that is, the Ka’ba.” What does “had to” show?
options: The move was necessary as part of Allah’s intention, not Abraham’s personal choice.
Abraham wanted to move because he preferred the new place to Palestine.
Abraham was used to moving from place to place, so it was a habit for him.
Abraham was not sure whether he would move.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Had to” is the past of “must/have to”: it expresses necessity. The chapter explains where the necessity came from: “According to Allah’s intention, Hagar and Ishmael had to leave Palestine …”. “That is” then clarifies the word “temple” by naming it: the Ka’ba.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Had to” shows necessity coming from Allah’s intention.
feedback.incorrect: Read the next sentences: “According to Allah’s intention …”. Is the move a wish, a habit, a doubt, or a necessity?

languageFocusExercises.title: Linking Across Generations
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 28 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words fit the lines about Ishmael’s family?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: … to reconstruct the Holy Ka’ba [blank] was lost after Noah’s Flood … Over the years, Ishmael’s children had children; one of [blank] was Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam (pbuh). [blank] spread all over the Arabian Peninsula [blank] their grandfather Abraham (pbuh)’s message of monotheism.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Which” adds background about a thing (the Ka’ba). “One of them” picks one person from the group just mentioned (Ishmael’s descendants), and “They” keeps the same group as the subject of the next sentence. “To + verb” gives the purpose of spreading: to carry the message. “For carrying” is not used for the purpose of a person’s action.

feedback.correct: Correct. You kept the reference clear and gave the purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is the Ka’ba a person or a thing? Who is “one of …” chosen from? Which form shows purpose after a verb? Check the end of Chapter 28.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Purpose-to-Legacy Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a community project and its long-term effect.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did a first need grow into a lasting result?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should show a clear discourse progression: necessity → clarification → immediate purpose → wider result → earlier/later background → long-term consequence.

feedback.correct: Check that every connector and reference choice helps the paragraph progress rather than merely adding another sentence.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Say what had to happen first: “The village had to … because …”
discussionPrompts.example: The village had to find a building first because books cannot be kept outside in the rain. The old school was the only empty place.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Explain a word: “…, that is, …”
discussionPrompts.example: The term “community library” needs clarification. It is run by volunteers, that is, local people who work without pay.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Link two aims: “They … in order to …, so that …”
discussionPrompts.example: They collected books in order to open the library, so that children could read after school. The second goal depends on the first.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Jump ahead in time: “Over the years, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Over the years, the children who read there became teachers and doctors. The library moved from an urgent need to a lasting effect on the village.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Which way did Abraham (pbuh) turn when he prayed?
options: towards the place where the Ka’ba stands today
beforeYouRead.quote: He turned his face towards the direction where the Ka’ba stands today

iCan: I can explain what Abraham (pbuh) asked for in his prayer for Mecca.
I can explain a word with “that is” and link two purposes.
I can write about a plan that had a long-term effect.

pages.title: Hagar’s Search for Water
pages.content:
Ibn Abbas, a companion of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) who narrated many hadiths, said, “Ishmael’s mother went on suckling Ishmael and drinking from the water. When the water in the water skin was used up, she became thirsty and her child also became thirsty. She started looking at Ishmael in grief. Hagar began searching for water. Leaving Ishmael under a tree, she began climbing the rocky slope of a nearby hill, Safa. ‘Maybe there is a caravan passing by,’ she thought to herself. Then, she moved across to the opposite hill, Marwa, but still saw nothing. She ran between the two hills of Safa and Marwa seven times looking for signs of water or help. Hagar’s patient search for water is directly comparable to the running (sa’y) between Safa and Marwah.” Her effort was later commemorated by Muslims during Hajj. Actually, there is almost no difference between the pilgrimage called by Abraham (pbuh) and the pilgrimage of Islam.

Exhausted and sad, she heard a voice but could not find where it came from.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-safa-and-marwa-ancient
Finished completely so that none was left.
Deep sadness, especially after a loss.
A group of travelers with animals crossing a desert together.
Remembered and honored with a special act or ceremony.
A journey to a holy place for religious reasons.

hotspots.title: Seven Runs
hotspots.description: Hagar ran between Safa and Marwa seven times, looking for water or help.

hotspots.title: An Echo in Hajj
hotspots.description: Muslims on Hajj repeat Hagar’s search when they walk between the two hills (sa’y).

exercises.title: Between Safa and Marwa
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 29 in order.
exercises.question: What did Hagar do when the water ran out?

sequencingItems.text: The water skin is empty, and mother and child become thirsty.
Hagar leaves Ishmael under a tree.
Hagar climbs Safa, hoping to see a caravan.
Hagar moves to Marwa but still sees nothing.
Hagar runs between the two hills seven times.

exercises.explanation: In Ibn Abbas’s account, “When the water in the water skin was used up, she became thirsty and her child also became thirsty.” Then, “Leaving Ishmael under a tree, she began climbing … Safa”, “moved across to the opposite hill, Marwa, but still saw nothing”, and “ran between the two hills of Safa and Marwa seven times”. Muslims remember her effort in the sa’y of Hajj.

feedback.correct: Well done. Hagar trusted Allah and still worked hard to find help.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Ibn Abbas’s account in Chapter 29: first the empty water skin, then Ishmael under the tree, then the two hills one after the other.

languageFocusExercises.title: Whose Voice?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it inside Ibn Abbas’s report, or told by the narrator? Sort the sentences.
languageFocusExercises.question: Where does Ibn Abbas’s report end?

items: When the water in the water skin was used up, she became thirsty and her child also became thirsty.
‘Maybe there is a caravan passing by,’ she thought to herself.
She ran between the two hills of Safa and Marwa seven times looking for signs of water or help.
Her effort was later commemorated by Muslims during Hajj.
Actually, there is almost no difference between the pilgrimage called by Abraham (pbuh) and the pilgrimage of Islam.
Exhausted and sad, she heard a voice but could not find where it came from.

Inside Ibn Abbas’s report: When the water in the water skin was used up, she became thirsty and her child also became thirsty.
‘Maybe there is a caravan passing by,’ she thought to herself.
She ran between the two hills of Safa and Marwa seven times looking for signs of water or help.
Told by the narrator: Her effort was later commemorated by Muslims during Hajj.
Actually, there is almost no difference between the pilgrimage called by Abraham (pbuh) and the pilgrimage of Islam.
Exhausted and sad, she heard a voice but could not find where it came from.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Ibn Abbas … said, “…”” frames a report from a named source, and the quotation marks show where it begins and ends. Inside it, “Maybe … she thought” is Hagar’s own possibility, not a fact. After the report, the narrator adds a later link (“was later commemorated”), a comment (“Actually, …”) and continues the story.

feedback.correct: Correct. You found where the report ends and the narrator continues.
feedback.incorrect: Find the closing quotation mark of Ibn Abbas’s report. Sentences after it belong to the narrator. Look for “later” and “Actually”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Naming the Source
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 29 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 29?

transformItems.source: Ibn Abbas, a companion of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) who narrated many hadiths, said, …
transformItems.frame: Ibn Abbas, [blank] a companion of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) and narrated many hadiths, said, …

transformItems.source: Her effort was later commemorated by Muslims during Hajj.
transformItems.frame: Later, Muslims [blank] her effort during Hajj.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A noun phrase after a name (“Ibn Abbas, a companion of …”) is an appositive: A short relative clause without “who was”. Adding “who was” lets it join another verb (“and narrated …”). Naming the source this way makes the report reliable. The passive “was commemorated by Muslims” keeps her effort in focus; the active makes Muslims the subject.

feedback.correct: Well done. You expanded the appositive and changed the focus.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: add the relative pronoun and verb that are understood. Item 2: make Muslims the subject of an active verb. Check Chapter 29.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Summary That Keeps the Certainty Levels
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the summary that keeps what Chapter 29 presents as fact, possibility and comparison.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which summary of Chapter 29 is faithful to the text?
options: Hagar hoped a caravan might be passing, but she saw nothing; her search is later remembered during Hajj, and the two pilgrimages are almost the same.
Hagar knew a caravan was passing by, so she ran to Safa to meet it, and her search was later added to the Hajj.
Ibn Abbas says that the Hajj began on the day of Hagar’s search, and that the two pilgrimages are exactly the same.
The narrator says that the pilgrimage of Abraham and the pilgrimage of Islam are exactly the same, and that Hagar saw a caravan from Safa.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Maybe there is a caravan …” is a possibility in Hagar’s mind, not a fact, and she “still saw nothing”. The later link to Hajj is the narrator’s, not Ibn Abbas’s. “Almost no difference” is a careful claim; “exactly the same” would overstate it.

feedback.correct: Correct. This summary keeps the possibility, the later link and the careful comparison.
feedback.incorrect: Check three things: Was the caravan a fact or a possibility? Who links the search to Hajj? Does the narrator say “almost no difference” or “no difference”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Write from Report to Later Interpretation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a rescue or a search from a news report.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened, and what did it mean later?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should show a controlled discourse progression: Attributed source → trigger → repeated or developing action → tentative possibility → contrastive result → later comparison/interpretation.

feedback.correct: Check that the paragraph makes clear what was reported, what was only possible, what happened, and what was interpreted later.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Name the source: “According to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: The local newspaper reported the event. I will begin: “According to the newspaper, two hikers got lost on the mountain.”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what someone thought might happen: “She thought there might be …”
discussionPrompts.example: One rescuer thought there might be a hut near the river. She was not sure, so I will use “might”.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Put the steps in order: “First, … . Then, climbing …, they …”
discussionPrompts.example: First, the rescuers searched the forest. Then, climbing the steep path, they reached the river. The -ing phrase compresses the climb into the background.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Add a later meaning: “Later, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Later, the town named the path after the rescuers. This meaning came afterwards and was not part of the rescue itself.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Who told this story about Hagar?
beforeYouRead.quote: Ibn Abbas, a companion of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) who narrated many hadiths

iCan: I can tell how Hagar searched for water between Safa and Marwa.
I can name a source and keep a report apart from a later meaning.
I can write about a search in a clear order.

pages.title: Zamzam Appears
pages.content: Looking down into the valley, Hagar saw the angel Gabriel standing next to her son, Ishmael. The angel hit the ground with his heel, and water immediately flowed out. It was a miracle! Hagar quickly made a small basin around the water to stop it from spreading, and she filled her water skin. The angel said, “Do not be afraid. This is the place for the House of Allah, which this boy and his father will build. Allah never abandons His people.” This well, called Zamzam, is flowing to this day in the city of Mecca in the Arabian Peninsula. This name was given to the water because the word Zamzam means “abundant and flowing, the voice of Gabriel, the sound water makes as it flows, the sound of thunder, a sound whose origin is unknown.” Not long after that, the tribe of Jurham that was moving from southern Arabia, Yemen, stopped by the valley of Mecca. They had seen the unusual sight of a bird flying in its direction, which could only mean the presence of water.

__historical_entity__:abraham-arabian-peninsula
__historical_entity__:abraham-yemen
__historical_entity__:abraham-zamzam
__historical_entity__:abraham-kaaba-abraham
__historical_entity__:abraham-jurhum

A low, bowl-shaped hollow that holds water.
Existing in large amounts; more than enough.
The place or point where something begins.
