hotspots.title: Water from the Ground
hotspots.description: The angel Gabriel struck the ground with his heel, and the water of Zamzam flowed out.

hotspots.title: A Bird over the Valley
hotspots.description: The tribe of Jurham saw a bird flying towards the valley and understood that there was water there.

exercises.title: News of Water
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 30.
exercises.question: How did the tribe of Jurham know that there was water in the valley of Mecca?
options: They heard the sound of the water flowing from far away.
They saw a bird flying in the direction of the valley.
Hagar sent them a message in Yemen and asked them to come.
exercises.explanation: The chapter says the Jurham “had seen the unusual sight of a bird flying in its direction, which could only mean the presence of water.” The sound of water appears in the meanings of the word Zamzam, not in how the tribe found the valley.

feedback.correct: Right. A bird flying towards the valley was a sign of water in the desert.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentences of Chapter 30. What unusual sight did the tribe see?

languageFocusExercises.title: Seeing the Sign
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the last sentence of Chapter 30. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: In “They had seen the unusual sight of a bird flying in its direction, which could only mean the presence of water”, the tribe had already seen the water itself before they stopped.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The tribe saw a bird, not the water. “Which could only mean …” marks a strong inference from that sign: The only possible explanation was water. The past perfect “had seen” shows that this sign came before their stop in the valley and explains it.

feedback.correct: Correct. They saw a sign and inferred the water from it.
feedback.incorrect: What exactly did the tribe see? Read the sentence again: “the unusual sight of a bird …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Event, Response and What Came Next
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 30 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened right away, and what came next?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: The angel hit the ground with his heel, and water [blank] flowed out. It was a miracle! Hagar quickly made a small basin around the water [blank] it from spreading, and she filled her water skin. … [blank], the tribe of Jurham that was moving from southern Arabia, Yemen, stopped by the valley of Mecca.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Immediately” shows that the result followed the action at once; “lately” means “recently” and does not describe how fast something happened. “To + verb” gives the purpose of Hagar’s action: she made the basin to stop the water spreading. “Not long after that” moves the story forward by a short time; “Long before that” would move it back.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed the immediate result, the purpose and the short time gap.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: How quickly did the water appear? Why did Hagar make the basin? Did the tribe arrive soon after or long before? Check Chapter 30.

languageFocusExercises.title: Names and Conclusions
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each part of Chapter 30 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 30?

transformItems.source: This well, called Zamzam, is flowing to this day in the city of Mecca …
transformItems.frame: This well, [blank] Zamzam, is flowing to this day in the city of Mecca …

transformItems.source: This name was given to the water because the word Zamzam means …
transformItems.frame: People [blank] to the water because the word Zamzam means …

transformItems.source: They had seen the unusual sight of a bird flying in its direction, which could only mean the presence of water.
transformItems.frame: They had seen a bird flying in its direction, so there [blank] water there.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Called Zamzam” is a short form of “which is called Zamzam”. The passive “This name was given to the water” does not name who gave it; the active needs a subject such as “People”. “Could only mean …” marks a strong inference; “must be” says the same thing with a modal of deduction.

feedback.correct: Well done. You expanded the name, named the agent and kept the inference.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: add the relative pronoun and verb. Item 2: use an active verb. Item 3: use a modal that shows a strong conclusion.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write from Sign to Settlement
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a discovery that changed what people did.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was found, and what did people think it meant?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should move coherently from an initiating event through purpose and time shifts to an evidence-based inference that motivates a later action.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph separates what happened, what was intended, what continues, what had happened earlier, and what was inferred.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Show a quick result: “…, and … immediately …”
discussionPrompts.example: A farmer’s plough hit a stone box, and old coins immediately spilled out.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say what someone did and why: “He called … to …”
discussionPrompts.example: He called the museum to protect the coins from thieves.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Say what people can still see: “Visitors can still see … to this day.”
discussionPrompts.example: Visitors can still see the coins in the museum to this day. They can read the dates and see a king’s face on them.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Make a careful guess: “Experts said that … could mean …”
discussionPrompts.example: Experts said that the coins could mean there was a market there long ago. “Could mean” shows that this is an inference, not the original observation.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Who hit the ground with his heel?
beforeYouRead.quote: The angel hit the ground with his heel, and water immediately flowed out.

iCan: I can tell how Zamzam appeared and how the tribe of Jurham found it.
I can mark a conclusion from a sign with “could mean”.
I can write about a discovery that changed what people did next.

pages.title: The Dream of Sacrifice
pages.content: They eventually settled in Mecca and Ishmael grew up among them. Ishmael learned Arabic from them and they all loved and admired Ishmael because of his gentle character. Growing up among the Jurham tribe, Ishmael married the daughter of one of their leaders. Abraham (pbuh) had a dream that he sacrificed his son, which was to be the ultimate test of his faith. In a dream, Abraham (pbuh) learnt that he must sacrifice his son. Joseph (pbuh) and Muhammad (pbuh), two of Abraham (pbuh)'s offspring, also had important dreams. “So We gave him the glad tidings of a forbearing boy. And when he (his son) was old enough to walk with him, he said: 'O my son! I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you (offer you in sacrifice to Allah), so look what do you think!' 'O my father! Do that which you are commanded InshAllah (if Allah wills), you shall find me of the patient” (Surah as-Saffat: 101–102). Ishmael knew the task of his father.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-mecca-valley-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-jurhum
Respected and liked someone very much.
Kind, calm and soft in manner.
The greatest and hardest trial of someone’s faith.
Good news that brings happiness.
Patient and calm, even when treated badly.

hotspots.title: Growing Up Among the Jurham
hotspots.description: Ishmael (pbuh) grew up among the Jurham, learned Arabic from them and married the daughter of one of their leaders.

hotspots.title: The Hardest Dream
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son, and Ishmael (pbuh) told him to do what he was commanded.

exercises.title: The Son’s Answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 31.
exercises.question: What does Ishmael’s answer to his father’s dream show about him?
options: He wanted to ask the leaders of Jurham before deciding.
He asked his father to wait until he was older.
He did not know what his father had seen in the dream.
He accepted Allah’s command and promised to be patient.
exercises.explanation: Ishmael answered: “O my father! Do that which you are commanded InshAllah (if Allah wills), you shall find me of the patient” (Surah as-Saffat: 102). The chapter adds that “Ishmael knew the task of his father.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Ishmael was a “forbearing boy”: he accepted the command with patience.
feedback.incorrect: Read Ishmael’s words in the verse at the end of Chapter 31. What does he tell his father to do, and how does he describe himself?

languageFocusExercises.title: Reading the Verses
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each part of the verses in Chapter 31 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happens in these verses, step by step?

matchingPairs.left: the glad tidings of a forbearing boy
matchingPairs.right: good news of a gentle, calm son

matchingPairs.left: when he (his son) was old enough to walk with him
matchingPairs.right: when the boy had grown up enough to go about with his father

matchingPairs.left: so look what do you think
matchingPairs.right: Abraham asks for his son’s opinion

matchingPairs.left: Do that which you are commanded
matchingPairs.right: Ishmael tells his father to obey the order

matchingPairs.left: you shall find me of the patient
matchingPairs.right: Ishmael promises to endure it

correctAnswer.the glad tidings of a forbearing boy: good news of a gentle, calm son
correctAnswer.when he (his son) was old enough to walk: when the boy had grown up enough to go about with his father
correctAnswer.so look what do you think: Abraham asks for his son’s opinion
correctAnswer.Do that which you are commanded: Ishmael tells his father to obey the order

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Glad tidings” means good news, and “forbearing” means patient and gentle. “Old enough to …” marks a stage of growth. In the dialogue, Abraham first tells his dream and then asks for his son’s view; Ishmael answers with an instruction to obey and a promise of patience, which he qualifies with “if Allah wills”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the verses from good news to consultation and commitment.
feedback.incorrect: Read the verses at the end of Chapter 31. Who speaks each line, and is it news, a time, a question, an instruction or a promise?

languageFocusExercises.title: Growing Up and Obligation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 31 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 31?

transformItems.source: Growing up among the Jurham tribe, Ishmael married the daughter of one of their leaders.
transformItems.frame: [blank] among the Jurham tribe, Ishmael married the daughter of one of their leaders.

transformItems.source: In a dream, Abraham (pbuh) learnt that he must sacrifice his son.
transformItems.frame: In a dream, Abraham (pbuh) learnt that he [blank] sacrifice his son.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The participle clause “Growing up among the Jurham tribe” gives background: It can be expanded into a time clause with “as”, “while” or “after”. In reported speech, “must” for obligation often becomes “had to” in the past; the chapter keeps “must” to stress how strong the command was.

feedback.correct: Well done. You expanded the background and reported the obligation.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: turn “Growing up” into a clause with a subject and a verb. Item 2: give the past form of “must” for obligation.

languageFocusExercises.title: Looking Ahead from the Dream
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 31. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Abraham (pbuh) had a dream that he sacrificed his son, which was to be the ultimate test of his faith.” What does “was to be” express?
options: What the dream would turn out to be, seen from the time of the dream.
An obligation that Abraham felt towards his son after he had the dream.
Something that was planned for the future but did not happen in the end.
A habit: Abraham often had dreams like this in the past.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Was/were to be” is a formal way to look ahead from a past moment to what was destined to happen. The narrator tells us, at the moment of the dream, that it would become the greatest test of Abraham’s faith. The relative clause “which …” adds this comment to the whole event.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Was to be” looks ahead to what the dream would become.
feedback.incorrect: Is the narrator describing a feeling, a habit, or what the dream would later prove to be? Read the chapter to its end.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Consultation under Pressure
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about two people talking about a hard duty.
languageFocusExercises.question: Whose duty is it, and what do they say?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should move from background to a turning point, distinguish obligation from preference, and use consultation language to develop the interaction.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph separates background, obligation, consultation, response and future commitment.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Give the background: “Over the years, … had become …”
discussionPrompts.example: Over the years, Zeynep had become the most experienced nurse on the ward.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Say where the duty comes from: “The rules said that … must …”
discussionPrompts.example: The hospital rules said that a senior nurse must stay on duty during the storm. It was part of her role, not her own wish.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Ask for an opinion: “What do you think? Can you …?”
discussionPrompts.example: She asked her younger colleague, “What do you think? Can you stay with me tonight?”

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Answer with a careful promise: “I will …, if all goes well.”
discussionPrompts.example: Her colleague answered, “I will stay, if all goes well with my children at home.” This shows willingness without promising full control.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Whom did Ishmael (pbuh) marry?
options: the daughter of a Jurham leader
beforeYouRead.quote: Ishmael married the daughter of one of their leaders.

iCan: I can tell what Abraham (pbuh) saw in his dream and how Ishmael answered.
I can show that a duty comes from an instruction, not from a wish.
I can describe two people discussing a difficult responsibility.

pages.title: Submission and Mercy
pages.content:
The Allah-fearing son of a faithful father promised to obey Allah. Abraham (pbuh) took his son to the place where he was to be sacrificed and laid him. “And when they both obeyed Allah’s command, and he (Abraham (pbuh)) laid him (Ishmael) face down upon his forehead (in order to be sacrificed)” (Surah as-Saffat: 103). A voice stopped Abraham (pbuh) just as his knife was about to touch Ishmael: “We called to him: O Abraham: You have indeed fulfilled the vision. Thus do We reward the good. That verily was a clear test” (Surah as-Saffat: 104–106). Here, Abraham (pbuh) showed his willingness to sacrifice all his belongings for Allah. Because of this, Allah made him the leader of humanity and brought Messengers from his children. “And when Allah tested Abraham with various commands, and he proved true to each one. He (Allah) said, indeed I have made you a leader of humanity.

He (Abraham) said (asking of Allah), ‘and from my children” (Surah al-Baqarah: 124). It was only a test; the substitute was a ram or goat.

vocabulary.definition: Deeply devoted and careful to avoid sin.
Placed someone down on the ground.
The state of being ready and happy to do something.
Something that takes the place of another.
An adult male sheep.

hotspots.title: A Voice at the Last Moment
hotspots.description: A voice stopped Abraham (pbuh) just as the knife was about to reach Ishmael (pbuh).

hotspots.title: A Leader for Humanity
hotspots.description: Because Abraham (pbuh) passed every test, Allah made him a leader for people and chose messengers from his children.

exercises.title: The Test and the Reward
exercises.instructions: Match each part with what Chapter 32 says about it.
exercises.question: How does Chapter 32 end the story of the sacrifice?

matchingPairs.right: It stopped Abraham just before the knife reached Ishmael.
A ram or goat took Ishmael’s place.
Allah made him a leader of humanity.

correctAnswer.The voice: It stopped Abraham just before the knife reached Ishmael.
correctAnswer.The substitute: A ram or goat took Ishmael’s place.
correctAnswer.Abraham’s willingness: Allah made him a leader of humanity.

exercises.explanation: “A voice stopped Abraham (pbuh) just as his knife was about to touch Ishmael.” Abraham “showed his willingness to sacrifice all his belongings for Allah. Because of this, Allah made him the leader of humanity.” The chapter ends: “It was only a test; the substitute was a ram or goat.”

feedback.correct: Well done. The test showed Abraham’s submission, and it ended in mercy and honor.
feedback.incorrect: Look for three places in Chapter 32: the moment of the knife, the sentence with “Because of this”, and the last sentence.

languageFocusExercises.title: The Last Moment
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 32. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “A voice stopped Abraham (pbuh) just as his knife was about to touch Ishmael …” What does “was about to” show?
options: The action was going to happen in the next moment, but it had not happened yet.
The knife had already touched Ishmael before the voice stopped Abraham.
The action was planned for a later day, not for that moment.
The knife stayed near Ishmael for a long time before anything happened.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Be about to + verb” describes something that is going to happen very soon. With “just as”, it marks the exact moment of the interruption: The voice came before the knife reached Ishmael. This timing creates the tension of the chapter.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Was about to” marks the moment just before the action.
feedback.incorrect: Did the knife reach Ishmael? What stopped Abraham, and when? Read the sentence again with “just as”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Promise, Consequence and Limit
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 32 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words fit the lines about the promise and the test?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: The Allah-fearing son of a faithful father promised [blank] Allah. … [blank] this, Allah made him the leader of humanity and brought Messengers from his children. … It was [blank] a test; the substitute was a ram or goat.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Promise” is followed by to + verb (“promised to obey”). “Because of” is followed by a noun or pronoun (this); “because” needs a full clause. “Only” limits the event: It was a test, not a real sacrifice, as the substitute animal shows. “Even” would suggest something surprising, not a limit.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed the promise, the consequence and the limit.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which form follows “promised”? Is “this” a noun or a clause? Which word limits the event to a test? Check Chapter 32.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build the Evaluation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to rebuild this sentence from Chapter 32.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Abraham show here?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The noun “willingness” is followed by to + verb (willingness to sacrifice), just like the adjective “willing to”. “Here” points back to the scene just told. The sentence turns the event into an evaluation, which the next sentence links to its consequence with “Because of this”.

feedback.correct: Well done. The noun “willingness” is followed by what he was willing to do.
feedback.incorrect: Start with “Here,” and the subject. Then say what he showed, and follow “willingness” with to + verb.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Turning-Point Evaluation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a test that stops at a key moment.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened, and what did it really show?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should separate event timing, interruption, evaluation and consequence, then use a final limiting expression to prevent overstatement.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph distinguishes the event itself from what it proves or leads to.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Set the moment: “… was just about to …”
discussionPrompts.example: The examiner was writing notes, and the learner driver was just about to drive through a red light.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show what stopped it: “Suddenly, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Suddenly, the examiner pressed the second brake, and the car stopped. This interrupted the expected mistake.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Say what it showed: “The event showed that … . Because of this, …”
discussionPrompts.example: The event showed that the learner needed more practice at busy crossings. Because of this, the test was stopped.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Do not say too much: “It was only …, not …”
discussionPrompts.example: It was only one mistake, not proof that the learner would never drive well.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did the voice say Abraham had fulfilled?
beforeYouRead.quote: You have indeed fulfilled the vision.

iCan: I can explain how the test ended and what Abraham (pbuh) was given.
I can describe a moment when something was about to happen.
I can evaluate what an event showed without saying too much.

pages.title: Sacrifice and Reunion
pages.content: Every year, hundreds of millions of Muslims perform this act of trust in Allah during the days of Hajj. This day is called “The Day of Sacrifice” or “The Celebration of Sacrifice.” At Abraham (pbuh)’s time, the practice of sacrificing the firstborn children was quite widespread in Arabia, Palestine, and Egypt. Actually, sacrificing animals was part of Abraham’s religion of monotheism. In Abraham (pbuh)’s religion, animal sacrifice was equivalent to human life, and for the people of that era, it meant safety, especially for children. In fact, animal sacrifice is not a form of worship that began with Abraham (pbuh). Prophets before him also sacrificed animals, while idolaters sacrificed humans. Abraham (pbuh) returned to Palestine. After a separation of several years, the father and son came together again. At that time, Ishmael was about thirty years old. Father and son embraced each other again with longing. Both were crying with joy. This time, they were going to build the honored House of Allah, which is a center of worship and the direction people face while praying, and to make it the site of Islamic pilgrimage, Hajj.

__historical_entity__:abraham-egypt-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-kaaba-abraham
Existing or happening in many places or among many people.
Equal in value or meaning to something else.
A long period of history.

A strong wish to see or have someone or something you love.

hotspots.title: The Day of Sacrifice
hotspots.description: Every year during Hajj, Muslims remember Abraham’s (pbuh) trust in Allah on the Day of Sacrifice.

hotspots.title: Father and Son Reunited
hotspots.description: After years apart, Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh) embraced each other and cried with joy.

exercises.title: Sacrifice in Abraham’s Time
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 33.
exercises.question: According to the writer, what did animal sacrifice in Abraham’s religion mean for the people of that time?
options: The start of the Hajj season
Wealth and power for the priests
exercises.explanation: The writer explains that “the practice of sacrificing the firstborn children was quite widespread”. In Abraham’s religion, however, “animal sacrifice was equivalent to human life, and for the people of that era, it meant safety, especially for children.”

feedback.correct: Right. Where people sacrificed children, animal sacrifice protected human life.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of Chapter 33. Find the sentence that says what animal sacrifice “meant” for the people of that era.

languageFocusExercises.title: Then or Now?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it about Abraham’s time, or about today? Sort the parts of Chapter 33.
languageFocusExercises.question: Is the claim about then, or about now?

items: At Abraham (pbuh)’s time, the practice of sacrificing the firstborn children was quite widespread in Arabia, Palestine, and Egypt.
In Abraham (pbuh)’s religion, animal sacrifice was equivalent to human life …
… for the people of that era, it meant safety, especially for children.
Every year, hundreds of millions of Muslims perform this act of trust in Allah during the days of Hajj.
This day is called “The Day of Sacrifice” …

Limited to Abraham’s time: At Abraham (pbuh)’s time, the practice of sacrificing the firstborn children was quite widespread in Arabia, Palestine, and Egypt.
In Abraham (pbuh)’s religion, animal sacrifice was equivalent to human life …
… for the people of that era, it meant safety, especially for children.
About today: Every year, hundreds of millions of Muslims perform this act of trust in Allah during the days of Hajj.
This day is called “The Day of Sacrifice” …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Time frames limit a claim: “At Abraham’s time”, “In Abraham’s religion”, “for the people of that era”. With these phrases and the past tense, the chapter does not claim that these ideas are true for all times. The present simple with “Every year” describes a practice that continues today.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the claims limited to that era from the present-day practice.
feedback.incorrect: Look for time frames (At Abraham’s time, that era) and the tense of the verb. Present simple with “Every year” describes today.

languageFocusExercises.title: Contrast and Plan
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 33 with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 33?

transformItems.source: Prophets before him also sacrificed animals, while idolaters sacrificed humans.
transformItems.frame: [blank] prophets before him also sacrificed animals, idolaters sacrificed humans.

transformItems.source: This time, they were going to build the honored House of Allah …
transformItems.frame: This time, their plan was [blank] the honored House of Allah …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “While” and “whereas” set two different practices side by side, and the contrast clause can come first or second. “Were going to” is the future seen from the past: At the moment of the reunion, building the House of Allah was the plan ahead of them.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved the contrast word and kept the plan.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use a contrast word at the start. Item 2: “were going to build” describes a plan; complete “their plan was …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Words of Practice and Reunion
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 33 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which expressions describe the old practices and the reunion?

matchingPairs.right: fairly common in many places
of the same value as
held one another in their arms
with a strong wish to be together again

correctAnswer.embraced each other: held one another in their arms
correctAnswer.with longing: with a strong wish to be together again

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Quite” before an adjective often means “fairly”. “Equivalent to” compares value, and in the chapter it is limited to Abraham’s religion and era. “Each other” shows a two-way action: Father and son embraced each other. “Longing” is a strong wish for someone you have missed.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each expression with its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Find each expression in Chapter 33: two are about old practices, and two are about the reunion of father and son.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Historically Framed Contrast
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences comparing a practice from the past with today.
languageFocusExercises.question: How was it then, and how is it now?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should distinguish historical context, contrast, clarification and later intention while keeping claims within their proper scope.

feedback.correct: Check that each claim is tied to its time, group or context where necessary.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Limit the claim to a time: “In the 1700s, many … believed …”
discussionPrompts.example: In the 1700s, many European doctors believed that removing blood cured fevers. This claim is limited to that period.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Compare then and now: “Doctors then …, while doctors today …”
discussionPrompts.example: Doctors then removed blood from their patients, while doctors today use medicines that are tested in laboratories.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Correct a wrong idea: “In fact, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In fact, those doctors did not want to harm anyone; they followed the best knowledge they had. This corrects the idea that they were cruel.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Show a later plan: “After several years, … were going to …”
discussionPrompts.example: After several years of research, doctors were going to replace this practice with safer treatments. I describe this plan from that past moment.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How old was Ishmael when he and his father met again?
beforeYouRead.quote: Ishmael was about thirty years old

iCan: I can explain what the book says about sacrifice and the reunion.
I can compare two practices with “while” and limit a claim to one time.
I can write a careful comparison of two times in history.

pages.title: Building the Ka’ba
pages.content:
Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said: “Indeed this place has been made sacred by Allah since the day He created the heavens and the earth, and it will remain so until the Day of Judgment” (Sunan an-Nasa’i, 2874). Abraham (pbuh) said to Ishmael: “O Ishmael, Allah has commanded me to do an important task, and you will help me in this task.” Ishmael replied, “I will help you for sure.” Abraham (pbuh) said, “The Almighty Allah commanded me to build a house for Himself.” Father and son found the foundations of the old structure and began to build the Ka’ba on it. When the building became high, the old man Abraham (pbuh) could no longer lift the stones to such a high position. So he stood over the stone of Al-Maqam, and Ishmael carried on handing him the stones. Both of them were saying: “O our Lord! Accept this service from us; verily You are the All Hearer, the All Knower” (Surah al-Baqarah: 127).

Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Mecca in response to Allah’s command to establish the sacred Ka’ba.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-mecca-valley-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-kaaba-abraham
Declared holy and protected from harm or disrespect.
The strong base under a building that supports it.
Passing something directly to another person.
An answer or reaction to something.
To set up something that will last.

hotspots.title: Standing on the Stone
hotspots.description: When the walls grew high, Abraham (pbuh) stood on the stone of Al-Maqam while Ishmael (pbuh) handed him the stones.

hotspots.title: A Prayer While Building
hotspots.description: As they built, father and son asked Allah to accept their service.

exercises.title: Building the House
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 34 in order.
exercises.question: How did Abraham and Ishmael build the Ka’ba?

sequencingItems.text: Abraham tells Ishmael that Allah has given him an important task.
Ishmael promises to help his father.
Abraham and Ishmael find the foundations of the old structure.
As the walls rise, Abraham stands on Al-Maqam and Ishmael hands him the stones.

exercises.explanation: Abraham said: “O Ishmael, Allah has commanded me to do an important task, and you will help me in this task.” Ishmael replied: “I will help you for sure.” They “found the foundations of the old structure and began to build the Ka’ba on it.” When the building became high, “he stood over the stone of Al-Maqam, and Ishmael carried on handing him the stones”, and both prayed: “O our Lord! Accept this service from us.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Father and son worked together and asked Allah to accept their work.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Chapter 34 from the conversation between father and son to the work itself. The stone of Al-Maqam is needed only when the walls are high.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Request, Not an Order
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the prayer at the end of Chapter 34. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “O our Lord! Accept this service from us; verily You are the All Hearer, the All Knower.” What does “Accept” do here?
options: It is a humble request made in prayer.
It is an order given to an equal.
It states that the service has already been accepted.
It is an instruction from Abraham to Ishmael.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The imperative form is not always an order. Addressed to Allah (“O our Lord!”), it is a humble request, a prayer. “From us” shows that father and son pray together, and “verily You are the All Hearer, the All Knower” gives the reason for their hope: Allah hears and knows.

feedback.correct: Correct. In a prayer, the imperative is a humble request.
feedback.incorrect: Who is being addressed with “O our Lord!”? Can the speakers give orders to Him?

languageFocusExercises.title: Reporting the Dialogue
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Report what Abraham and Ishmael said in Chapter 34. Complete each sentence.
languageFocusExercises.question: What changes when we report their words?

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) said to Ishmael: “O Ishmael, Allah has commanded me to do an important task, and you will help me in this task.”
transformItems.frame: Abraham told Ishmael that Allah [blank] him to do an important task.

transformItems.source: Ishmael replied, “I will help you for sure.”
transformItems.frame: Ishmael replied that he [blank] him for sure.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In direct speech, the present perfect “has commanded” shows that the command is still relevant when Abraham speaks, and “will” shows commitment. In reported speech after a past verb, the tenses move back: has commanded → had commanded, will help → would help.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved the tenses back correctly.
feedback.incorrect: Move each tense one step back: present perfect → past perfect, will → would. Check the dialogue in Chapter 34.

languageFocusExercises.title: Building Together
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapter 34.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each sentence about the building?

formChoices.sentence: Father and son found the foundations of the old structure and began to build the Ka’ba [choice] it.
When the building became high, the old man Abraham (pbuh) could [choice] lift the stones to such a high position. So he stood over the stone of Al-Maqam …
… and Ishmael carried on [choice] him the stones …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A building goes “on” its foundations. “No longer” shows that an earlier ability has stopped (“any longer” needs a negative verb: could not … any longer). “Carry on + -ing” means continue an activity: Ishmael kept handing him the stones while Abraham built.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right preposition, the change and the continuing action.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Where does a building stand? Which phrase means “not any more” with a positive verb? Which form follows “carry on”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Shared-Task Sequence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about two people doing a hard job together.
languageFocusExercises.question: How do they share the work?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should organize time, stance and coordinated action across a coherent paragraph rather than as isolated grammar examples.

feedback.correct: Check that your forms create a clear progression from instruction to shared action and adaptation.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Give the task and a promise: “The teacher has asked us … . I will …”
discussionPrompts.example: The teacher has asked Ela and Deniz to build a garden bed. When Ela says, “I will carry the bricks for you,” the task becomes a personal promise.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Show a change: “She could no longer …, so …”
discussionPrompts.example: When the wall became high, Deniz could no longer reach the top. So she stood on a wooden box.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Show two actions at once: “… carried on …ing while … kept …ing.”
discussionPrompts.example: Ela carried on passing the bricks while Deniz kept laying them.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — End with a polite request: “Please …”
discussionPrompts.example: At the end they wrote a note: “Please water the plants during the holiday.” It is a polite request, not a command.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: According to the hadith, since when has this place been sacred?
options: since Allah created the heavens and the earth
beforeYouRead.quote: this place has been made sacred by Allah since the day He created the heavens and the earth

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael built the Ka’ba.
I can use “no longer” for a change and “carried on” for a continuing action.
I can describe two people sharing a hard task.

pages.title: The Legacy of Abraham
pages.content:
He was but the restorer of the structure that was originally built long before. No other place of worship is older than the Ka’ba of Mecca. Reconstruction of the Ka’ba and the call to pilgrimage (see Surah al-Hajj: 27) are clear evidence that Prophet Abraham (pbuh) established the religion and invited those living in that region at that time to embrace it. This belief is known as Hanifism. Reconstructing the Holy Ka’ba was the completion of Abraham (pbuh)’s mission. He built a place of worship for all people, not just people of a chosen race or color. This actually reminds us of the oneness of Allah. During Hajj Muslims are reminded of many events of Allah’s beloved “friend” Abraham (pbuh) and his family. Before his death, Abraham (pbuh) left Palestine to Isaac and Mecca to Ishmael, and sent his other children eastward. His son Ishmael taught his father Abraham (pbuh)'s faith in the Hijaz region, and in this region, his Hanif faith coexisted with idolatry.

The ‘Beloved servant of Allah’ about whom Allah said, “I will make you a leader to the nations,” returned to Palestine and died there. When people have lost their way and are looking for salvation, Abraham (pbuh) has always been there to show them the right path. This is especially true in societies where morals have worsened and the real path that Allah showed them has been corrupted.

__historical_entity__:abraham-palestine-ancient

exercises.title: The Writer’s Evidence
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer from Chapter 35.
exercises.question: What does the writer present as clear evidence that Abraham established the religion in that region?
options: His rebuilding of the Ka’ba and his call to pilgrimage
The fact that he sent his other children eastward
The fact that his faith existed side by side with idolatry in the Hijaz
The fact that he returned to Palestine and died there
exercises.explanation: The chapter says: “Reconstruction of the Ka’ba and the call to pilgrimage (see Surah al-Hajj: 27) are clear evidence that Prophet Abraham (pbuh) established the religion and invited those living in that region at that time to embrace it.” The other options are facts from the chapter, but the writer does not use them as evidence for this claim.

feedback.correct: Correct. The writer names the Ka’ba and the call to pilgrimage as the evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of Chapter 35. Find the words “clear evidence” and look at what comes just before them.

languageFocusExercises.title: Careful Claims About a Legacy
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each expression from Chapter 35 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these words say about Abraham’s legacy?

matchingPairs.left: was but the restorer of the structure
matchingPairs.right: only rebuilt something that already existed
the final stage of what he was sent to do

matchingPairs.left: not just people of a chosen race or color
matchingPairs.right: nobody excluded because of their origin
lived side by side with the worship of idols

correctAnswer.was but the restorer of the structure: only rebuilt something that already existed
correctAnswer.the completion of Abraham (pbuh)’s missi: the final stage of what he was sent to do
correctAnswer.not just people of a chosen race or colo: nobody excluded because of their origin
correctAnswer.coexisted with idolatry: lived side by side with the worship of idols

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “But” can mean “only” (was but the restorer = was only the restorer): it limits the claim because the Ka’ba “was originally built long before”. “Not just X” widens the scope to everyone. The prefix co- in “coexisted” means “together”: the two beliefs were present in the same region at the same time.

feedback.correct: Correct. You read the limiting, widening and coexistence expressions.
feedback.incorrect: Find each expression in Chapter 35. Which one limits Abraham’s role, which widens who the Ka’ba is for, and which shows two things existing together?

languageFocusExercises.title: How Far Does the Evidence Go?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 35. Then choose the statement that keeps its scope.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Reconstruction of the Ka’ba and the call to pilgrimage (see Surah al-Hajj: 27) are clear evidence that Prophet Abraham (pbuh) established the religion and invited those living in that region at that time to embrace it.” Which statement keeps the scope of this claim?
options: The reconstruction and the call to pilgrimage are presented as evidence of Abraham’s mission in that region at that time.
They prove that everyone in the region accepted Abraham’s religion at that time and never worshipped idols again.
They prove that Abraham built the very first Ka’ba and that no building stood there before him.
The chapter says there is no clear evidence for Abraham’s mission in that region at that time.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The claim is limited in place and time: “those living in that region at that time”. It says Abraham invited people, not that everyone accepted. The chapter also calls Abraham “the restorer” of an older structure, so the evidence does not show he built the first Ka’ba.

feedback.correct: Correct. This statement keeps the limits of place, time and invitation.
feedback.incorrect: Check the limits in the sentence: Which region, which time, and did people accept or were they invited? Also compare the first sentence of the chapter.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Lasting Guide
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Abraham’s legacy?

errorItems.sentence: When people have lost their way and are looking for salvation, Abraham (pbuh) always was there to show them the right path.
This is especially true in societies which morals have worsened and the real path that Allah showed them has been corrupted.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The present perfect “has always been” connects the past with the present: Abraham’s example has guided people in every period up to now. The past simple would end the connection in the past. “Where” (= in which) links the claim to societies as situations; “especially” narrows the general claim to these cases.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the time link and the relative word.
feedback.incorrect: Does the guidance stop in the past or continue until now? Which relative word means “in which”? Check the last paragraph of Chapter 35.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Qualified Legacy Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about the legacy of a famous reformer or idea.
languageFocusExercises.question: What has lasted, and how far did it reach?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should distinguish event, evidence, interpretation, scope, coexistence and continuing relevance across a coherent paragraph.

feedback.correct: Check that your paragraph moves from evidence to a qualified interpretation and then explains why the legacy still matters.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Keep the claim small: “… was but one of many …”
discussionPrompts.example: Florence Nightingale was but one of many people who improved hospitals. This sentence stops my claim from becoming too strong.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Link evidence to meaning: “This is evidence that …”
discussionPrompts.example: After the war, many hospitals began to keep their wards clean and to record every patient. This is evidence that her ideas spread, at least in Britain.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Widen the claim: “… not just … but …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her ideas helped not just soldiers but all patients. Later, her methods were used in many other countries too.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Show it still matters: “… has remained … . Whenever …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her idea that clean hospitals save lives has remained important to this day. Whenever a new hospital is planned, nurses still follow her principles.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Which place of worship is the oldest?
beforeYouRead.quote: No other place of worship is older than the Ka’ba of Mecca.

iCan: I can explain what the book says about Abraham’s legacy.
I can make a claim smaller or wider with “was but” and “not just”.
I can write about a legacy that has remained important.

groupTask.title: A Legacy Within Its Limits: A Class Exhibition

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You copy one legacy sentence from Chapter 35 and one supporting sentence from an earlier chapter, exactly as they are written.

roles.name: Scope Checker

roles.name: Writer

roles.name: Designer and Presenter

steps: Choose one legacy claim from Chapter 35, for example “He was but the restorer of the structure that was originally built long before.” or “He built a place of worship for all people, not just people of a chosen race or color.”
Find one earlier chapter that supports your claim, for example Chapter 34 for the building or Chapter 2 for Hanifism, and copy one sentence from it exactly.
Use the scope questions to write your summary. Keep each claim inside its limits, as the book does with “in that region at that time”.
End with one sentence about why this legacy still matters today. Nobody speaks as a person from the story, and the poster has no pictures of people; you only report and explain what the book says.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its poster or plays its audio report, reads its two exact quotes aloud and explains which words limit or widen the claim.

legend.route:toMecca: From Palestine to the valley of Mecca

places.name: Babylon or Ur
places.text: There are different ideas about Abraham (pbuh)’s birthplace. Most generally, the book says he was born in the city of Ur or Babylon, the country of King Nimrod. He is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC, and some sources suggest 2200–2000 BC. At that time, the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in agriculture and industry.
places.teacherNote: The book gives both names, so the pin marks Babylon and the small dot marks Ur; neither is presented as certain. Chapter 5 adds that he was born in a cave where his mother was hidden from Nimrod. The dates are hedged (“believed”, “some sources”).
places.question: Why does the book give two names for Abraham (pbuh)’s birthplace?

places.name: Harran
places.text: Some sources say that Abraham (pbuh) was born in the land of Sumer, Mesopotamia, and migrated from there to Harran. The book presents this as one of several ideas about his early life. That is why this line shows a possibility, not a certain journey.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say when or why this migration happened, so the line is drawn from the area of Ur (Sumer). The pin marks ancient Harran, in south-eastern Türkiye today. Ask learners to find the hedging language in chapter 4.
places.question: Which words in chapter 4 show that the Harran journey is not certain?

places.name: The fire
places.text: All the citizens were ordered to gather wood, and for several days they collected fuel. They dug a deep pit, set it on fire and threw Abraham (pbuh) in with a catapult. Allah commanded the fire to be coolness and safety for him. Afterwards, his fame spread throughout the entire kingdom of Babylonia.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say where the fire was, so the pin beside Babylon only marks the event. The debate with King Nimrod follows in chapters 23–24, after which only Sarah and Lot shared his belief.
places.question: Why did the people decide to burn Abraham (pbuh) instead of admitting they were wrong?

places.name: Egypt
places.text: When Abraham (pbuh) realized that no one else was going to believe in his call, he decided to emigrate. He left his people and traveled with his wife Sarah and Lot to Egypt. While they were in Egypt, Sarah was given an Egyptian woman, Hagar, as a servant.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say which way Abraham (pbuh) traveled from his people to Egypt, so no line is drawn to Egypt. The circle is approximate.
places.question: Who traveled with Abraham (pbuh) to Egypt?

places.name: Palestine
places.text: After Egypt, Abraham (pbuh) traveled to Palestine and settled there, calling people to Allah and judging fairly between them. Years later, he returned to Palestine from Mecca. Before his death, he left Palestine to his son Isaac, and he died there.
places.teacherNote: Ishmael was born when Abraham (pbuh) was an old man; the book does not say where, though chapter 28 says Hagar and Ishmael had to leave Palestine. In chapter 33 the return to Palestine and the reunion with Ishmael are told briefly; chapter 34 then says he traveled to Mecca to build the Ka’ba.
places.question: Which son received Palestine, and which son received Mecca?

places.name: Mecca
places.text: Abraham (pbuh) walked through cultivated land, desert and mountains to an uncultivated valley near the hills of Safa and Marwa. There, Zamzam water flowed for Hagar and Ishmael, and it still flows in the city of Mecca today. Years later, father and son built the Ka’ba on the foundations of the old structure. Before his death, Abraham (pbuh) left Mecca to Ishmael.
places.teacherNote: While building, Abraham (pbuh) stood over the stone of Al-Maqam (chapter 34). Hagar’s running between Safa and Marwa is remembered in Hajj. Chapter 35 adds that Ishmael taught his father’s faith in the Hijaz region.
places.question: Why does the book call the Ka’ba the oldest place of worship?

places.name: Yemen
places.text: The tribe of Jurham was moving from southern Arabia, Yemen. When they saw a bird flying towards the valley of Mecca, they knew there was water, so they stopped there. They settled in Mecca, and Ishmael grew up among them and learned Arabic from them.
places.teacherNote: The book does not give Jurham’s route; the line only joins Yemen to Mecca. The circle is approximate. Ishmael later married the daughter of one of Jurham’s leaders (chapter 31).
places.question: How did the tribe of Jurham know that there was water in the valley?

challenge.prompt: Find the area of Abraham (pbuh)’s birthplace. The book names two cities in the country of King Nimrod.
Find Egypt. Abraham (pbuh) traveled there with Sarah and Lot, and Hagar came from there.
Find Palestine. Abraham (pbuh) settled there after Egypt and died there.
Find Mecca. Zamzam water still flows there today.
Find Yemen. The tribe of Jurham came from this part of southern Arabia.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your understanding of the complete Prophet Abraham B2 story.

exercises.title: A Claim and Its Example
exercises.instructions: Connect the two parts of the book and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Abraham’s night on the mountain (Chapters 8–9) best illustrates which claim from Chapter 2?
options: The existence of Allah can be found through reasoning.
Hanifism later became mixed with idolatry and was corrupted.
Islam and Hanifism differ only in the acts of worship.
Every prophet before Abraham taught exactly the same details.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “Human beings are capable of discovering Hanifism; that is, the existence of Allah can be found through reasoning.” In Chapters 8–9 Abraham watches the planet, the moon and the sun set, and concludes that they “had been created; they appeared and disappeared at the Creator’s command.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. On the mountain Abraham reaches Tawhid step by step, by observing and reasoning, which is what Chapter 2 claims is possible.
feedback.incorrect: Compare what Abraham does on the mountain with the sentences in the second paragraph of Chapter 2. Which one describes how a person can reach belief in Allah? Also check whether every option is really stated in Chapter 2.

exercises.title: A New Idea?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 4.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 4, belief in one God had existed in Mesopotamia before, but people had forgotten it.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “Abraham (pbuh)’s message of monotheism was a belief that had existed in these lands before, but it had been forgotten over time.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The writer presents Abraham’s message as a forgotten belief being renewed, not an invention.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 4. Does the writer say monotheism was unknown, or that it had been forgotten?

exercises.title: What the Verses Leave Out
exercises.instructions: Choose the writer’s interpretation in Chapter 11.
exercises.question: Abraham’s people tried to prove their beliefs, but the verses do not record their arguments. What does the writer conclude from this?
options: The arguments were lost when the story was passed on.
The people were too afraid of Abraham to speak openly.
The arguments were too long to include in the verses.
Their claims were ridiculous and not worth reporting.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “His people attempted to argue with him and present evidence to prove the correctness of their beliefs. That these arguments are not told in the verses shows the ridiculousness of their claims.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer reads the silence itself as a judgment: The claims did not deserve to be repeated.
feedback.incorrect: Find the sentence after the verses in Chapter 11 that begins “That these arguments are not told …”. What does the writer say this silence shows?

exercises.title: From Words to Proof
exercises.instructions: Connect Chapter 18 with the chapters before it.
exercises.question: Chapters 11–16 are full of Abraham’s arguments. What does Chapter 18 say breaking the idols added?
options: a practical proof that the people could see
a punishment for the priests who had left
a warning to Nimrod that his rule would end
a way to take back his father’s lost trade
exercises.explanation: Chapter 18: “He had fulfilled his duty to show his people a practical proof of their foolishness in worshipping something other than Allah.”

feedback.correct: Well done. His words had not changed their minds, so he gave them something to see: Gods that could not even protect themselves.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the sentences just after Abraham leaves the temple in Chapter 18. What kind of proof does the writer say he gave?

exercises.title: Blackened Faces, a Bright Face
exercises.instructions: Choose the best reading of the writer’s contrast in Chapter 22.
exercises.question: “The smoke blackened their faces, yet his face was bright.” What does this contrast suggest?
options: The watchers stood too close, while Abraham stood far away.
The fire was weaker than the people had hoped it would be.
Those who meant to harm him were shamed; he was honored.
Abraham was still afraid, but he hid it from the crowd.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 22: “The smoke blackened their faces, yet his face was bright.” The same chapter quotes: “They wanted to harm him, but We made them the worst losers” (Surah al-Anbiya: 70), and adds, “This miracle shamed the despotic rulers.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. The physical detail matches the verse: The planners of harm became “the worst losers”, while Abraham came out honored.
feedback.incorrect: Read the contrast together with the verse and the sentence about the rulers later in Chapter 22. Who ended up shamed, and who did not?

exercises.title: Another Test
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: The story presents taking Hagar and Ishmael to Mecca as one of Abraham’s tests, like the tests mentioned in Chapter 2.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “During his struggle, he had very difficult tests and he passed the tests with his full trust in Allah.” Chapter 26: “This was another test for Abraham (pbuh) while Ishmael was still a little child. It was part of Allah’s master plan.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The word “another” links this journey to the earlier tests, which Abraham passed through trust in Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the middle of Chapter 26. Which word does the writer use for this journey, and what does “another” connect it to?

exercises.title: Two Pilgrimages
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 29.
exercises.question: The writer says there is almost no difference between the pilgrimage of Islam and the pilgrimage that Abraham called people to.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 29: “Actually, there is almost no difference between the pilgrimage called by Abraham (pbuh) and the pilgrimage of Islam.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The writer stresses continuity: Hajj today is almost the same as the pilgrimage of Abraham.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 29, just after the sentence about Hajj.

exercises.title: Words That Come True
exercises.instructions: Connect Chapter 30 with Chapter 27 and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: The angel tells Hagar, “Allah never abandons His people.” Which earlier words of Hagar does this confirm?
options: “Has Allah commanded you to leave us here?”
“We are not going to be lost, since Allah is with us.”
“Maybe there is a caravan passing by.”
“Yes. I am leaving you to Allah’s care.”
exercises.explanation: Chapter 27: “I am satisfied to be with Allah! We are not going to be lost, since Allah is with us.” Chapter 30: “Do not be afraid. This is the place for the House of Allah, which this boy and his father will build. Allah never abandons His people.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Hagar’s trust in Chapter 27 is answered in Chapter 30: Allah did not leave them, and the water appeared.
feedback.incorrect: Check who says each option: One is Abraham’s answer, and two are Hagar’s question and thought. Which sentence expresses the same trust as the angel’s words?

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the story in one place.

vocabulary.definition: A person who speaks or acts for a group, a belief or an idea.
vocabulary.storyExample: In the Holy Qur’an, Prophet Abraham (pbuh) is presented as the messenger and representative of the monotheistic belief.

vocabulary.definition: Believing that there is only one God.
vocabulary.storyExample: In the Holy Qur’an, Prophet Abraham (pbuh) is presented as the messenger and representative of the monotheistic belief.

vocabulary.definition: Someone or something that competes with another for the same position.
vocabulary.storyExample: He has no partner, rival, or helper.

vocabulary.definition: A person from an earlier generation of your family; an ancestor.
vocabulary.storyExample: Prophet Ishmael (pbuh) is the direct forefather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

vocabulary.definition: Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else.
vocabulary.storyExample: Allah is unique in every way.

vocabulary.definition: The Islamic belief that Allah is one and has no partner.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qur’an presents in detail his discovery of the oneness of Allah (Tawhid) in the middle of an idol-worshipping nation.

vocabulary.definition: Worshipping statues or objects as gods.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qur’an presents in detail his discovery of the oneness of Allah (Tawhid) in the middle of an idol-worshipping nation.

vocabulary.definition: Being one and only one.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qur’an presents in detail his discovery of the oneness of Allah (Tawhid) in the middle of an idol-worshipping nation.

vocabulary.definition: An important task or purpose that someone is given or chooses to follow.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Hanifism and the One True Faith
vocabulary.storyExample: His life mission was to spread the message of Tawhid—the belief that Allah is One and He has no partners.

vocabulary.definition: A long, hard effort against difficulties or opposition.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Hanifism and the One True Faith
vocabulary.storyExample: During his struggle, he had very difficult tests and he passed the tests with his full trust in Allah.

vocabulary.definition: Honest, fair and always behaving in a decent way.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Hanifism and the One True Faith
vocabulary.storyExample: In the Holy Qur’an, Abraham (pbuh) is often described as a hanif; a hanif is a monotheist who is not a Jew, a Christian, or an idolater (see Surah Al Imran: 67) and is also morally upright.

vocabulary.definition: The process of thinking about something in a logical way to reach a conclusion.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Hanifism and the One True Faith
vocabulary.storyExample: Human beings are capable of discovering Hanifism; that is, the existence of Allah can be found through reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: The abilities that people have to understand or do things.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Hanifism and the One True Faith
vocabulary.storyExample: As human conditions and capacities changed over time, some changes in details became necessary.

vocabulary.definition: To pray to someone or something and show it great love and respect.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Hanifism and the One True Faith
vocabulary.storyExample: He challenged the idol worship of his time and taught people to believe in Allah alone.

vocabulary.definition: The worship of statues, stars or other created things instead of Allah.
vocabulary.storyExample: They stayed away from idolatry and its practices.

vocabulary.definition: Changed from its pure, original form into something false.
vocabulary.storyExample: However, later on, this belief became mixed with idolatry and, like Judaism and Christianity, it was corrupted.

vocabulary.definition: A message from Allah given to a prophet.
vocabulary.storyExample: When the first revelation (wahy) came to Muhammad (pbuh), Waraqa ibn Nawfal welcomed his prophethood.

vocabulary.definition: The position of someone chosen by Allah to carry His message to people.
vocabulary.storyExample: When the first revelation (wahy) came to Muhammad (pbuh), Waraqa ibn Nawfal welcomed his prophethood.

vocabulary.definition: Accepted something gladly and with approval.
vocabulary.storyExample: When the first revelation (wahy) came to Muhammad (pbuh), Waraqa ibn Nawfal welcomed his prophethood.

vocabulary.definition: The town or country where a person came into the world.
vocabulary.storyExample: There are different ideas about the birthplace of Abraham (pbuh).

vocabulary.definition: According to history or to what is known about the past.
vocabulary.storyExample: Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC.

vocabulary.definition: Rich and successful.
vocabulary.storyExample: During the time of Abraham (pbuh), the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in many aspects, such as agriculture and industry.

vocabulary.definition: The work of making goods, especially in large amounts.
vocabulary.storyExample: During the time of Abraham (pbuh), the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in many aspects, such as agriculture and industry.

vocabulary.definition: Particular parts or sides of something.
vocabulary.storyExample: During the time of Abraham (pbuh), the Sumerian/Mesopotamian country was prosperous in many aspects, such as agriculture and industry.

vocabulary.definition: The general mood and influences that surround a person or place.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh) was born into that atmosphere and family.

vocabulary.definition: People who claim to know the future by studying the movement of the planets.
vocabulary.storyExample: Nimrod, the king of Babylon, had many fortunetellers and astrologers.

vocabulary.definition: Said that something would happen in the future.
vocabulary.storyExample: One year, around the 20th century BC, they predicted that a child named Abraham (pbuh) would be born in the region, would change the religion of the people, and would end the reign of Nimrod.

vocabulary.definition: The period during which a king or queen rules.
vocabulary.storyExample: One year, around the 20th century BC, they predicted that a child named Abraham (pbuh) would be born in the region, would change the religion of the people, and would end the reign of Nimrod.

vocabulary.definition: A report of past events passed on from person to person.
vocabulary.storyExample: According to another narration, Nimrod had a dream that a child in the region would challenge his throne.

vocabulary.definition: Made something pure and free from anything wrong or confusing.
vocabulary.storyExample: Allah cleared up Abraham (pbuh)’s heart and mind and gave him wisdom from childhood.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to make wise and sensible decisions.
vocabulary.storyExample: Allah said: “And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgement before, and We were of him well-Knowing” (as to his belief in the Oneness of Allah etc.) (Surah al-Anbiya: 51).

vocabulary.definition: Extremely surprised.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh) was astonished and he spontaneously rejected the idea.

vocabulary.definition: Naturally and immediately, without planning or being told.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh) was astonished and he spontaneously rejected the idea.

vocabulary.definition: Figures of people or animals made from stone, wood or metal.
vocabulary.storyExample: During his early childhood, Abraham (pbuh) realized that his father made strange statues, sculptures.

vocabulary.definition: A very strong feeling of dislike.
vocabulary.storyExample: From childhood, his heart was full of hatred for these idols.

vocabulary.definition: Without life; not living and unable to move or feel.
vocabulary.storyExample: He realized these statues were lifeless, silent, and entirely helpless; when they fell, they could not get back up.

vocabulary.definition: Completely unable to act or to protect oneself.
vocabulary.storyExample: He realized these statues were lifeless, silent, and entirely helpless; when they fell, they could not get back up.

vocabulary.definition: A hollow space in a wall where a statue or object is placed.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh)'s people had a big temple full of idols, in the middle of which was a niche housing the biggest gods.

vocabulary.definition: Asking for something in a desperate and humble way.
vocabulary.storyExample: It shocked him to see people bowing, crying, and begging the idols for help, as if those lifeless idols were capable of hearing their prayers!

vocabulary.definition: A person who performs religious duties in a place of worship.
vocabulary.storyExample: His father wanted him to become a priest when he grew up, which made things even worse.

vocabulary.definition: A very large area, or everything, under the rule of one power.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Holy Qur’an told this incident in Surah al-An’am, verses 75–79: “Thus, We showed Abraham the empire of the heavens and the earth, that he might be one of those with certainty.

vocabulary.definition: An event, especially an important or unusual one.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Holy Qur’an told this incident in Surah al-An’am, verses 75–79: “Thus, We showed Abraham the empire of the heavens and the earth, that he might be one of those with certainty.

vocabulary.definition: Complete confidence that something is true.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Holy Qur’an told this incident in Surah al-An’am, verses 75–79: “Thus, We showed Abraham the empire of the heavens and the earth, that he might be one of those with certainty.

vocabulary.definition: (Of the sun, moon, stars or planets) went down below the horizon.
vocabulary.storyExample: But when it set, he said, ‘I do not love those that set.’” Abraham (pbuh) saw that the stars couldn’t show up when they wanted to because they could only do so at night.

vocabulary.definition: Having nothing to do with something wrong.
vocabulary.storyExample: But when it set, he said, ‘O my people, I am innocent of your idolatry.

vocabulary.definition: Natural objects in the sky, such as the sun, the moon, stars and planets.
vocabulary.storyExample: He was astonished that these heavenly bodies were worshipped by people, while in fact all those stars, asteroids, the Sun, the Moon, etc., had been created; they appeared and disappeared at the Creator’s command.

vocabulary.definition: Small rocky objects that travel around the sun.
vocabulary.storyExample: He was astonished that these heavenly bodies were worshipped by people, while in fact all those stars, asteroids, the Sun, the Moon, etc., had been created; they appeared and disappeared at the Creator’s command.

vocabulary.definition: A discussion in which people give opposing opinions and arguments.
vocabulary.storyExample: In that debate, Abraham (pbuh) demonstrated to the people that these heavenly bodies cannot be worshipped as partners with Allah.

vocabulary.definition: Turned or pointed something towards a particular person or thing.
vocabulary.storyExample: I have directed my attention towards Him Who created the heavens and the earth—a monotheist—and I am not of the idolaters.’” His young heart was filled with severe pain.

vocabulary.definition: Lasting for ever; never ending.
vocabulary.storyExample: Allah is without end, everlasting without disappearance.

vocabulary.definition: Not deserving respect, attention or a particular treatment.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh) clarified the situation for them, firstly, that the heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship and, secondly, that they are the signs of Allah.

vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh) clarified the situation for them, firstly, that the heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship and, secondly, that they are the signs of Allah.

vocabulary.definition: Gives special importance to an idea.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Qur’an emphasizes this with simple logic: “And of His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon.

vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh)'s rational thinking helped to uncover the truth, and then the conflict between him and the worshippers of the stars and planets started.

vocabulary.definition: To give reasons for or against something, often angrily.
vocabulary.storyExample: “And his people argued with him.

The writer passes on a source or traditi: In the Holy Qur’an, Abraham (pbuh) is often described as a hanif …

The narrator tells an event directly: A bitter struggle began between Abraham (pbuh) and his people.

exercises.explanation: Framing words show where a claim comes from. “is often described as”, “is presented in Islamic sources as” and “According to another narration” pass on what a source or tradition says. “We may say that”, “It is understood from … that” and “are clear evidence that” mark the writer’s own reasoning: A view the writer offers, or a conclusion drawn from evidence. A past simple sentence with no frame (began, learned, returned) tells an event directly. A careful B2 reader keeps these three voices apart.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated the source, the writer’s reasoning and the narrator’s account.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the start of each sentence: Is there a source frame (described, presented, According to), a reasoning frame (may say, understood, evidence), or no frame at all?

exercises.title: Notice: Looking Ahead from the Past
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapters 17 and 25. Then choose the best explanation.
exercises.question: Chapter 17: “He knew that there was going to be a great celebration outside the town.” Chapter 25: “When Abraham (pbuh) realized that no one else was going to believe in his call, he decided to emigrate.” What does “was going to” do in these sentences?
options: It shows a plan that was never carried out, because something stopped it before it could happen.
It describes an action that was repeated many times in the past, like a habit or a yearly custom.
It looks forward from a moment in the past (what he knew or realized then) to something that was still ahead.
It shows that the writer doubts whether the event really took place, because the sources do not agree about it.
exercises.explanation: “Was going to” is the future seen from the past. The verbs knew and realized put us at a past moment; from there, the celebration and the people’s refusal were still in the future. The form itself does not say whether the event really happened: the context does, and here both did. Chapter 5 takes the same viewpoint: “Very soon, he was going to fight against his family and the whole system in his society.” Would can do the same job: “All the people would attend it.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The narrator stands at a past moment and looks ahead.
feedback.incorrect: Find the past moment first (he knew, he realized). Is the celebration before or after that moment?
