errorItems.sentence: Abraham (pbuh) was put on the catapult; his hands and feet were tying.
Cries of astonishment was heard from the unbelievers.
Abraham (pbuh) has aged and his hair was gray after many years spent in calling people to Allah.

exercises.explanation: A passive needs be + past participle: Someone tied his hands and feet, so they were tied (were tying would mean the hands were doing the tying). The verb agrees with the plural subject Cries, so were heard. Had aged steps back from the moment of the story: By the time Sarah made her suggestion, Abraham had already grown old. The present perfect has aged belongs to the present, not to a past story.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the passive, the agreement and the earlier past.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Who did the action, is the subject singular or plural, and does the verb look back from a past moment? Compare with Chapters 20, 22 and 25.

exercises.title: Build: Report the Words
exercises.instructions: Report the words from Chapters 6 and 15. Complete each new sentence.
exercises.question: What changes when we report words in a past story?

transformItems.source: His father continued, “These big ears show his deep knowledge.”
transformItems.frame: His father added that those big ears [blank] his deep knowledge.

transformItems.source: they responded: “Are you criticizing our gods and our forefathers? …”
transformItems.frame: They asked Abraham (pbuh) [blank] their gods and their forefathers.

exercises.explanation: After a past reporting verb, the tense usually moves back and these becomes those: show → showed. The father’s claim is reported, not shared by the narrator. A reported yes/no question uses whether or if + statement word order, with no question mark: Are you criticizing …? → whether he was criticizing …. The pronouns change too: you → he, our gods → their gods.

feedback.correct: Correct. You moved the tense back and used statement word order.
feedback.incorrect: Move the tense one step back (show → showed, are → was). For a yes/no question, start with whether or if, then subject + verb.

exercises.title: Build: Keep the Writer’s Certainty
exercises.instructions: Choose the summary that keeps how sure the writer is and how many people are meant.
exercises.question: Chapter 4: “Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC.” Chapter 24: “Only one woman and one man of his people shared his belief in Allah.” Which summary is the most faithful?
options: It has been proven that Abraham lived in the 20th century BC; only two of his people, a woman and a man, shared his belief.
Abraham is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC; after the fire, many of his people shared his belief.
Abraham is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC; only two of his people, a woman and a man, shared his belief.
Abraham is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC; in the end, not a single person shared his belief.
exercises.explanation: “is believed to have lived” keeps a distance: It reports a belief about a date, so ‘It has been proven’ overstates it. “Only one woman and one man” gives an exact scope: ‘many’ inflates it, and ‘not a single person’ erases the two believers. A good B2 summary changes the words but keeps the strength of the claim and its scope.

feedback.correct: Correct. The summary keeps both the certainty and the size of each group.
feedback.incorrect: Check two things: Does the summary make the date more certain than the book does, and does it keep many … but some …?

exercises.title: Build: Link, Limit and Collocate
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines from the book with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
exercises.fillBlanksText: … he was determined to [blank] to these practices … Allah also will cause them to die and bring them back to life again. [blank], idolaters would not give up but held on tightly to their idols. … Sarah thought she could not have a child. [blank], she suggested Abraham (pbuh) get married to Hagar. … He built a place of worship for all people, [blank] people of a chosen race or color.
exercises.explanation: Put an end to + noun is a fixed collocation meaning ‘stop something completely’; give an end is not English. However turns to something unexpected: Allah’s power is described, yet the idolaters still refused to give up. Therefore gives a result: Sarah believed she could not have a child, so she made her suggestion. Not just widens the scope: The place is for everyone, not only for one group. Although needs a full clause after it (Although she thought …, she …), so it cannot stand alone before a comma.

feedback.correct: Well done. You chose the collocation, the contrast, the result and the scope marker.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Is it part of a fixed phrase, a surprise, a result, or a wider group? Check Chapters 14, 17, 25 and 35.

exercises.title: Use: Our Town’s Old Fountain
exercises.instructions: This new text is from a school newspaper report. Choose the form that fits each sentence.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s language in a new text?

formChoices.sentence: According to a sign in the town museum, the old fountain in the square [choice] in 1890.
Some older residents [choice] that its water once came from a spring in the hills, but no written record confirms this.
Last year the council was going to close the fountain because of repair costs; [choice], our class collected signatures, and it is still open today.

exercises.explanation: A fountain does not build itself, so the passive is needed: was built. The source is named at the start (According to a sign …). Believe keeps the claim as a belief; prove or have shown would contradict the next words: no written record confirms this. Was going to close is a plan seen from the past, and however shows that the plan did not happen. In spite of needs a noun after it, not a comma and a clause.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new report.
feedback.incorrect: For each sentence, ask: Who did the action? How sure can we be? Does the next part give a result or something unexpected?

exercises.title: Use: Say It More Carefully
exercises.instructions: These sentences are not from the book. Make each one less certain, or report it as a belief.
exercises.question: Can you report a belief and soften a claim that is too strong?

transformItems.source: People believe that the Romans built the old bridge.
transformItems.frame: The old bridge [blank] by the Romans.
answers: is believed to have been built

transformItems.source: The survey proves that students want a longer break.
transformItems.frame: The survey [blank] that students want a longer break.

transformItems.source: The new timetable will reduce lateness.
transformItems.frame: The new timetable [blank] lateness.

exercises.explanation: Is believed to have been built reports a belief about a past event: believed + to have + past participle, here in the passive. Suggests or indicates presents a survey as evidence without calling it proof. May, might or could turn a certain prediction into a possibility. The book makes the same moves: “is believed to have lived” and “Some sources suggest that he lived between 2200–2000 BC.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Your sentences report and qualify the claims carefully.
feedback.incorrect: Use is believed to have been + past participle for the belief, a verb like suggests for the survey, and may/might/could for the prediction.

exercises.title: Use: Argue a School Decision
exercises.instructions: Write 6–8 sentences about a decision in your school or town. Plan with a partner first.
exercises.question: Can you argue for your view carefully?
exercises.explanation: Example: “In my view, our school should keep the library open at lunchtime. According to a class survey, about sixty students use it every week. Before this year, the library had already become a quiet place for homework. Last spring the school was going to close it at lunch because of staff costs; however, some parents offered to help as volunteers. The survey suggests that students value a quiet space, although it may not show what every student thinks. Therefore, the library should stay open at lunch, not just for readers but for anyone who needs to study.”

feedback.correct: Check your paragraph: a position (In my view …), a source (According to …), background (had + past participle, was going to), a contrast (however, although), a careful claim (suggests, may), a result (Therefore) and a scope marker (not just).

discussionPrompts.question: Step 1 — Give your view and a source: “In my view, … . According to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In my view, phones should be collected at the start of every lesson. According to our class survey, most students check their phones during lessons.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 2 — Give the background: “Before …, … had already …” or “… was going to …; however, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Before the new rule, teachers had already asked students to keep their phones in their bags. The school was going to ban phones completely; however, parents asked for a softer rule.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 3 — Give evidence carefully: “The survey suggests that …, although it may not …”
discussionPrompts.example: The survey suggests that students concentrate better without phones, although it may not show the full picture. Only one class answered it.

discussionPrompts.question: Step 4 — Conclude: “Therefore, …, not just … but …”
discussionPrompts.example: Therefore, a phone box in each classroom is the best solution, not just for students but for teachers too.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Demonstrate whole-book B2 mastery through analysis, evidence, comparison, and synthesis.

exercises.title: A Unique Name
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer the story states.
exercises.question: Chapter 1 calls “Allah’s friend” a unique name. What makes this title unique, according to the story?
options: It was not given to any other prophet before Abraham.
It was the name his father Azer gave him as a child.
It is the name of the fourteenth surah of the Qur’an.
The people of Babylon used it for their own king.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 gives Abraham the name “Allah’s friend” and adds: “This title was not given to any other prophet before.” The last chapter returns to the title: “During Hajj Muslims are reminded of many events of Allah’s beloved “friend” Abraham (pbuh) and his family.” (Chapter 35)

feedback.correct: Yes. The word “unique” is explained in the next sentence: no prophet before him had this title.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence that follows the title in Chapter 1. What does it say about other prophets?

exercises.title: A Question to the Statues
exercises.instructions: Choose the purpose the story gives.
exercises.question: In the temple Abraham asks the statues: “Will you not eat of the offering before you?” What was his real purpose?
options: He hoped that the statues would finally move.
He was mocking them, since he knew they could not eat.
He wanted the priests to hear him and come back.
He was checking whether the food was still warm.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 18 explains: “He was mocking them, for he knew they would not eat.” His question showed that the statues were “lifeless, silent, and entirely helpless” (Chapter 7).

feedback.correct: Yes. The question was ironic: Abraham asked something he knew the statues could never do.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence right after the question in Chapter 18. What was Abraham doing?

exercises.title: Fame Without Followers
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer the story supports.
exercises.question: After the fire and the debate with Nimrod, Abraham’s fame spread throughout Babylonia. What was the result of his call among his own people?
options: Most of the people followed him to Egypt.
The king’s priests finally accepted his message.
Only one woman and one man shared his belief.
His father Azer left the idols and joined him.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 24 says: “However, in spite of his love and care for his people, they left him alone. Only one woman and one man of his people shared his belief in Allah.” Chapter 22 gives one reason: “people did not dare to follow Abraham (pbuh) out of fear of rulers.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Everyone talked about Abraham, but fear of the rulers kept almost everyone away from his faith.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 24. How many of his people believed, and who were they?

exercises.title: A Father’s Plan
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: Abraham’s father wanted his son to become a priest one day.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8 says: “His father wanted him to become a priest when he grew up, which made things even worse.” Azer “only wanted his son to show respect to those statues”.

feedback.correct: True. Azer planned a life in the temple for his son, the very place Abraham disliked most.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 8. What did Azer want Abraham to become?

exercises.title: Father and Son Again
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: When Abraham and Ishmael met again to build the Ka’ba, Ishmael was still a little child.
exercises.explanation: Ishmael was “still a little child” when he was taken to Mecca (Chapter 26), but Chapter 33 says: “After a separation of several years, the father and son came together again. At that time, Ishmael was about thirty years old.”

feedback.correct: Right. Many years had passed, and Ishmael was a grown man who could help his father build.
feedback.incorrect: Compare Chapter 26 with Chapter 33. How old was Ishmael when the building began?

exercises.title: People Around Abraham
exercises.instructions: Match each person or group with what the story tells about them.
exercises.question: Who are these people in Abraham’s story?

matchingPairs.right: presented as Nimrod’s idol maker
suggested that Abraham marry Hagar
believed in Abraham and later became a prophet
the people Ishmael learned Arabic from

correctAnswer.Lot: believed in Abraham and later became a prophet
correctAnswer.the Jurham tribe: the people Ishmael learned Arabic from

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “Azer is presented in Islamic sources as Nimrod’s idol maker.” Chapter 25: “Therefore, she suggested Abraham (pbuh) get married to Hagar.” Chapter 24: “The man’s name was Lot and he later became a prophet.” Chapter 31: “Ishmael learned Arabic from them and they all loved and admired Ishmael because of his gentle character.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Each of these people plays a part in Abraham’s life, from his father’s house to Mecca.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 4, 24, 25 and 31. What does each chapter say about these people?

exercises.title: Words and Attitudes
exercises.instructions: Match each of Abraham’s sayings with the attitude it shows.
exercises.question: What does each saying show about Abraham?

matchingPairs.right: complete trust just before the fire

matchingPairs.left: “I will ask my Lord to forgive you”
matchingPairs.right: kindness towards a father who threatened him

matchingPairs.left: “I will emigrate for the sake of my Lord.”
matchingPairs.right: leaving his homeland for Allah
humility while doing a great task

correctAnswer.“Allah is sufficient for me.”: complete trust just before the fire
correctAnswer.“I will ask my Lord to forgive you”: kindness towards a father who threatened him
correctAnswer.“Accept this service from us”: humility while doing a great task

exercises.explanation: Chapter 22: these were “His last words before entering the flames”. Chapter 14: Abraham answers his father right after “If you do not stop this, I will stone you.” Chapter 25: he speaks when he “realized that no one else was going to believe in his call”. Chapter 34: Abraham and Ishmael pray while they build the Ka’ba.

feedback.correct: Yes. In every scene, Abraham’s words show the same trust in Allah, in a different way.
feedback.incorrect: Think about where each saying comes: Before the fire, after a threat, before a journey, or during the building.

exercises.title: Wood for the Fire
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 20 with one word: service, gift, warning or punishment.
exercises.question: How were the citizens told to see their work of gathering wood?
exercises.fillBlanksText: All the citizens were ordered to gather wood as a [blank] to their gods.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 20 says: “All the citizens were ordered to gather wood as a service to their gods.” The rulers presented their revenge as worship, although these gods could not even protect themselves from Abraham’s axe (Chapter 18).

feedback.correct: Yes. The word “service” shows how the rulers turned their revenge into a religious duty.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 20. The people were told that gathering wood was something they did for their gods.

exercises.title: A House for All People
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 35 with one word: race, city, age or language.
exercises.question: Who was the Ka’ba built for?
exercises.fillBlanksText: He built a place of worship for all people, not just people of a chosen [blank] or color.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 35 says: “He built a place of worship for all people, not just people of a chosen race or color. This actually reminds us of the oneness of Allah.”

feedback.correct: Yes. One house for all people reflects the belief in one Allah for all people.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 35. Which word goes together with “color”?

exercises.title: From Babylon to Mecca
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: How does Abraham’s life unfold from Babylon to Mecca?

sequencingItems.text: Nimrod frees one man sentenced to death and puts the other to death.
Abraham laughs when his father says Marduk’s big ears show deep knowledge.
Abraham stands on the stone of Al-Maqam while Ishmael hands him the stones.
Abraham hangs his axe on the neck of the one idol he did not break.
Abraham leaves Hagar and Ishmael with a skin of water and a bag of dates.
Abraham sits in a cave on a mountain and looks at the planets and stars.

exercises.explanation: Marduk (Chapters 6–7), the night on the mountain (Chapter 8), the broken idols (Chapter 18), Nimrod (Chapter 23), the valley of Mecca (Chapter 27) and the building of the Ka’ba (Chapter 34).

feedback.correct: Yes. The story follows Abraham from his father’s workshop to the House of Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Nimrod called Abraham only after he “had emerged from the fire unharmed”.
